#8207. 32 Old-Fashioned Girl Names Pulled Straight Out Of Vintage Cookbooks

These will take you right back to Grandma’s recipe box.

I still remember walking into my grandma’s kitchen, with its scuffed-up parquet floors and antique wooden dining table, and pulling a spiral-bound community cookbook from a makeshift shelf in the corner. Maybe it was the writer in me, but I always loved to leaf through the names of the women who’d put the book together and picture them, like my grandma, sprinkling herbs into a bubbling pot over the stove or putting the finishing touches on a latticed holiday pie. At least for me, a big part of the magic in those books was the bylines. Every dip, casserole, and suspiciously gelatinous salad came with a name attached, and those names were *chef’s kiss.*

I unfortunately have no idea where my grandma’s collection of yellowing community cookbooks went, but thankfully the internet lives forever. I found and flipped through vintage collections published from 1947 to 1988 (from the deep South to a historic church in Hawaii), pulling some of the best first names off the recipe cards. Not surprisingly, many are straight-up coastal-grandma-coded (looking at you, Maude). Others I’d never heard of prior to stumbling upon them.

And how fun that there’s a sweet little origin story to go along with each one? If you name your baby Bea, you can tell people it was inspired by a woman who made very good baked clams in 1983. Charming! So, with further ado, here are 32 vintage baby names straight from old cookbooks.

Inspired by: Josephine Marner’s shrimp cocktail dip, Centennial Cookbook (1979)

I’m a sucker for a name that's easy to shorten, and you can’t ask for an easier one than Josephine: Jo, Josie, even Posey or Fifi work here. Of Hebrew origin, it means “God will increase.”

Inspired by: Ida Gilberg Spitzer’s braided egg twist, Heritage Cookbook (1975)

This short and sturdy name most likely makes you think of Ida B. Wells, a journalist, educator, and early leader in the Civil Rights Movement. And, really, who wouldn’t want a name shared by such an icon? German and Greek in origin, it means “hardworking.”

Inspired by: Thora Hawkins Linebaugh’s butter flake rolls, Heritage Cookbook (1975)

Any ‘90s kid will tell you this name has coolness to spare thanks to Hocus Pocus star Thora Birch. But it’s also the feminine form of Thor, aka a Norse thunder god, which makes it feel a little tough, too.

Inspired by: Maude Lyman’s chicken casserole, West Oakland Soul Food Cookbook (1963)

Thanks to Judd Apatow and Leslie Mann’s daughter, Maude Apatow, this one reads less like a church potluck and more like It Girl these days. A medieval form of Matilda, it means “mighty in battle.”

Inspired by: Viola Taylor’s deep-dish peach pie, West Oakland Soul Food Cookbook (1963)

This name conjures up a lot: Shakespeare’s clever heroine in Twelfth Night, a flower, an instrument, and of course, our queen Viola Davis. Latin, it means “purple flower.”

Inspired by: Rosemary Riglar’s cheese netties, Lula No Ke Kuke Ana Historic Hawaiian Church Cookbook (1983)

Any herb name comes with built-in kitchen cred, and Rosemary happens to be one of the absolute prettiest. Bonus: Rosie, Romy, and Mae are all on the table for nicknames.

Inspired by: Gertie Carey’s fresh lemon cake, West Oakland Soul Food Cookbook (1963)

I can’t be the only one who thinks this name is off-the-charts adorable, can I?! It always makes me think of Drew Barrymore’s character in E.T., which endeared it to an entire generation. The cute short form of Gertrude, it means “spear strength.”

Inspired by: Clarinda Ward’s oatmeal bread, Centennial Cookbook (1979)

A truly unique option, Clarinda is a literary invention built on Clara, which means “bright.” Poet Robert Burns used it as a pen name for the woman he wrote swoony letters with. Romantic-era BookTok vibes!

Inspired by: Estelle Braaf’s Pate “En Croute,” The Good Neighbor’s Cookbook (1983)

I mean, any woman serving pâté en croûte at a neighborhood potluck was clearly the Estelle Getty of her block, y’know? This name serves serious Hollywood glamour with a meaning to match: “star.”

Inspired by: Tibby Ellison Simmons’ fresh mint punch, Heritage Cookbook (1975)

While this is historically an old Scottish nickname for Isabel or Elizabeth, millennials will recognize it as the name of Amber Tamblyn’s character in The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants.

Inspired by: Ione Jones’ baked popped corn, Lula No Ke Kuke Ana Historic Hawaiian Church Cookbook (1983)

Pronounced eye-OH-nee, this Greek name means “violet.” It’s definitely not one you have to worry about five other kids on the playground having, and it’s got a bit of Gen X dreaminess to it thanks to Ione Skye.

Inspired by: Nora Kremers’ Tillamook Bay clam chowder, Tillamook County Bicentennial Cookbook (1976)

Already a modern favorite, this name is traditionally short for Honora or Eleanor. Although if you grew up in the ‘90s, you probably associate it most with Nora Jones or the Blessid Union of Souls song by the same name.

Inspired by: Virgie Dow’s butterhorns, Community Cookbook Order of Eastern Star (1981)

Admittedly, I’m a bit partial to this one; it was my great-grandmother’s name! It’s sweet, Southern, and folksy… just like she was. Of Latin origin, it means “maiden” and would make an excellent nickname for the longer Virginia.

Inspired by: Lenora Buck’s party meatballs, Pine to Prairie Cookbook (1988)

A diminutive of Leonora or Eleanor, this name has a touch of moodiness because it echoes Poe’s “Lenore.” Nora and Lennie are the easy nicknames here, although you could go more gender-neutral with Len or even Leo.

Inspired by: Jetta Meads’ Y-U-M-M-Y cocoa pie, Community Cookbook Order of Eastern Star (1981)

Often a Dutch nickname for Henrietta, Jetta is also derived from the English word for a glossy black gemstone. It has a bit of old-school Hollywood sophistication to it as well, seeing as Jetta Goudal was a prominent Dutch-American silent film actress from the ‘20s.

Need even more inspo? Here are a few more, pulled straight from cookbooks of yore.

#8205. 6 Berry-Bearing Shrubs to Plant Now and Feed Hungry Birds Through Winter

Plant a pantry of nutritious berries for winter birds and pretty-up your garden at the same time!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Feeding garden birds in winter is such an easy way to support wildlife, and growing berry-bearing shrubs is a great way to supplement birdseed and fatballs. So many avian species depend on berries to survive winter, so planting a berried shrub to feed birds is a great way to attract feathered visitors to your yard. Waxwings and American robins gather into berry-seeking flocks once temperatures drop and, once insects become scarce, many rare garden visitors such as bluebirds, warblers and woodpeckers can be tempted in with a feast of plump berries.

Not all shrubs with berries are created equal when it comes to winter food, however. Some berries are incredibly high in fat, carbohydrates or anti-oxidants, offering birds highly nutritious, energy-rich fuel to stay warm, and stay alive. Others are the equivalent of avian junk food. It’s good to offer a variety of berries, too: some super-tasty treats to be gobbled up in fall, and some that are too tart to eat before the freeze-thaw of deep winter sweetens them up to provide a late-season larder.

All these shrubs grow energy-dense berries for winter birds, so they’ll bring feathered garden friends flocking. All are well-behaved ornamental plants you’ll welcome in your garden, as they don’t take much looking after but easily earn their yard space with plenty of color. And all are best planted right now in fall so they have time to grow their roots deep into the soil before winter arrives. So which will you choose to feed birds in winter?

Ilex verticillata ‘FarrowBPop’ tops our list of berried shrubs for birds, producing a profusion of red berries rich in nutrients. It’s a dwarf cultivar of a native deciduous holly so it drops its leaves in fall to create a highly visible feast of berries that will act as a magnet for over 40 species of birds including waxwings, robins, bluebirds and northern cardinals. As it’s a compact and grows berries all along its stems, foraging birds like thrushes and sparrows will benefit, too.

Berry Poppins winterberry holly is a great asset to any garden as its berry-packed branches are an eyecatching sight for us humans, too. Because the berries start off firm and tart, it's an enduring display as the fruit only gets eaten up in January or February once it's sweetened up into a late-season lifeline for birds.

Growing to just 3-4 feet high and wide in zones 3-9, this is a neat, disease-resistant shrub that’s easy to grow. There’s one catch, however! Berry Poppins is a female plant, and needs a male plant nearby to produce berries. Mr Poppins winterberry holly, also available from Plant Addicts and a similar size, is the ideal choice of male plant to partner Berry Poppins. While Mr Poppins doesn’t produce berries, it’s a pleasant zero-maintenance foliage shrub and can be planted up to 50 feet away; one male plant will service up to five females, too.

Next on the list of shrubs for winter birds is Viburnum nudum ‘Bulk’, sold as Brandywine. There are so many berry-bearing viburnums to choose from but this cultivar wins hands-down for its abundant high-fat berries and incredible garden beauty.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Green berries start forming in late summer then, in fall, shift into stunning pink and blue shades, often with different-hued fruit in the same cluster. As the days grow darker, so do the berries, turning a glossy purple-black as the surrounding foliage takes on fiery red hues. Brandywine viburnum is another late-winter pantry for birds as the berries only sweeten once the deepest winter weather sets in.

Hardy in zones 5-9, this low-maintenance shrub reaches 5-6 feet high and wide in five or so years, and you will need to let it grow to its natural height as it flowers and fruits on 2-year-old wood. But then you can expect to see waxwings, robins, bluebirds, thrushes and even woodpeckers feasting on its berries.

If you don’t have the garden space for a Brandywine viburnum, then Berry Box Pyracomeles is a smart choice. Staying compact at just 2-3 feet high and wide, this evergreen shrub looks good year-round and while its berries are small, they start out a bright orange in late summer before transitioning to a vibrant red in winter, and the sheer number creates an impressive display. Because of its small size, Berry Box thrives in a container, making it a lovely choice for colorful fall planters that last into winter. Growing this shrub in a pot also means that if you’re a little outside its growing zones of 7-9, you can keep it in a sheltered spot.

Pyracomeles is a cross between Pyracantha and Osteomeles and has inherited the high-nutrient berry and heavy-fruiting genetics of the former and the compact nature of the latter. With fruit persisting on the branches well into winter, Berry Box berries are a valuable food source for robins, waxwings and thrushes, and small birds will find shelter in the shrub's dense evergreen foliage.

Aronia shrubs create a valuable winter resource for birds with dense growth offering shelter as well as long-lasting berries that offer a life-saving pantry when most other food has been gobbled up. Chokeberries have a high level of tannin which gives them a bitter taste but also acts as a preservative, so they last all through fall and early winter. Freezing weather breaks up those tannins, however, so these berries bring an emergency food supply high in antioxidants through the coldest days of late winter.

Chokeberry’s fire-engine-red fall foliage makes these low-maintenance shrubs fabulous plants for the garden, too, and this native shrub is a great substitute for invasive burning bush. And whatever the size of your yard, there’s an Aronia to suit.

If you have the room then Aronia ‘Viking’ should be your go-to as it was originally bred as an orchard crop so has big black berries and lots of them, that will attract American robins, eastern bluebirds, cedar waxwings and even blue jays; it grows to 4-6 feet high and wide in zones 3-8. Turn chokeberries into jam, jelly and syrup to enjoy the health benefits of these anti-oxidant-rich berries yourself, too. Berry Scape Chokeberry, available from Plant Addicts, is more ornamental with pretty bright red berries, growing to 4-5 feet high and wide in zones 4-9. If you’re short on space, then LowScape Mound Chokeberry, available from trees.com, only reaches 1-2 feet high and wide but still produces plenty of purple-black berries that ground-dwelling birds will appreciate.

Another useful emergency supply of late-winter berries is Proud Berry Pink coralberry. Symphoricarpos orbiculatus is a close native relative of the snowberry and, like chokeberry, has berries high in tannins that only become palatable after many freeze-thaw cycles. That’s a bonus for gardeners as well as birds because the large pink berries, that gradually become more vibrant as temperatures drop, are so decorative. Coralberry's arching branches and rounded blue-green leaves are pretty, too.

Ornamental coralberry, also known as Indian currants, grows to 3-4 feet high and wide but because it fruits on new wood, it’s easily kept smaller without sacrificing the berry supply. Hardy in zones 3-7, plant this shrub now for berries next year.

Of course, you need some berries for birds to scoff through fall and early winter, and Callicarpa is the garden-worthy beauty to pick. But don’t just plump for the native American beautyberry. Pearl Glam offers all the same nutritional, high-moisture berries that cardinals, robins and bluebirds love, but has a much tighter, upright habit, reaching 4-5 feet high and 3-4 feet wide in zones 5-8. As well as a profusion of violet-purple berries, Pearl Glam also boasts deep purple foliage (the native beautyberry has regular green leaves).

While Plant Addicts stocks Pearl Glam in a garden-ready #3 container, if you’re on a budget and have a little patience then Lowe’s offers the same Proven Winners shrub in a great-value gallon pot.

Any or all of these shrubs will give your feathered friends a feast and help them survive through winter. They'll attract birds into your yard, too, so be sure to plant them in view of a window. All well as adding winter color to your backyard, these beauties are easily smart and low-maintenance enough to work as front-yard shrubs that add curb appeal, too. They'd also make welcome Christmas gifts for bird-loving friends. And don't forget, it's also perfectly acceptable to gift your garden birds the best-ever present of a berry-bearing shrub!

Emma is an avid gardener and has worked in media for over 25 years. Previously editor of Modern Gardens magazine, she regularly writes for the Royal Horticultural Society. She loves to garden hand-in-hand with nature and her garden is full of bees, butterflies and birds as well as cottage-garden blooms. As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

#8202. The Only Time I Felt Allowed To Be Overweight Was When I Was Pregnant

Pregnancy didn't make me comfortable gaining weight. It made my weight explainable.

I'd never gone 24 hours without thinking about my weight. Never a day where I didn’t feel guilty for overeating and what the scale would look like the next morning. Forever overweight and forever ashamed.

Then I got pregnant. I arrived at my new high-risk OB-GYN, the one I had to search for because my BMI alone made me automatically high risk. No preexisting medical conditions, no concerning family history… just FAT. And before I could even wrap my head around the fact that I was growing an actual human being, my new doctor told me that because of my BMI, I should only gain 11 pounds over the next nine months.

I was supposed to grow a whole ass baby, and only gain 11 pounds? Historically, I could gain 11 pounds overnight if I put my mind to it! I thought pregnancy was the one time I could finally embrace getting bigger. I actually envisioned stepping on the scale at the doctor's office without fear, maybe even getting a little golf clap from my doctor for gaining a few pounds. Like the prize pig at the county fair.

I understood there were medical reasons behind the recommendation, but I couldn't help feeling defeated. Here I was, finally experiencing something I had dreamed about, and somehow, the conversation had already come back to my weight. Even when my body was literally supposed to get bigger, there was a limit.

I felt ashamed. And that shame quickly turned into anxiety. I'd spent my entire life fearing weight gain for myself, but now I was terrified it could hurt someone else: my baby. Instead of embracing my growing body, I spent my first trimester afraid of what would happen if it grew too much.

By week 12, stress and morning sickness had caused me to lose 10 pounds. I stepped on the scale at my next ultrasound, secretly excited and doing some quick math. Did that mean I could gain 21 pounds now? Did the math carry over? I was already calculating how to earn more weight gain. But when I spoke with my doctor, he didn't mention the weight loss at all. He wasn't proud, he wasn't mad. Not a peep.

And somehow, this felt like a green light to me. Like actually, maybe he isn’t THAT focused on the scale and more focused on the baby (duh). After that appointment, I felt my jaw unclench, and something in my brain shifted. I had made it through the first trimester, the baby was healthy and I had lost weight. For thatI was not punished nor rewarded. It was finally, just a number.

So I announced my pregnancy to family and friends and a sudden weight was lifted (and soon gained). Eventually, even the morning sickness let up and I reverted back to the old me. And just like that, I was back in my safe space, scrolling DoorDash.

I started eating whatever I wanted and felt no shame. I ate mozzarella sticks for a snack at 10am. Bagels before bed. I would end every meal with a “treat” of Phish Food ice cream or a couple peanut butter cups for good measure. It’s called palate cleansing.

It felt like FREEDOM. I didn't have to suck in my stomach or hide my rolls. No worrying about posing for a picture to make myself look smaller or hide my sins. I didn't have to wonder if someone was looking at what was on my plate, because honestly I DARE YOU. I didn't have to promise myself I'd “be good tomorrow.” My belly was supposed to get bigger. My clothes were supposed to stop fitting. I was supposed to gain weight. It was like a fun topic of conversation with my girlfriends and people who were already moms… “eating myself through house and home, you know how it goes!”

Well, spoiler alert, I saw their 11 pounds and ended up raising them 50. And honestly? I wasn't that scared. I'd been that weight before. I knew what it was like to live in that body. The number I was supposed to fear reaching was a number I'd already seen on my own scale. But more than that, for the first time in my life, my growing body came with an explanation.

The craziest part? My doctor didn’t bring up my weight again until after I had the baby. Sure, it still made the occasional cameo, like when I needed an anesthesia consultation before birth because of my BMI. But it made my weight felt more like a supporting character instead of the entire plot. It felt like a huge relief.

Pregnancy didn't make me comfortable gaining weight. It made my weight explainable. Because the reality is, I didn't suddenly stop being plus-size. For once in my life I felt normal…like maybe this is how regular people go about their day. Like I was in a new tier of women, one where people were going to celebrate my growing belly. My dad would make us dinner on Sundays and say “Mary gets extra, she’s eating for two!” This is what dreams were made of.

Before I knew it, nine months had flown by and I'd given birth to my baby boy. Less than 12 hours postpartum, a visiting doctor looked at my legs and asked, “Do your legs typically look like this, or are you really swollen?”

Nope, that's just what my legs look like. I'd barely had a minute to process giving birth before I was back to feeling self-conscious about my body. Nine months of freedom, gone in one sentence.

And that was just the beginning. Soon, doctor's appointments included questions like, “So, what's your plan for weight loss?” and suggestions about GLP-1 medications. My health was otherwise good, but once again, my weight was the conversation.

I remember thinking, how am I supposed to diet on no sleep? I'm just trying to keep a newborn alive, recover from childbirth, and make it through the day. Could my body just exist for a minute without needing to be fixed?

But still, I felt the pressure to lose weight, like my body was a project that was never finished. I even caught myself feeling relieved on days when I was so busy caring for my baby that I barely had time to eat.

I've spent my entire life trying to make my body smaller, and for most of my pregnancy, I finally got to celebrate getting bigger. I wish I could say that experience changed the way I see myself forever, but the truth is, I still think about my weight every day. I still feel the guilt, still do the mental math, still wonder what the scale will say tomorrow. My brain is programmed this way. But pregnancy gave me a taste of freedom I never knew was missing. For once, I got to exist in my body without feeling like I owed anyone an explanation.

Sometimes I wonder if I will ever feel that free again. After giving birth to two beautiful boys, I don’t long for another pregnancy, though I have to admit, nine more months of not obsessing over the scale sounds pretty damn appealing.

I don’t want another excuse to love my body, I just want to stop feeling like I need one.

Mary Burnham is a plus-size boy mom of two who manages software by day and chaos by night. She’s highly susceptible to a viral product and even more susceptible to self-diagnosing the latest health scare. Virality at all costs. Follow her at @maryuburnham.

#8200. Beautiful Eastern Orthodox Baby Names and Their Meanings

Timeless Eastern Orthodox baby names that celebrate heritage, culture, and tradition across generations

Have you ever wondered how a name can carry the weight of centuries?

When it comes to naming a baby, tradition often speaks louder than trends. For families connected to Eastern Orthodox heritage, names are more than labels. They’re echoes of centuries of culture, history, and community. These names have been passed down through generations, carrying stories of emperors, scholars, saints, and everyday people who shaped Orthodox life.

From the regal Constantine to the graceful Anastasia, this list of Eastern Orthodox baby names celebrates timeless choices that honor tradition while remaining beautiful and relevant today.

Names are more than words. They’re vessels of memory, culture, and continuity. Within Eastern Orthodox tradition, baby names reflect centuries of heritage, often inspired by Byzantine rulers, revered scholars, and beloved figures whose stories shaped communities across Greece, Russia, the Balkans, and beyond. Choosing an Orthodox baby name isn’t just about finding something elegant; it’s about honoring the past while giving your child a timeless identity that will carry meaning for generations.

From Greek Orthodox names that sparkle with classical charm to Slavic Orthodox names rooted in resilience, these choices embody tradition in its purest form. They remind us that while trends may fade, tradition endures, and a name chosen with care becomes a lasting gift.

Strong, dignified, and steeped in tradition, these boy names have been passed down through centuries of Orthodox heritage. They carry echoes of emperors, scholars, and timeless figures, making them enduring choices for families who value culture and continuity.

Aaron – Exalted, strong; St. Aaron the Priest

Abraham – Father of many; Patriarch of Israel

Achilles – Hero of the Greeks; symbol of courage

Adrian – From Hadria; St. Adrian the Martyr

Alexander – Defender of men; borne by saints and emperors

Alexios – Defender, helper; St. Alexios the Man of God

Anastasios – Resurrection; linked to Easter tradition

Anthony (Antonios) – Priceless one; St. Anthony the Great

Aristides – Best purpose; early Christian philosopher

Aristotle – Best purpose; classical Greek heritage

Arsenios – Virile, strong; St. Arsenios the Great

Athanasios – Immortal; St. Athanasius of Alexandria

Basil (Vasilios) – Royal, kingly; St. Basil the Great

Benjamin – Son of the right hand; biblical patriarch

Christos – Anointed one; direct reference to Christ

Christopher – Bearer of Christ; St. Christopher the Martyr

Constantine – Steadfast, constant; Emperor Constantine the Great

Cosmas (Kosmas) – Order, harmony; St. Kosmas of Aetolia

Damian – To tame, subdue; St. Damian the Martyr

Demetrios – Devoted to Demeter; St. Demetrios of Thessaloniki

Dimitri – Earth lover; Slavic Orthodox tradition

Dominic – Belonging to the Lord; Western Orthodox usage

Elias – The Lord is my God; Prophet Elijah

Emmanuel – God with us; messianic prophecy

Ephraim – Fruitful; Old Testament patriarch

Eugene (Eugenios) – Well‑born; St. Eugene of Trebizond

Eustace – Fruitful, steadfast; St. Eustace the Martyr

Fabian – Bean grower; early Christian saint

Fedor – Gift of God; Russian Orthodox tradition

Florin – Flower; Romanian Orthodox heritage

Francis – Free man; St. Francis, widely venerated

Gabriel – God is my strength; Archangel Gabriel

Gavriil – Slavic form of Gabriel; Orthodox archangel

George (Georgios) – Farmer; St. George the Great Martyr

Gregory (Gregorios) – Watchful, alert; St. Gregory the Theologian

Haralambos – Shining joy; St. Haralambos the Martyr

Hilarion – Cheerful; St. Hilarion the Great

Ignatius (Ignatios) – Fiery; St. Ignatius of Antioch

Ioannis (John) – God is gracious; St. John the Theologian

Isaiah – Salvation of the Lord; Old Testament prophet

Isidore – Gift of Isis; St. Isidore of Pelusium

Ivan – Slavic form of John; deeply Orthodox name

Jacob (Iakovos) – Supplanter; Apostle James

Jerome – Sacred name; St. Jerome, translator of scripture

Plant These 7 Flower Seeds in November for Gorgeous Early Blooms Next Year

These 7 Flower Seeds to Sow in Fall Are the Best Investment You'll Make for Next Year's Garden

8 Fling-and-Forget Seeds to Scatter in Fall for Flowers that Grow Themselves – it’s Practically Magic!

Even the loveliest flowering ornamentals can cause problems if left to self-seed. Fall is the time to remove these key bloomers before they take over your backyard

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Self-seeding flowers initially seem like a delight, particularly in a cottage garden border. There’s an effortless charm to volunteer blooms filling bare gaps between perennials, softening hard edges, and lending an organic, spontaneous feel. However, what starts out as a free-flowering companion can sometimes become an aggressive garden interloper. Left unchecked, enthusiastic self-sowers can quickly wind up in walkways, lawns, vegetable patches, and even your neighbors’ yards.

As their blooms fade, seed heads get ready to burst, scatter, or get carried away by animals to fill new areas. Once the seeds disperse, you’re facing a lot of cleanup in spring. The real danger with these prolific self-seeders lies in their competitive vigor. When permitted to drop seeds in fall, they naturally get a head start on anything you might add in spring, hogging nutrients, and casting shade over slower-growing sunseekers. So fall is an important time to keep key self-seeding flowers in place.

By intervening now to deadhead mature capsules, sever seed stems, and clear away dropped seed heads, you prevent billions of viable seeds from ever hitting the soil. And if there are any standout heirloom varieties you want to keep, you can save their seed for controlled sowing in spring, keeping all the beauty while sparing yourself lots of backbreaking pulling and digging next year. Here are the key culprits you need to control now, with insights on what to do with seed heads so you can still continue to enjoy them on your terms.

Some self-seeders are more aggressive than others, so you need to focus your efforts. Try the strategies that work best for your climate, yard and gardening goals, as well as your USDA hardiness zone. In colder zones 3-5, severe early frosts can sometimes halt late-forming seed heads before they mature. In milder southern and coastal regions (6-9), extended warm falls can give plants weeks of extra time to disperse seed capsules, making rapid intervention vital. Wind patterns and heavy rain can also transport tiny seeds across garden beds in a single afternoon.

The primary defense is regular deadheading. While removing spent flowers in summer promotes reblooming, autumn deadheading is about containment. As petals drop and seed heads swell, snip them away before they turn dark brown, dry out, or split. Always carry a deep bucket or paper sack with you. Tossing cut seed heads onto the ground or moving bare stems across the yard will inadvertently broadcast thousands of seeds hither and yon. Bag up seed heads and discard them in the household trash, never into home compost heaps, which rarely sustain the high internal temperatures required to destroy persistent weed seeds.

Not all self-seeders deserve eviction, however. Native wildflowers like purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) and native black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia hirta) produce sturdy seed cones that feed foraging goldfinches and native songbirds through winter without becoming overly thuggish. Choose this option for an area where you don’t mind some seed dispersal or with flowers that are less aggressive.

Additionally, selective seed saving is a great way to hang onto more unusual or heirloom bloomers. Harvest mature, unopened seed pods on a dry sunny afternoon. Use snips like Fiskars Micro-Tip Pruning Snips, available from Amazon, to remove the heads. These spring-action blades give targeted deadheading without dropping loose seeds. Spread your collected seeds on paper towels to cure, then store them in labeled paper envelopes in a cool, dark drawer for measured sowing next spring.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

With their feathery foliage and cheerful daisy blooms, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) add delicate color and movement to beds and borders. However, beneath their dainty features lies a fierce capacity for uninvited propagation. A single plant can produce dozens of flower heads from midsummer through frost, each maturing into a cluster of needle-like seeds with barbed tips that catch on fur, gloves, and clothing.

To prevent cosmos from transforming into an unruly forest next year, inspect the fading flower heads now before the central florets turn black and stiff. Cut off spent blooms while the seed heads are still green or pale tan, or shear the entire plant to ground level once the first frost blackens the stems. If you wish to save seed, snip off a few brown heads on a dry day, strip the spiky seeds into paper envelopes, and store seeds in a cool, dark drawer for sowing next spring. For a good storage tin, try the Pethiy Green Storage Seed Tin, available from Walmart, which I love for its rustic appearance and enduring, airtight reliability.

Also known as cleome, spider flowers (Cleome hassleriana) produce spidery floral globes with extra-long stamens for brilliant late-season drama in borders. Yet few cottage annuals reseed with as much ruthless efficiency. As petals drop along the lengthening flower stalks, they leave behind long, slender, bean-like seed pods held on wiry pedicels. As these mature from green to brown, they dry out, crack open, and fling dozens of seeds across the yard.

Tackle your cleome before the seed pods reach the brittle stage. However, take care, as mature stems develop sharp spines and sticky hairs. Wear heavy gauntlet gloves and long sleeves. If you need a good pair of long-lasting gauntlet gloves, I love the Womanswork Arm Saver Garden Gloves, available from Anthropologie, with their gorgeous floral pattern and comfy fit. Snip off those green pods and bag them, or sever the entire stalk. If you love their height, keep a few ripe, unopened pods in a paper bag to dry, ensuring you dictate where they grow next season.

Pretty, delicate forget-me-nots (Myosotis sylvatica) are cherished for their sea of sky-blue flowers, creating a romantic underplanting beneath tulips and flowering shrubs. However, their common name carries a double meaning: if you forget to remove their seed heads, you will spend years pulling up unwanted seedlings from rockeries and paving cracks. Each spent flower produces tiny nutlets with barbs that cling to animal fur and shoelaces, scattering those seeds far and wide.

Ideally, it’s wise to deadhead right after flowering, but this month is the deadline to scout your beds for lingering plants that set seed during late summer. Rake through mulch with a hand cultivator to expose any dry, brown seed clusters that escaped summer snipping. Sever any remaining seed stems, bag the debris, and apply a 2-inch (5cm) layer of clean mulch where needed. Go for an organic wood-based option such as team favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon. This smothers new seeds by depriving them of the sunlight and winter chilling triggers they need to germinate in spring.

Revered by landscape designers for its airy stems topped by vivid violet and pinky-purple blooms, Verbena bonariensis (aka tall verbena or purpletop vervain) is a pollinator magnet that butterflies adore. However, in zones 7-10, this designer darling can be an invasive self-seeding powerhouse. Just a single plant produces tens of thousands of dust-like seeds capable of surviving freezing winters. These germinate with wild abandon in spring.

The challenge lies in how easily mature seed heads shed. The moment the blooms turn from purple to a dull brown, the tiny seeds loosen and scatter at the slightest brush of a breeze or sleeve. Cut back the flowering stems now, while flower clusters still hold a hint of lilac, or cup a bucket beneath the stems as you snip to catch dropping seed heads. Use wipes, such as Clorox Disinfecting Wipes 3-Pack from Walmart, to protect your snips and shears from clinging micro-seeds. Bag cut stems immediately to prevent contaminating lawn edges.

This vintage cottage garden annual is admired for its blue, pink, and white blooms nestled within a fluffy ruff of misty green bracts. Following bloom, love-in-a-mist (Nigella damascena) flowers transform into intriguing striped seed capsules that look like paper lanterns. While these pods look stunning in dried floral arrangements, it’s risky to leave them in the garden. Once they burst, they will shed hundreds of seeds across your yard like demented pepper shakers.

So, as soon as you see their green lanterns developing dark striping and they start to feel papery to the touch, harvest them with snips before the top horns split. Cut the stems long and tie them upside down inside a paper sack. The seeds will drop into the bag as the capsules dry. Save these in airtight tins for controlled springtime planting. If you need seed-saving envelopes, Artrylin Self-Seal Seed Envelopes (150-Pack) from Walmart are great for labeling, dating, and organising your seeds.

Also known as pot marigold, calendula (C. officinalis) is a hardworking cool-season annual that brightens borders and edible gardens, and continues blooming late into fall. However, each spent bloom forms a dense ring of seeds with hooked backs, which cling to tools, garden clothing, and pet fur, hitchhiking to new corners of your yard. If left undisturbed, fallen seeds create thick mats of seedlings that can choke out early spring bulbs. Deadhead those spent blooms the moment the petals wilt, snipping just below the green seed ring before it gets rigid.

If self-sown seeds have already scattered across the topsoil, lightly skim the surface with a hand rake to collect the seeds. Then cover the area with compost or shredded bark mulch to prevent early spring calendula germination. If you fancy adding some compost but don’t have enough of your own, The Home and Country USA Store do lovely little Mushroom Compost Pails from Amazon, to help you create a good soil blanket after sorting out your seed heads.

Few annuals provide the explosive vigor of the Mexican sunflower (Tithonia rotundifolia). Reaching 6-8 feet (1.8-2.4m) tall with brilliant orange blooms, it can draw monarchs and hummingbirds from miles around. However, that size poses a major problem when it self-seeds. Spring volunteer seedlings grow with ferocious speed, quickly developing thick stems and umbrella-like leaves that cast deep shade over surrounding perennials and crops.

By October, spent blooms transform into dark seed heads packed with dozens of stiff, pointed seeds that shatter outward at the slightest bump. Cut fading flowers back promptly before the centers turn dry and brittle. Once frost claims the foliage, chop down the hollow stalks and take them to the municipal waste. If you need strong debris sacks, Lowe’s Heavy Duty Debris Bags hold coarse stalks and seedheads securely for curbside yard disposal. Never toss mature heads into your home compost, or you will see hundreds of giant seedlings in beds next season.

Self-seeding can bring dynamic energy to the landscape, but if you want to prevent unwanted thuggish invasions (and all the gardening chores that go with that) then take timely fall action. The trick is deciding which flowers to allow to spread, which to manage, and how extensively to manage them.

By snipping off ripe seed heads and clearing away loose seed clusters, you can eliminate hours of weeding next spring. It might take a little trial and error, but don’t ignore your self-seeders or you might well regret it come spring. Harvest the seeds you want to keep, dispose of the rest, and enjoy a beautifully balanced and better behaved space next year.

#8194. 250 Turkish Baby Names Inspired by Nature, Strength and Beauty

Discover the beauty, meaning, and cultural stories behind 250 captivating Turkish names.

Have you ever met someone and immediately thought, Of course that’s their name?

Maybe their name sounds soft and peaceful, and that is exactly how they carry themselves. Perhaps it feels bold and powerful, matching their confidence before they have even said a word. It can make you wonder how parents choose the perfect name for a baby they have only just met, and how they somehow know which name will grow to suit them.

Choosing a name often means imagining who that baby might become. Parents may be drawn to a particular meaning, family tradition or simply the way a name sounds, hoping it will feel right both in the first moments of life and many years later.

Names become part of how we understand people. Over time, they collect memories, personality traits, family stories and emotions. A name chosen for a newborn may begin with a meaning, a tradition or simply a beautiful sound, but it eventually becomes inseparable from the person carrying it.

Names can carry the same meaning and still sound completely different from one language to another. A name inspired by the moon may feel soft and luminous in one culture, yet bold, mysterious or quietly powerful in another.

Turkish names are especially rich in imagery. Many draw from the sky, the sea, the seasons and the natural world, turning a single word into something vivid and memorable. Aylin evokes a halo around the moon, Deniz and Derya call to mind the sea, Gunes means sun and Yildiz means star.

Others reflect qualities parents may hope their children will carry through life. Eren is associated with wisdom, Mert with bravery and honesty, and Umut with hope.

With roots in Turkic, Arabic, Persian and neighboring traditions, names used in Türkiye reflect a layered cultural history shaped by poetry, nature and generations of meaning.

Below are 100 names commonly used in Türkiye, presented in alphabetical order. The list includes feminine, masculine and gender-neutral options.

Alara – water fairy or mythic river spirit

Ebru – marbled pattern or cloudlike design

#8193. What Couples Who Survive A Betrayal Do In The First Six Months

These steps apply to more than just cheating.

Your partner is your person, your safe place, your rock — so when they betray you unexpectedly, it can feel like the ground split open beneath you, and there’s no more safety net. Maybe you’re not sure what to do next. Maybe you’re thinking of ending things, or you want to try and work on it first. Whatever happened and wherever you are, there are certain steps couples take after a betrayal that relationship experts say predict whether or not they’ll move forward together or fall apart.

For starters, a betrayal doesn’t just mean someone cheated. Any breach of trust can feel like betrayal, says Blythe Landry, M.Ed., licensed clinical social worker, author of Trauma Intelligence, and founder of Grief to Purpose. Quitting a job without letting your partner know, buying a car or adopting a pet without discussing it first, or parenting in a way your partner is opposed to behind their back — these are all betrayals. So too are having affairs and endangering your kids, like drinking and driving with them in the car, Landry explains.

Those first six months after a betrayal are when the pain is most acute, Landry says. And following any type of betrayal, each partner is going to face their own unique hurdles.

“Oftentimes, the betrayed partner has difficulty determining if things are safe emotionally, as well as being uncertain of what they can believe about their relationship,” Suzanne Koch Eckenrode, licensed marriage and family therapist at Carlsbad Beach Recovery. “The person responsible for breaking the trust may be experiencing feelings of guilt, shame, or defensiveness. One of the biggest obstacles to healing is the fact that both parties will heal at a different rate. It can be very challenging to begin the process of healing when one feels ready to proceed while the other does not feel ready.”

So, how do you begin to move forward at all? Here’s what the experts advise.

Instead of trying to immediately forgive and move on, couples who stick together put their energy toward being consistent with one another, says Koch Eckenrode. This is what rebuilds trust in the long run.

“The couple establishes clear boundaries, communicates in an open manner when they feel uncomfortable or angry, and takes responsibility without blaming the other person,” she says. “Typically, rebuilding a relationship is not achieved by a single grand action but through many actions, to create enough positive interactions so the two people begin to trust each other again gradually.”

In most cases, the “perpetrator” has not suddenly turned evil and betrayed their partner. These things don’t happen in a vacuum.

“There is often a history of communication differences and things that are going on that lead one party to do something,” Landry says. “Now, that does not make the other person responsible for their choice to betray. But for example, if someone is constantly criticized and they are afraid to tell the truth because [of it], they may be much more likely to do something that they don’t tell their partner about. So one very positive sign is if both parties can look at their accountability.”

One partner may feel chronically unheard, rejected, or disrespected, which ultimately leads to a betrayal of some kind, Landry says. While it doesn’t excuse them, it does explain the behavior — and it reveals what needs fixing to move forward in your relationship together.

When a normally good, moral person betrays their partner, typically something inside of them is not OK. Either because they don’t want to or don’t know how to process those feelings, they look for something external to help. Maybe it’s an affair partner because their spouse no longer seems sexually interested in them. Maybe it’s drinking too much because it takes the edge off the bad feelings. But their commitment to understanding their own behavior plays a major role in healing and rebuilding trust.

And, importantly, the other partner is patient while they suss out what led them to stray.

“It’s always easy to see when it’s not you,” Landry says. “That’s what I would say to anyone going to couples counseling or even going to a pastor or whoever you go to for help. When it’s inside of you, it’s so evasive sometimes.”

Thinking back to her own clients, Landry says the couples in which both partners were genuinely invested in fixing things — those were the ones who repaired their relationships. That meant both showing up for counseling, both taking accountability, and both being vulnerable throughout the process.

5. They communicate, communicate, communicate until that becomes the norm.

Let’s say one partner travels often for work, and has also used that time to gamble away large sums of money in secret before. Short of quitting that job and never traveling again, how can the couple handle this scenario in a way that rebuilds trust?

“Discuss your travels beforehand and establish reasonable times for checking in with one another, then immediately inform each other of any changes from the plan,” says Koch Eckenrode. “The person doing the travel will be expected to follow through and do as agreed upon without having to constantly be reminded. The purpose here is not to provide some sort of long-term surveillance system; it’s to create an environment where each person feels safe enough that they are transparent about their actions naturally because it has become a part of who they are as opposed to being something they need to do.”

If you had good communication before the betrayal, that’s usually the biggest indicator that you two will successfully get through this as a couple, Landry says.

This has more to do with your personalities than the relationship itself, Landry notes, but the ability to see each other in a positive light will get you far. When the betrayed party has the capacity to look at their partner and say, “This is a good person who did a bad thing,” that’s a really good sign.

Of course, there are those people who don’t deserve this level of grace. “There’s a difference between giving someone another chance and holding them in high regard and letting someone abuse you. Make sure that you’re not so attached to someone that they’ve done something repeatedly to betray you and you’re holding onto it in the name of compassion, and really you’re harming yourself,” she says.

Again, it’s impossible to see yourself and your behaviors clearly all the time, Landry says. This is where the support of a therapist, family member, religious leader, or other non-biased third party can be helpful.

“Before you go to a professional, make sure to ask them questions like, ‘What have you done before? Have you worked with other couples in this situation? Do you work on yourself?’ I have never had a pre-client ask me if I go to therapy, but I really wish they would because you really shouldn’t be helping people unless you're helping yourself,” Landry says.

If you do opt to lean on a pastor or church elder for guidance, make sure they are not going to encourage you to stay in an unhealthy relationship, she adds. “The cool thing about therapy is that the therapist will have to see each of you individually prior to doing couples counseling. And they are doing that to make sure the relationship is safe.”

These 7 Flower Seeds to Sow in Fall Are the Best Investment You'll Make for Next Year's Garden

Remove These 7 Flower Thugs Before They Self-Seed Everywhere – Or You’ll Be Digging Them Up Next Year

We all dream of a perennial that keeps the garden looking good long after summer has packed its bags, don't we? You know, the kind that keeps producing beautiful flowers just when you think the growing season has nothing left to give.

It's fair enough; as temperatures dip and fall settles in, even the prettiest garden can start looking a little lackluster. The summer blooms start fading, the flower beds lose their sparkle, and you're probably wondering whether it's time to call it a year.

Thankfully, there's one unusual perennial that can bring a welcome splash of late-season color just when you need it most... and, despite its rather unflattering name, it looks seriously beautiful while doing it.

The toad lily (Tricyrtis), a shade-loving perennial with intricate, orchid-like flowers covered in colorful spots. Blooming in late summer and fall, it offers a surprisingly exotic display at a time when many other plants are winding down.

And despite its rather unflattering name, this little-known garden gem has plenty going for it. With delicate blooms that look more at home in a tropical greenhouse than a shady backyard, the toad lily is the sort of plant that makes you stop, take a closer look, and wonder why you aren't growing it already.

Let's get one thing straight: the toad lily isn't actually an orchid, no matter how much it might look like one. Rather, as the name suggests, it's a member of the lily family, and its botanical name is Tricyrtis.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Depending on the species or variety, the blooms may feature white or pale lavender petals, deep purple freckles, and contrasting yellow or purple centers. Some have a star-shaped appearance, while others look more like tiny funnels. Either way, though, their delicate details are best appreciated up close, rather than from the other side of the yard, as they look almost as though someone has taken a miniature paintbrush to every flower.

In other words, this isn't just another pretty perennial that relies on enormous flowers to make an impression; it's all about the details. And those details are exactly what make it such a charming addition to a shady garden.

Spring and summer get most of the attention when it comes to flowering perennials. By the time fall rolls around, many gardeners are left with attractive foliage, fading blooms, and a growing collection of plants preparing for winter.

The toad lily, however, usually begins flowering in late summer or early fall, with some continuing into October and, under favorable conditions, even November. (The exact timing depends on the variety, local climate, and when the first hard frost arrives in your USDA Planting Zone).

If you're looking for a plant that helps bridge the gap between summer color and the quieter months of winter, then, this is one of those flowers you've never heard of that's worth considering, especially as many varieties prefer partial to full shade, making them particularly useful beneath trees, along woodland borders, or in those awkward shade garden corners where sun-loving flowers struggle.

Despite their exotic appearance, toad lilies aren't especially demanding when planted in the right conditions. Pop yours somewhere it won't get too much direct sun, as this can scorch the foliage (particularly if the soil dries out), and keep the soil consistently moist.

That being said, make sure excess water can drain away because, while moist soil is good; persistently waterlogged roots are another matter. Many toad lilies spread gradually through creeping underground stems or rhizomes, forming attractive clumps over time, so they appreciate a bit of space, too.

There's something especially satisfying about discovering a fall flowering perennial that offers something different from the usual lineup of autumn mums and asters, especially one that brings delicate orchid-like flowers, attractive foliage, and a welcome burst of color just when the garden might otherwise be winding down.

Honestly, if anyone asks why you've planted something called a toad lily, simply invite them over for a closer look. Once they see those extraordinary little blooms, the name might be the last thing on their mind.

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. And what trends we may see more of in 2027.

Each year, BabyCenter compiles all the data from their users and publishes a list of the year’s most popular baby names. The official rankings from the Social Security Administration, based on actual issued birth certificates, usually don’t come in until months into the new year, so this is our first peek at which names might have been given to the most babies born in 2026. But they also spot names that have risen quickly in popularity, helping identify what’s coming next in baby-naming trends.

The most popular baby names of 2026 are a predictable pair: Olivia for girls and Noah for boys. Olivia was also the most popular girl name of 2025, according to the SSA, and Noah was #2 on the boys’ chart.

Here’s how the rest of the top 10 shook out, according to BabyCenter’s data:

Many of these names have fallen somewhere in the top 10 for multiple years running, but Evelyn in particular rejoins the chart after falling off in 2024. And five completely new monikers broke into the top 100 this year. Making their debuts are Magnolia, Milo, Dean, Archer, and Stetson.

Speaking of Magnolia, long baby names are generally gaining in popularity, according to BabyCenter’s report. In fact, 29% of the top girl names and 31% of the top boy names had seven or more letters (21% had four or less, by comparison). Perhaps parents are opting for longer names that sound good on an adult’s resume, with cute nickname options to use ‘til then.

If you’re big into initials, you’ll like to know that E is currently the most popular first initial for girls (15% of BabyCenter’s top 100 girl names begin with it), while J ranks highest for boys at 14%.

Western-inspired baby names have been trending for a couple of years now, and that doesn’t seem to be slowing down. BabyCenter noted big jumps in popularity for Stetson, Wilder, Callahan, Sadie, and Sutton, to name a few. Names that include an X got a lot of use this year too, according to BabyCenter’s Steph Coffield. Prepare to see even more baby Jaxsons, Maximillians, Ximenas, Xaidens, X-cetera (sorry).

And thanks of course to the eponymous movie, the name Odysseus rose an astronomical 1,456 spots on BabyCenter’s popularity charts. While it won’t be everyone’s first choice for a baby boy in the new year, it does seem like more parents are leaning into Greek mythology for name inspo. Monikers like Atlas, Ares, Evander, Daphne, and Gaia are all scooching their way up the rankings as we speak.

While it’s hard to say exactly what 2027’s baby name trends will bring (you never know when a pop culture moment like Odysseus will change the charts), we can’t wait to hear more interesting names being called across the playground.

#8186. Don't Cut Down That Tree Yet – It Could Be Legally Protected, Even if It's on Your Own Property

That troublesome tree might be yours, but removing it isn't always your decision. A few important checks could save you a costly mistake.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As homeowners, we tend to be proud and possessive. My house, my lawn, my trees. But don’t make the mistake of thinking you can chop down those trees just because you feel like it. Owning a tree doesn’t necessarily give you the unrestricted right to remove it.

We tend to think of trees and plants as our personal property, and in many cases that is true. If you plant a hydrangea bush on property you own this year, you can take it out the following summer. The same goes for a rose bush or a cherry tree. But that principle doesn’t apply to every single tree. In fact, removing trees without doing your research can leave you open to legal liability.

Some trees are legally protected under a variety of laws, ranging from municipal ordinances to HOA restrictions to environmental and wildlife protections. As a former attorney, I advise on issues like this in my Gardening Lawyer series. Read on for the whole scoop.

Everyone knows that certain animals are protected by national and state laws in this country. The animals are often endangered species, such as whales, dolphins, and manatees, protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. But many people don’t realize that laws also protect some types of trees. Most protections are at a local level, but a few national protections exist too.

Laws relating to tree removal are generally handled at the city or county level. Local municipal ordinances may require a homeowner to obtain a permit to remove a mature tree or a protected species. The types of trees most often protected include heritage trees or native species.

If your property is part of a Homeowners Association community, your landscaping rights are governed by HOA rules, also called CC&Rs – Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions. These rules can forbid tree removal without approval by the HOA architectural committee. And this doesn't depend on whether your town requires a permit.

Property laws may also affect your right to remove a tree. If the tree is planted in the center of your yard, property laws probably will not be a concern. But if the tree trunk sits on the property line, it is jointly owned, and you and your neighbor must agree before you can remove it.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Finally, you’ll want to check both federal and state environmental rules before taking out a tree if you live in an environmentally fragile area like a wetland. This can also be an issue if the area is a site where birds nest.

If you are asking this question, you are fairly new to a Homeowners Association (HOA). Yes, if your home is part of an HOA, you agreed to follow the CC&Rs.

Most HOAs require you to request and obtain board approval before pruning or cutting down a tree on your property. The Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions are legally binding rules that are part of the price you pay to be part of the HOA. The administration has every right to stop you from cutting down or even trimming a tree on your property if the action violates the community's recorded CC&Rs.

There are those risks you can’t afford to take but also risks you can’t afford not to take. The choice is always yours – to follow the laws or to close your eyes to the legalities and chop chop chip. (I mean, George Washington cut down a cherry tree and look how far he went!) But know your risks before you decide.

The average fine for cutting down a tree in a city without getting a permit is $10,000. That’s the fine in San Francisco too. In NYC, it’s $15,000. In Visalia, California, cutting down a protected valley oak without a permit is a cool $20,000.

What about HOA fees? Homeowners Association fees vary from one HOA to the next. But they typically charge administrative fines of up to $1000 plus tree replacement costs that run into the thousands of dollars. If the tree is in a protected common area or protected by local laws, fees can go up quickly to over $20,000.

If you cut or damage trees on federal public lands without federal protection, you can face criminal fines or up to one year in prison. Municipal and county governments impose direct administrative fines of up to $10,000 per tree for removing protected or wetland-adjacent trees without a local permit.

It would be nice if a homeowner could contact one agency to determine whether a tree is protected. But alas, that is not the case. You’ll have to do a little research or hire someone to do it for you. Here are some tips to get you started.

First, consider the tree's origin. Did you buy it as a young sapling from the garden store? That probably means that it is not an endangered species. Is it still a young tree, slender and only half its full height? You probably won’t be impeded by city permitting requirements, since these often apply only to mature trees of a certain height and girth. A call to city hall can confirm this.

Second, is your home part of an HOA community? If not, HOA rules won’t apply. If so, you'll likely have to jump through hoops, so review the CC&Rs.

Third, is the tree on the property line? If not, you won't need the neighbor’s permission. If so, you’ll need to arrange a conversation about the tree. Put any agreement in writing.

Fourth, is your tree on a public right-of-way or sidewalk strip? You will probably need a permit to remove it. Ask your town’s City Hall.

Last, is your property part of a wetland, a riparian buffer, or a bird nesting zone? You may not know. If you aren’t sure, start by asking your City Forester or Urban Forestry Department for direction.

Every rule has exceptions. Many local governments allow you to remove a tree without a permit if it is dead, severely diseased, or dangerous. For example, if the tree is leaning or uprooted and poses an immediate threat to your home or to passersby, the odds are good that you can remove it. Call city hall first to confirm.

This is probably also an exception in HOA restrictions. Read your CC&Rs or just call the office and ask.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#8184. 13 'Practical Magic' Baby Names Sure To Charm You

Who else wants to see a future generation full of baby Jets?

Pop culture baby names don’t always age well (we’re looking at you, Daenerys), but you certainly boost your odds when you pluck a name from a beloved cult classic. And if a timely sequel just happens to arrive right before your own production does, well, even better! That’s why we’re here for Practical Magic baby names.

Alice Hoffman’s bestselling 1995 book spawned a movie by the same name, and its long-awaited sequel, Practical Magic 2, hit the big screen just ahead of the spooky season. True fans know that the saga of the love-cursed Owens women actually spans four books — and we’ve combed through them to find the best Practical Magic names for your own wee witchy woman. Of course, like any good coven, there are 13.

Sandra Bullock’s Sally is fiercely protective and somewhat magic-averse… until she isn’t. The name, originally a diminutive for Sarah, means “princess,” so it’s especially fitting for a little girl. Even better, it’s just starting to climb back up the Social Security Administration’s list of popular baby names, meaning you can jump on this name before the spell of uniqueness is broken.

Practical Magic’s other protagonist is the free-spirited Gillian. Beautiful and impulsive, she’s Sally’s more-fun little sister whose main fault is having terrible taste in men. But let’s focus on the positive, shall we? Gillian — or Jillian — means “youthful,” making it another apropos choice for a baby. And just like sister Sally, it hits that classic-but-not-common sweet spot. Call it baby name magic!

One of the two feisty aunts who raise the young Owens sisters, Bridget is the proper name of Jet and is one of the main protagonists in The Rules of Magic, the second book in the series. Also the name of another literary darling (that’d be Bridget Jones, of course), the Irish name conjures up pluckiness and means “power.”

Hear me out: Aunt Bridget’s nickname is a standout choice for a baby girl all on its own! I mean, if Bridget means power, what more powerful image is there than… a jet? And as played by absolute screen legend Dianne Wiest, Aunt Jet is nothing if not powerful — in both love and magic.

Frances, along with the nickname Franny, is another one of those granny-chic names that is so old-fashioned it feels modern again. (Indeed, it reached number 318 on the SSA’s most recent list of baby names — and Stockard Channing’s return to the role might help it keep soaring.) Plus, it’s wise, eccentric Aunt Frances who has one of the book's most enduring lines: “My darling girl, when are you going to realize that being normal is not necessarily a virtue? It rather denotes a lack of courage.”

Practical and dutiful, Sally’s oldest daughter (played by Maisie Williams in the sequel) grows up to be a med student. But as a name, Antonia has a flowy, delicate feel that’s, dare we say, ethereal in nature. Sitting outside of the top 1,000 baby names, it’s a vintage name that’s more than ready for a comeback. We think it’s spellbinding.

And you thought Kylie Jenner made this name famous! In the Practical Magic series, Kylie Owens is Sally’s youngest daughter (except, oddly, in the sequel, where she’s the elder sister), and she shares her Aunt Gillian’s flaming red hair and rebellious streak. While Kylie as a name is on a bit of a downward trajectory, it’s still a very popular choice, coming in at number 204 on the SSA list.

The original witch and matriarch of the Owens family, Maria mysteriously arrives in America in 1680 (just in time for the Salem witch trials!) and was feared because of her magical gifts. She cast the spell that ultimately cursed any man who fell in love with an Owens woman. What a legacy! As a name, Maria has enduring popularity and multiple meanings, including “beloved.”

Faith Owens is Maria’s daughter and a character in Magic Lessons, the first book chronologically in the series but the third written. Separated from her mother, Faith becomes headstrong and practices blood magic. (Can you blame her?) As a name, Faith has long been a popular choice, although it’s not usually associated with witchcraft!

In Magic Lessons, Hannah Owens is the one who finds baby Maria, raises her, and teaches her the “nameless arts.” She even gives her the “Grimoire”: a leather-bound book of spells. Hannah means “grace” or “favor.”

In Practical Magic, Regina is Sally and Gillian’s deceased mother. While her storyline may not be a happy one, the name itself conjures up regal elegance and means “queen” or “lady.” Dare we say, it’s a magical choice.

Aunt Frances and Aunt Jet’s mother, Susanna stars in the prequel book The Rules of Magic. You won’t find Susanna anywhere on the SSA’s list of the top 1000 baby names, so it’s a clever pick for anyone who wants a name that’s classic but not common.

April Owens is Regina’s mother and Sally and Gillian’s grandmother; she appears in The Rules of Magic. April comes from Latin and means “to open.” It hits that popular-but-not-too-popular sweet spot, ranking at 542 on the most recent SSA baby names list.

If there’s one takeaway from this list, it’s that the baby girl names in the Practical Magic universe are less stereotypically witchy or pop culture-trendy than they are enduringly classic and granny-chic. So tell us: Which name has cast a spell on you?

#8182. Jefferson Fisher Has The Secret to Getting Along Better With Absolutely Everyone

The lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less. He might just be onto something.

If being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything. Also, most of us suck at communication.

For once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity. We can only blame ourselves because, hey, communicating is hard. Getting your point across to a group, your nuclear family, or one single person takes practice and discipline, mistakes and learning. I don’t think we ever get it entirely right.

Well, most of us don’t. There are some communicators in this world that are … blessed. Jefferson Fisher is one such individual. Fisher is a Texan, dad, husband, and personal injury attorney who has made a name for himself through social videos that teach us all how to communicate better.

The videos offer pithy lessons like this: Instead of saying I disagree, “tweak it a little and say, I see things differently.” Why? “When you talk in terms of perspective, you find more connection.” Here’s another: “How I talk to my kids will affect how they talk to their kids.”

Simple, pointed, and poignant. You can see why millions tune in.

Fisher’s goal is to make people talk more and argue less. It says just that on the cover of his fantastic, practical, wonderfully written book The Next Conversation — a must read for all of us who strive to get along a little better with those around us.

We caught up with Fisher to talk about his new book and, naturally, anoint him as the latest Cool Dad. Here are some excerpts from our talk, including extras from the Cool Dad Questionnaire and his advice for the most important conversations you’ll ever have.

What’s one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood?

Probably more of a reckless abandon about what they ate. I grew up in just every Little Debbie from Cosmic Brownies to ... everything you could think of that was probably terrible for us, but we didn't know any different.

I mean, this is my guess ... I would say what Sierra loves about me is my steadiness. When things don't go to plan, I'm pretty rock steady. So when there is something unexpected or the kids go into what we call their midnight madness, when it's right there at bedtime and they're absolutely losing their minds, that's when I'm able to step in and I think I'm able to really notice when she's overwhelmed, and take over.

And what do you think they maybe find annoying about you?

I mean, there's lots. I'm trying to find a really good one like she finds the most annoying about me is sometimes I can be a little bit occasionally of like a party-pooper where the kids are just ... all going nuts and I'm like, "Can we just not yell so much in our house?" So there's that.

Probably the bigger thing she gets more annoyed about is my relationship with money. Its just money. So I'm the spender and so she is the saver. If it's something that's like, "Hey, but this would be fun, even though it's not something we exactly need right now, but it would be a cool memory," I think there's a lot of that.

What does fatherhood mean to you in our current world?

Fatherhood, with the caveat of doing it well to be a good father, I think, is knowing it's a discipline and not a destination. It's a daily devotion to putting your wife, your spouse, your partner, your kids before you. And it's this idea of ... are you inconveniencing them for your comfort or is it the opposite, are you willing to inconvenience yourself for their comfort?

There are times where it's going to be uncomfortable. I don't want to be the one carrying all the bags all the time, but is it what my family needs in that moment in the airport? Yeah, that's what they need. Can I do it? Yeah.

I got to say that the carrying bags all the time is a wonderful metaphor.

Yeah. You're the one that is supposed to shoulder the heavy. So you're supposed to carry what they can't. I'm sure there's a similarity to this phrase of to be what others cannot, you must be willing to suffer what others will not, and so it's like that. To be the dad that others can't, you got to be able to do what others won't.

How do you better communicate with your partner in parenting? Do you think there's ways that you, something that don't apply, or do you follow the advice in your book and have great arguments and conversations with your spouse?

I wouldn't say there are things that don't apply. I would say what it would need to go deeper on is the theme of repair specifically. So you could have the mindset of arguments and that's something that's very helpful. There's the idea of saying things with control, meaning be regulated and knowing when you need to take that timeout, and using the pauses. But the turn the book doesn't make with regard to marital relationships is repair.

We are talking about words of affirmation, affirming somebody's feelings, being able to take ownership of your words and what that actually sounds like ... how to truly use words of empathy and affirm how they feel, how to say things that are going to bring. We hit on connection in the book, but more in the way of framing non-relationship conversations.

In repair, there is a lot of something as simple as, "Yes, I said that. Yes, I did that. I absolutely can see how that would have frustrated you or upset you," or "I think it's totally reasonable for you to feel this way. I don't blame you for being upset about that. I could have done that better." And then how to actually, words of apology, how to repair after a rupture, that to me is, that's a whole different ballgame, whole different set of skills.

What do you think about checking in? I'm wondering where that falls in the communication line. It's maybe a little bit of the repair, but is that an important thing to do or how do you feel about just what a felt of unspoken understanding between family?

There's an element that my wife and I do and that's check-ins and check-outs. I mean, it's what we call them, things that we do in the morning and things that we do in the evening. Otherwise, there are times you may never talk to your spouse in the day and you know what that's like. Before you know it, you're just two people, somehow there's a woman who lives with me. I don't know who she is, but she's here and you can be roommates that way if you're not checking in with each other. The other is that unspokenness of knowing when something is wrong and that you feel like you might be approaching things from a different vantage. I like asking the phrase, "What's coming up?" "What's coming up for you?"

Instead of me saying, "What's wrong with you" or even, "What's up with you?" That tends to get a pretty defensive response. But if I say something as simple as what's coming up, there's a difference between [that and] saying, "How are you and how's your heart?"
