#8168. Can Trap-Neuter-Return Solve the Feral Cat Crisis?

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Trap-neuter-return, better known as TNR, is one of the main ways communities try to manage feral cat populations. The idea is relatively simple: instead of removing cats born outdoors or those that have reverted to a semi-wild state, cats are trapped, sterilized, vaccinated, and returned to the place where they were found.

But TNR is also the subject of an ongoing debate over animal welfare, wildlife impact, and public health. With a push to make October Feral Cat Awareness Month, and National Feral Cat Day coming up on October 16th, we thought it would be time to look at this in more detail.

The scale of the problem helps explain why TNR has become so widely used. Roughly 3.3 million cats enter US shelters each year, while the feral cat population has been estimated at as many as 100 million nationwide. With unspayed females capable of producing one to two litters a year, and uncastrated males able to father an immeasurable number of litters in their lifetime, sterilization is essential to stopping the cycle.

In the past, dealing with increasing feral cat numbers meant eradication. Not only is culling cats cruel, but it has also been proven, time and time again, to be ineffective, with new cats migrating into the area to fill the void left by those who have been removed or destroyed.

By sterilizing cats in a feral colony, population control happens gradually. There is less fighting, less roaming, and less disease spread. Populations naturally dwindle as the number of fertile cats is reduced.

A feral cat is humanely trapped, examined, vaccinated, and neutered before being marked with a small notch in its ear. The cat is then returned outdoors rather than placed for adoption, since genuinely unsocialized cats are often unlikely to adapt to life as pets.

Anyone considering TNR should ideally start by contacting a local shelter or TNR organization. Experienced volunteers may be able to handle the process themselves and will also know the local rules governing trapping and release.

For those doing it independently, a proper humane trap is essential, as is a legal location where there is a genuine concentration of cats. Local regulations vary, so checking with animal control or a wildlife agency beforehand is important.

Once baited, usually with wet cat food, traps need to be checked at least every 12 hours. Other animals, including raccoons, can sometimes be caught accidentally, and different rules may apply to releasing them. Cats should remain inside the trap during transport, and veterinary care needs to be arranged beforehand because not every clinic treats feral cats.

The basic argument for TNR is that sterilizing cats prevents them from producing more kittens. Over time, that can reduce the size of a colony and the number of feral cats entering shelters.

That matters for shelters already dealing with large numbers of animals. Fewer feral cats arriving can leave more resources available for cats and other animals that are suitable for adoption.

TNR also offers an alternative to simply removing cats from an area, something that can be difficult when dealing with large outdoor populations.

Some research has questioned whether TNR consistently reduces feral cat populations, since new cats can be introduced into established colonies and abandoned cats can add to the numbers. Tracking colonies accurately is also notoriously difficult.

Only an estimated 2 percent of feral cats are currently sterilized, compared with roughly 85 percent of owned pets, highlighting how much of the population remains outside the reach of traditional veterinary care.

Animal welfare groups, including PETA, argue that returning feral cats outdoors can amount to abandonment. However, in established feral cat colonies, relatively few can adapt to life in a home, but for those that can, rehoming is always the preferred option.

Public health is another concern. Maintaining vaccinations and preventive health across an unowned population can be extremely challenging. One study found that 92 percent of captured feral cats carried fleas. Feral cats have also been associated with typhus, plague, internal parasites, and toxoplasmosis, and, at roughly six times the rate of dogs, they are the domestic animal most frequently diagnosed with rabies in the US.

Perhaps the most contentious part of the TNR debate concerns wildlife.

The American Bird Conservancy has linked cats to the extinction of 40 bird species, 21 mammals, and two reptiles. Hundreds of additional species are affected by feral and outdoor cats more broadly.

Sterilization prevents reproduction, but it does not remove a cat's instinct to hunt, and a neutered cat can still kill birds, mammals, and reptiles, making population control only one part of the wider environmental debate.

Some evidence suggests that keeping cats well-fed with a high-protein diet may reduce their prey drive; however, this requires continued management of the colony.

Few researchers argue that TNR alone can solve the feral cat problem. Even supporters generally see it as one part of a broader approach that includes sterilizing owned pets and reducing the number of cats entering the outdoor population in the first place.

At the same time, critics point to the potential consequences for wildlife, public health, and the cats themselves.

That leaves TNR in an awkward position. It can reduce reproduction without necessarily eliminating the wider problems associated with free-roaming cats, but whether it is the most ethical approach ultimately depends on how the competing welfare concerns involving cats, wildlife, and people are weighed.

Ultimately, feral cats are a human-created problem, and it is up to us to work towards a solution. TNR may not be the only answer, but it has, in many cases, proven to be a humane and effective way to control feral cat populations.

#8167. 17 Easy Holiday Cocktail Recipes That'll Make You Feel Merry & Bright

Whether you’re hosting a holiday party or just want to sip on a special beverage alone by the fire, now is the time when much of the world goes searching for easy holiday cocktail recipes. We all deserve a little treat after the year that was 2025. Well, rest assured, there’s a fun and festive drink out there for every palate (including if mocktails are more your speed). From spiked hot chocolate and eggnog concoctions for sweets lovers to wintry old-fashioneds and martinis, here are some of the best easy holiday cocktails on the internet.

If you’ve never put Bailey’s in your eggnog, now’s the time. Averie Cooks’ recipe for Santa’s magic potion will help you get the ratio just right, and hit it with a little cinnamon and nutmeg for that perfect holiday flavor.

Mimosas are a crowd-pleasing cocktail, so why not just put a holiday spin on them for your winter party? Damn Delicious’ cranberry mimosas blend orange, pineapple, and cranberry juice with sparkling white wine. Just top with a sprig of rosemary and a couple cranberries and serve.

If you’re not a bourbon fan, might I recommend Princess Pinky Girl’s drunken Rudolph, a hot chocolate cocktail spiked with Fireball instead? This recipe is even less work and is sort of the everyman’s version, if you will.

Family Fresh Meals’ starry night punch recipe is nonalcoholic, but obviously you can just swap the sparkling grape juice for the real thing. It will yield a classic Christmas red sangria, which you can top with star-shaped apple cutouts for the perfect finishing touch.

If you want a cocktail that absolutely screams Christmas, then Dude That Cookz’ peppermint cream martini is the drink for you. It’s a delicious mix of peppermint schnapps, white cream liqueur, and vanilla vodka, with the cutest crushed-candy-cane rim.

Why haven’t I thought of apple cider sangria before? Averie Cooks explains everything you’ll need and how to get the perfect balance of flavors. Then just load ‘er up with apples, cinnamon sticks, oranges, pomegranate, and whatever else your holiday heart desires.

Personally, I swore off blue drinks after one particularly rough hangover in college, but Princess Pinky Girl’s Jack Frost cocktail is admittedly very fun-looking. Just blend your ingredients together, rim your glass, and clink it with a friend’s.

One last mimosa idea before you go, courtesy of Budget Bytes: simply swap out orange juice for apple cider, pour it into your champagne flute until the color is just right, and bada bing bada boom. It doesn’t get any easier than that, and you know it’s going to be delish.

Oh, so you’re having a holiday party party — love that. Then you have to try Princess Pinky Girl’s Instagram-worthy candy cane shots, which only take about five minutes to whip up. Adding a little sweetened condensed milk to the gelatin mix gives it a sweet, creamy base that makes the candy cane flavor really come alive.

Biscuits & Burlap’s spiced pear and chai bourbon drink is the perfect reminder that apples are not the only seasonal fruit worth celebrating. It’s a bit more involved (you’ll need to make a fresh pear simple syrup), but the end result looks so worth that little bit of time and effort.

Speaking of pears, you’ve gotta try Dinners Done Quick’s pear gin fizz. When’s the last time you actually ordered a gin fizz out? They’re so good but they’re never really on cocktail menus anymore, and they give me an old-timey celebratory feel every time.

Moscow mules are the perfect drink to serve to guests if you’re not much of a bartender and you’re just out here doing your best as a host. Fresh Apron’s recipe is a matter of a few simple steps (complete with exact measurements); it’s the festive garnishes and copper mugs that really make this beverage shine.

Savory Spice’s recipe will teach you how to make a chai simple syrup (very useful if you’re an at-home coffee enthusiast, by the way) and how to balance it perfectly within a cranberry fizz. It’ll add a seasonal, cozy depth of flavor that’s unexpected yet oddly perfect.

White russian drinkers, you’ll love this easy apple pie cocktail, made with Crown and RumChata, from Dinners Done Quick. You can easily customize it to make it sweeter, heavier on the cinnamon, extra apple-y, however you take your cocktails.

Be honest: How many gallons of apple cider did you just add to your grocery list?

This article was originally published on Dec. 12, 2025

When a room fills with Broadway stars, an evening at The Carlyle could easily become another glamorous New York event. But on October 19, the spotlight wonât be on those performing onstage; it will be shining on shelter dogs looking for homes.

The second annual Fetch Pet Gala will bring musical superstars Bernadette Peters, Darren Criss, and Ariana DeBose together for a night of performances, dinner, and fundraising in support of pets and the people who care for them. Hosted by Fetch Pet Insurance, the gala has already sold out, with an overflowing waitlist.

The evening will begin with a Green Carpet featuring adoptable dogs from North Shore Animal League America, one of the countryâs largest no-kill animal rescue and adoption organizations. The dogs will have a chance to bathe in the limelight and meet potential adopters before guests head into CafÃ© Carlyle for dinner and performances.

For anyone who works with animals, the purpose behind a night like this is easy to recognize. Giving a pet a second chance often takes much more than finding an empty spot on someone's couch. There may be veterinary care, foster placement, rehabilitation, transportation, or other support needed before a dog or cat is ready to start over.

Sometimes, getting an animal ready for adoption means more than just a makeover. Addressing problems that have been overlooked for months or even years, like dental disease, skin conditions, parasites, chronic pain, and behavioral challenges can all become part of the journey toward a new home.

The same is true for pets already living with families. When people face illness or financial hardship, keeping up with a pet's needs can become difficult, even when the bond between them remains as strong as ever.

For many pet parents, the idea of giving up a beloved animal is heartbreaking. But when money is tight or a family is dealing with a serious illness, even routine veterinary care can suddenly feel out of reach.

That is where the Fetch Pet Gala becomes about much more than a glamorous night in New York. Behind the performances and the photographs are animals waiting for a second chance and families desperate to keep caring for the pets they love. The money raised can help transform lives in more ways than one.

For these dogs, walking the Green Carpet is much more than a glamorous photo opportunity. They are there in search of a happy ending to their story.

North Shore Animal League America works with animals rescued from overcrowded shelters, puppy mills, and natural disasters, preparing them for adoption by providing veterinary care and other support. Since its inception, more than 1.2 million animals have been saved through the organizationâs efforts.

Putting adoptable dogs in the middle of an evening filled with Broadway stars is a pretty effective way to remind us that rescue animals deserve their own spotlight, too. And maybe, just maybe, their Broadway moment will end with a happily ever after.

Once the Green Carpet wraps up, guests will move into CafÃ© Carlyle for dinner and performances from Peters, Criss, and DeBose.

Peters brings a particularly strong connection between Broadway and animal welfare. She co-founded Broadway Barks with Mary Tyler Moore, an organization that brings Broadway performers and animal shelters together to help dogs and cats find homes.

Criss and DeBose bring their own Broadway credentials to the evening. Criss, known by many for playing Blaine Anderson on televisionâs musical superhit, âGleeâ, recently earned a Tony Award for his performance in Maybe Happy Ending. Not to be outshone, DeBose won the 2022 Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Anita in Steven Spielbergâs remake of West Side Story.

The evening will conclude with the Fetch Pet After Party and another performance from a surprise guest. Last year it was John Legend, so the bar has been set pretty high for this yearâs mystery guest!

The celebrities and performances may be what catch people's attention, but the real purpose of the gala is fundraising.

The 2026 gala will benefit four organizations: Broadway Cares/Equity Fights AIDS, Broadway Barks, Wags & Walks, and North Shore Animal League America. Together, their work touches different parts of the challenges facing pets and the people who care for them, from shelter and adoption services to helping families continue caring for their animals during difficult circumstances.

Broadway Cares is supporting another side of the human-animal relationship. Through grants to organizations around the country, it helps people living with HIV/AIDS and other serious illnesses, including programs that help them continue caring for their pets. When someone is dealing with a serious illness or financial hardship, paying for a pet's food, medications, or veterinary visits can become difficult. For veterinary professionals, this is a familiar reality: the ability to pay for care can sometimes determine what happens next for an animal, even when the family desperately wants to do what is best for them. Yet giving up a beloved animal can be another painful loss at an already difficult time. Helping people meet their pets' basic needs can allow those animals to stay where they belong: with the people who love them.

Wags & Walks focuses on rescue dogs and reducing euthanasia, while Broadway Barks works to connect shelter animals with adoptive families. North Shore Animal League America brings the rescue and adoption side directly into the gala through the dogs appearing on the Green Carpet.

The Fetch Pet Gala is still a relatively new event, but its first year showed what this combination of entertainment and philanthropy can accomplish.

The Fetch Pet Gala is part of a greater charitable effort from Fetch Pet Insurance. The company says it has raised more than $14.6 million for organizations and initiatives supporting pets, animals, and the people who care for them.

For the 2026 event, the formula remains much the same: bring people together, put rescue animals in the spotlight, and turn an evening of entertainment into funding for organizations doing hands-on work. And ultimately, that is what makes a night like this worth paying attention to.

The dresses, performances, and famous faces will make for a wonderful night, but the heart of the evening is in the animals waiting for a family and in the people doing everything they can to keep their pets healthy and by their side. After all, a pet's home is more than a place to live. It is where they are loved, cared for, and, very often, where they are part of the family.

The Green Carpet may be where the night begins, but for the dogs waiting for homes and the families trying to care for their pets through difficult circumstances, the impact of the evening will extend well beyond one fun night in New York.

#8164. Chatting About Weird Cat Behaviors, Hissing, & Cats Who Hump | Chatty Cattys, Episode 37

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

In this episode of Catster's Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole dive deep into the peculiar yet normal world of feline behavior, unraveling the mysterious reasons behind common cat habits. From unpacking why domestic pets bring home "gifts" like dead prey or hair ties to setting the record straight on why cats "make biscuits," they share what it truly means to listen to, understand, and care for our feline companions. Instead of advertising a one-size-fits-all approach to pet discipline, the conversation focuses on the importance of understanding a cat's instincts and body language. The hosts chat about how speaking a cat's natural language leads to better communication, proving that forcing a feline into a human mold rarely ends well.

Tune in to find out why your indoor or outdoor cat feels driven to bring home dead preyâor stolen household objects like hair tiesâeven when they are fully fed. Dr. Karyn breaks down the hardwired hunting instincts that persist despite domestication, explaining how cats view their owners as substitute family members to provide for. You will also learn about the true origin of kneading (or "making biscuits"), why it brings adult cats so much comfort, and why some male cats awkwardly take the habit a step further.

Plus, this episode sheds light on hilarious personal pet stories. You will find out what happened when Dr. Karyn caught her neutered cat making eyes at her while humping a cozy blanket, why traditional deterrents like spray bottles or double-sided tape often backfire into fun games, and how a simple, gentle "hiss" can instantly communicate boundaries to your pet!

Hunting Instincts Realities: Dr. Karyn and Nicole address why cats bring home dead animals or scavenged items, clarifying that hunting is an automatic survival drive with no time for logical processing, meaning even well-fed cats will pounce on instinct.

Klepto Cats & Treasure Hunting: The hosts reveal that some cats redirect their hunting drive entirely onto non-living household items, such as hair ties, bringing "treasure" home to their owners as part of their natural drive to provide for their substitute family.

The "Making Biscuits" Origin: Dr. Karyn explains that kneading originates from suckling behaviors in kittenhood; while grown cats no longer need to nurse, they carry the motion into adulthood because it triggers a cozy, endorphin-filled state of comfort and security.

Arousal and Humping Habits: The episode explores how kneading can sometimes lead to unexpected sexual arousal or humping in cats, noting that while humping is typically associated with dog dominance, cats display it purely as a cozy or quirky behavior rather than a social hierarchy tool.

Misinterpreting Body Language: Dr. Karyn clarifies that cat facial expressions and body language require full context; wide pupils can mean fight-or-flight adrenaline or catnip excitement, while a swishing tail can signal playfulness or an impending scratch.

Effective Boundaries Over Punishment: The hosts highlight why yelling, spray bottles, or double-sided tape fail to stop bad behavior, sharing Dr. Karyn's top tip of using a brief, clear "hiss" to instantly speak their language and set boundaries without causing distress.

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. #8162. Are You Gonna Finish That? Why Some Dogs Always Leave Something In the Bowl

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Most dogs don't need much encouragement to finish a bowl of food, which makes it especially curious when one or two pieces of kibble are consistently left behind. It can happen meal after meal, with the same tiny piece sitting untouched at the bottom of the bowl.

There may not be one definitive reason for the habit. Instead, several explanations could account for why a dog decides that one last piece isn't worth eating, from instincts inherited from wild ancestors to simple anatomy.

One explanation goes back to the way dogs' wild ancestors had to deal with food. Unlike domestic dogs with meals that follow a predictable schedule, wild canines could never assume when, or even if, their next meal was coming.

Holding something back after eating could have provided a small reserve if the next opportunity to find food didn't go as planned. A dog leaving a single piece of kibble behind may be displaying a faint version of that old instinct, even though there is no real need to save food when another meal is readily available.

Similar behavior can be seen when dogs stash food somewhere or bury it in the yard. Wild canines would hide food after a successful hunt and return to it during leaner periods. That instinct has carried over to domestic dogs, though the original reason for it is no longer relevant.

Another possibility is that some dogs simply don't like the idea of an empty bowl.

A dog may have unconsciously associated a full bowl with having food available and, therefore, security. Leaving one piece behind means the bowl is never completely empty, avoiding that association with an empty food source.

The bowl itself could also play a role. Dogs eating from stainless steel bowls can sometimes see their reflection in the metal, which for some, may be unsettling enough that they don't want to put their face right down to the bottom of the bowl.

In that case, leaving one piece behind could have nothing to do with the food itself. The remaining kibble may simply make the bottom of the bowl, and the reflection in it, less noticeable.

The simplest explanation may also be the most obvious. A dog might leave one piece of kibble behind because it has had enough to eat.

Many dogs can regulate how much they eat and stop once they are satisfied, even when there is still a small amount of food left. If this seems to be happening, offering a slightly smaller portion at the next meal can provide an easy test.

If the bowl is consistently emptied after the portion has been reduced, the original serving size may simply have been more than the dog needed.

A vet can also help determine the appropriate amount of food based on a dog's size, age, and activity level.

There is another explanation that has nothing to do with instinct or appetite. It could simply be difficult for the dog to see the final piece.

Many dogs have a visual blind spot directly beneath their nose and snout. That means a small piece of kibble sitting at the bottom of a bowl can end up in a surprisingly awkward position.

The dog may not be deliberately refusing to eat it at all. The kibble could simply be sitting somewhere that is difficult to see.

That makes the behavior look much more deliberate than it really is. From the dog's perspective, the final piece may effectively be invisible.

One piece of kibble left in the bowl at the end of a meal is generally not something to worry about. If a dog is otherwise eating normally, the habit is likely to be one of those harmless quirks that can have a surprisingly simple explanation.

The situation is different if the amount of food being left behind gradually increases. A growing loss of appetite can sometimes point to an underlying health issue, particularly when it represents a noticeable change from the dog's usual eating habits.

Any significant change in eating habits that continues for more than a day or two is worth mentioning to a vet.

For dogs that consistently leave exactly one piece behind, though, there may be nothing mysterious or concerning happening at all. It could be an old instinct, an aversion to an empty bowl, a sign that the dog is satisfied, or simply a tiny piece of kibble hiding in a visual blind spot.

#8160. 6 Tips For Getting Through The Holidays When You’re A Mom With ADHD

Strategies for ditching the burnout, surviving the chaos, and rediscovering holiday magic.

Kids losing sleep during the holidays basically a rite of passage. But for moms with ADHD? By that point, the holiday sleep deprivation started weeks ago.

Here’s how mom-of-two Alba C. puts it: “[During the holidays] my mind races to the point that it can take me hours to fall asleep, or fall back asleep. I’ll have thoughts like, ‘Did I buy enough presents?,’ and ‘I have so many presents to wrap!’ Those thoughts start piling up, and that can put me in a moody state where I get irritated very easily.”

Nobody wants to be the holiday Grinch. But when you toss executive dysfunction into the mix with social obligations, family drama, and midnight present-wrapping marathons, the holidays become a brutal obstacle course for moms with ADHD.

“Mothers are often responsible for much of the invisible labor associated with the holidays, from coordinating family schedules, to purchasing and wrapping gifts, moving the Elf on a Shelf, making the ‘holiday magic,’ and keeping a pulse on everyone’s logistical and emotional needs,” explains neuropsychologist Dr. Jessica McCarthy. “For women with ADHD, these responsibilities can become especially overwhelming.”

So moms with ADHD, hear this: You aren’t failing at the holidays — they’re just intense. We talked to experts — and some moms who’ve been through it — to find out how to ditch the burnout, survive the chaos, and rediscover holiday magic this season. Here are some ways to cope.

The holidays amplify struggles with executive dysfunction like forgetfulness, task avoidance, or missing details, explains Dr. Ifeanyi M. Olele, a board-certified psychiatrist with Genesis Psychiatric Solutions. To ease holiday stress, he recommends delegating responsibilities to other family members and asking for help wherever possible.

“Moms shouldn't feel that they have to do everything themselves. If you have a spouse or partner, communicate and divide responsibilities. If there are teenagers or adult children in the house, ask them to help with some of the holiday preparations,” he says.

Holiday parties are where Jacquelyn D.’s ADHD symptoms — including sound sensitivity and social self-consciousness — feel the most intense. To avoid spoiling the party, the 47-year-old mom of two always comes prepared with an escape plan.

“I take a break when I need to, and don't feel bad taking a few minutes to regulate myself,” she explains. “I have some social masking techniques as well, like keeping conversations short and directed outward, and using checking on the kids as a reason to step away and get some fresh air.”

During the merriest season, many moms stay up late wrapping gifts, organizing events, or completing tasks they couldn’t get to during the day. Since sleep deprivation magnifies difficulties women with ADHD are already working hard to manage — like attention, working memory, impulse control, and emotional regulation — Dr. McCarthy advises that sometimes the most productive thing a mom can do is leave something unfinished, and go to bed.

“My advice is to treat sleep as a priority rather than something that happens after everything else is finished,” says McCarthy. “Set realistic cutoff times for holiday tasks, maintain consistent sleep routines when possible, and resist the pressure to sacrifice rest to meet unrealistic expectations.”

One of the biggest mistakes busy moms make during the holiday season is assuming that because there’s technically room on the calendar for another activity, they have the emotional capacity for it, explains Kristen Carder, an ADHD coach and author of You're Not in Trouble: The ADHD Guide to Building Healthy, Connected Relationships.

“If you know that an afternoon with extended family is going to be emotionally taxing, don't schedule another demanding activity immediately afterward. Build in downtime, protect your routines when possible, and pay attention to early signs of dysregulation.”

Amy H., an author and mother of eight, keeps her own ADHD symptoms in check by planning ahead. Her advice? Start your preparations early. Like, early, early.

“Start earlier than feels reasonable,” Amy recommends. “ If the prep is done early, December gets to be about the good stuff instead of the panic. Your future self will thank you — and so will everyone who has to live with that future self.”

While social media scrolls portrays picture-perfect holiday decor and flawless family photos, Emily M., a mom of five, reminds us that real life is rarely as immaculate as it appears through tiny screens — especially for moms with ADHD.

“When I feel myself starting to spiral and feel like I’m not enough, I look at my husband, my kids, and my friends, and I remind myself that I’m worthy even when I’m not perfect. Some days I have to come back to that over and over again, and that’s okay,” she says. “That is the practice.”

Learn more about how to handle your ADHD symptoms at https://www.reframeadhd.com/

#8158. Thor: The Golden Retriever Who Changed My Life

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

On July 5, 2025, I said goodbye to my best friend. His name was Thor.

It's strange how a year can pass so quickly and yet still leave you feeling like a part of your heart is frozen in time. There are moments when I still expect to hear his paws on the floor behind me or feel him brush against my leg as I make coffee in the morning. Sometimes I catch myself looking toward the front door, half expecting him to come trotting inside with his favorite ball in his mouth.

People say time heals all wounds. I don't think that's true.

Thor came into my life as a fluffy Golden Retriever puppy, full of curiosity and joy. Like most Golden Retrievers, he loved everyone. He had an uncanny ability to make strangers smile. We'd walk through town or down the beach, and people couldn't help but stop to tell me how beautiful he was. They'd ask if they could pet him, and Thor never met a person he didn't think was a friend.

We lived just across the street from the dog beach in Ormond Beach, Florida, and he knew exactly where we were going every time we picked up his leash. He would practically lead me there, tail wagging the entire way.

He wasn't much of a swimmer, but he loved to wade into the surf just enough to cool his paws before racing back onto the sand. More than anything, he loved his tennis ball. It didn't matter where we were or what else was happeningâif he had his ball, life was good.

Looking back now, those ordinary days became the moments I cherish most.

Then, one morning, our lives changed forever.

I had worked for a neurologist for years. If anyone should have been prepared for something like that, I thought it would have been me, but nothing prepares you for watching it happen to someone you love.

From that day forward, epilepsy became part of our daily lives.

Our world revolved around medications, specialists, emergency hospitals, blood work, and carefully planned routines. Every dosage or missed meal mattered. Every subtle change in his behavior made me wonder if another seizure was coming.

I learned to recognize things most people would never noticeâa certain look in his eyes, a slight change in how he walked, moments when he seemed just a little different.

Hope became measured in days without a seizure.

Then another seizure would come, and we'd start over.

Most people saw the happy Golden Retriever. They saw the dog running down the beach, wagging his tail, carrying his ball. They didn't see the nights spent sleeping lightly because I was afraid I wouldn't hear him if he seized. They didn't see the medication schedules taped around my life or the emergency plans rehearsed in my head over and over again.

One morning stands out more than any other.

Thor wasn't a cuddler. As much as I wished he were, he usually preferred to sleep nearby rather than pressed against me. But that morning, he climbed into bed and lay back-to-back with me.

I woke up to him having a seizure beside me and rushed him to the emergency hospital.

I didn't know then that it was the beginning of the hardest chapter of our journey.

Epilepsy is cruel because it gives you hope just often enough that you believe tomorrow might be different.

We fought with everything we had for months, celebrating every seizure-free stretch, no matter how short, because when you love a dog with epilepsy, you learn to celebrate the smallest victories.

Despite everything he was carrying, Thor never stopped being Thor.

He still greeted people with excitement, still insisted on bringing me his ball.

He still looked at me with complete trust, as if I could fix anything.

That trust was both the greatest gift and the greatest responsibility I've ever known. As the months passed, one question kept finding its way into my thoughts:

What if something happened when I wasn't there?

What if he had a seizure while another family member was watching him?

His collar carried my phone number. His microchip could identify himâbut only if someone thought to take him to a veterinary clinic or shelter to have it scanned.

Thor couldnât tell a stranger that he had epilepsy. He couldnât explain which medications he took or where to find them, or which neurologist knew his case.

After months of fighting with incredible strength, Thor lost his battle with epilepsy.

Suddenly, my life was divided into 'before' and 'after.'

His toys were exactly where he'd left them.

It's realizing that the routines you built your life around disappeared overnight.

People asked me if I would get another dog, but what they didn't understand is that another dog could never replace Thor. Love doesn't work that way.

As the weeks turned into months, I found myself returning to the thoughts that had haunted me throughout Thor's illness. Some things are beyond our control, but maybe there was a way to make sure another family wouldn't have to worry that critical information would be unavailable during an emergency.

I wasnât looking to start a business or be known for inventing something. But grief has a remarkable way of asking you one impossible question:

For me, the answer became honoring the dog who had given me so much.

Everything I've built over the past year in creating Bark-ID: The Worldâs Smartest Dog Tag has been my way of making sure Thor's life continues to matter.

His legacy isn't a product; itâs the love that inspired it.

If you've ever loved a dog, you understand that they leave paw prints on more than your floors.

They leave them on your routines. Your memories. Your heart.

Thor taught me patience, resilience, and he taught me how fiercely we can love another living creature.

And in losing him, he taught me that grief and gratitude can exist together.

I still miss him every single day, and I probably always will. But when I think about Thor now, I try not to think about the day I lost him.

The tennis ball that never stayed clean for long and strangers who smiled because they met him.

The countless ordinary moments that, in hindsight, became extraordinary.

Some dogs make the world happier simply by being in it, and Thor was one of those dogs, and I was lucky enough to be his person.

If there's one thing I hope his story reminds people, it's that we never get enough time with the dogs we love.

So throw the ball one more time. Take the walk. Let them stop and sniff.

Take too many pictures. Sit with them a little longer.

Because one day, those ordinary moments become the memories you'll treasure most.

Thor gave me a lifetime of love in the months we had together, and if his story encourages even one person to cherish their dog a little more today, let that be his legacy.

Kimberly Sanders is a Golden Retriever enthusiast, pet safety advocate, and founder of Bark-ID: The Worldâs Smartest Dog Tag. After losing her beloved Golden Retriever, Thor, to epilepsy in 2025, she turned her grief into a mission to help other pet families be better prepared for emergencies. She lives with her Golden Retrievers in Ormond Beach, Florida, where she spends most of her happiest days at the dog beach. âThe Golden Retriever Who Changed My Lifeâ is her first published personal story.

Picture the fun and spectacle of Comic-Con, the annual Pasadena event that celebrates comics, movies, television, gaming, celebrities, and cosplay. Now, imagine that, instead of Marvel, DC, Trekkies, or Star Wars, it's about cats. This is CatConâ¢.

âCatCon plays a huge role in the rescue community. Not only do they get a few hundred cats adopted at the event, but it also gives rescues a place to meet each other and share what they do with the general public. It's also great for rescues to connect with amazing pet brands in hopes of getting donations.

âWhen I was interviewed at CatCon 2018, they asked, âWhat is one thing I wanted to accomplish?â I said I want cat people to be as trending and âcoolâ as dog people. Five years later, I was interviewed again, and this time the question was: âHow do you feel that the hashtag CatDad is trending?â

âSo, now that it's cool to own cats, my next goal is to make it cool to give back and help less fortunate animals.â

The CatCon event program is packed with exhibits, shows, stalls, and celebrities. Here are some of the highlights:

Nostalgic Cat Art Show: This one-of-a-kind art exhibit will feature artists across the generational spectrum and showcase pieces that show how cats have been represented in visual culture throughout time. Youâll have the chance to meet a handful of these talented artists at the convention, including @BunnyDee, @NikitaChanArt, and Laura Keenados. The exhibit will be dedicated to the late Sid Krofft, the creator of shows such as HR PufnStuf and Land of the Lost, and will tap into feline nostalgia through the work of the amazing artists, as well as a collection of cat ephemera from the 1950s through the 2000s to view on display. All works are for sale, with a portion of proceeds going to help cats in need.

The Heroes of the Australian Firefighters: The world-famous Australian Firefighters are returning to CatCon. These heroes have raised over $3.5 million for various charities with their iconic calendar each year, and will be at CatCon to raise funds for cat charities and support on-site adoptions. Additionally, you can watch their panel, moderated by comedian and host of the podcast We're Here to Help, Gareth Reynolds, on Sunday, October 11th at 3pm.

Bob Baker Marionette Theater: Come see the countryâs most iconic nonprofit puppet theater as they take the stage at CatCon. On Saturday, October 10th at 4pm, wrap yourself up in strings and join the world-famous Bob Baker Marionettes for their mew-sical revue, especially brought to you by our captivating clowder in residenceâ¦ and perhaps a few mice, too!

Paw Promise Adoption Village sponsored by NexgardÂ® COMBO: Pasadena Humane is back for another year at CatCon giving folks the opportunity to rescue a cat in need of a home. Stop by the adoption village to meet your next feline friend and bring them into a loving home.

PrettyLitter Poops & Hoops: Returning to CatCon for the first time in 8 years, PrettyLitter is not holding back on their message: when it comes to cat litter, PrettyLitter is the real MV-Pee. Visitors are invited to shoot hoops with poops (poop-shaped stuffies) and take home an assortment of free cat toys to keep the games going at home. Other giveaways include a limited-edition tote bag, mini lint rollers, and exclusive offers for CatCon attendees.

Celebricat & Creator Meet-and-Greets: In addition to @NathanTheCatLady, youâll get the chance to rub shoulders with some of the internet's most famous celebri-cats and pet-centric creators, including @One_Eared_Uno, @CatNamedCalvin, @Lily_Rose_Adventures, @StevenRayMorris, @Dr.MattMcGlasson, and so many more. Plus, youâll get to meet some new talent, including @Gareth Reynolds, @VonFluffernutter, and @Donât Stop Meowing.

WHEN: Saturday, October 10th & Sunday, October 11th | 10:00 AM - 5:00 PM PST

WHERE: Pasadena Convention Center, 300 East Green St., Pasadena, CA 91101

#8156. The 10 hottest kids’ Halloween costumes of 2026, according to Google

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 20, 2026

Every October, parents become amateur anthropologists, scouring the internet for a Halloween costume that will satisfy one small, extremely opinionated client. (Or, more likely, researching a request for a character we’ve never heard of.)

Now, Google has put all that frantic searching into one place. Its new site, Frightgeist, tracks which costumes are top ranked in search, and the kids’ top ten for 2026 is a gloriously incoherent collection. We’ve got a country legend we’re still mourning, a Thriller-era King of Pop, a web-cartoon jester, and, with no explanation offered, a dumpling.

There’s no tidy theme to sum it up, and I’ve stopped trying. Here’s what you need to know about this year’s top costumes, along with advice for putting a look together.

It just makes sense that our dearly departed Saint of Tennessee comes in at No 1. And since Dolly sported so many iconic looks across a long parade of eras, you have the opportunity to seem like you’re presenting your child with options even when there’s a solid chance this was your idea, not theirs. The only must is a blonde wig that defies gravity. A stuffed bra is optional but encouraged–Dolly would have wanted it that way.

Makes sense she’s spiking, since she’s leading this year’s CMA nominations with nine nods and “Choosin’ Texas” made her the only woman to top the Hot 100, Hot Country Songs, and Country Airplay charts at once. That said, I’ll be honest. Unless said trick-or-treater is belting out “Choosin’ Texas,” this costume will be lost on me. But any excuse to pile on some rhinestones is a good one. (See above.)

The lone non-celebrity in the lineup and, I’d wager, the only costume on this list your kid actually chose for themselves. Chalk it up to the squishy dumpling toys, the brightly colored, bamboo-steamer-packaged squishies that have been dominating TikTok and every kid’s pocket this year. On the plus side, the costume is cozy, warm, and fully nap-compatible. No notes.

Between her two World Cup performances last summer and the early-2000s revival in full swing, she was overdue. I recently combed the attic for my old low-rise jeans, the ones with the half-inch zipper, because my teenage daughter asked for them in earnest. The horror.

Pokémon turns 30 this year, which makes it officially old enough to have trained a generation of parents before becoming their kids’ obsession. Give them a backwards red cap, tuck a Pikachu they already own under one arm, and you’ve got the cheapest, most comfortable costume on the list. Additionally, they’ll be recognizable to every other kid on the block which, for better or worse, is more than I can say for the country singers above.

The show hit its 20th anniversary this year, which means the early-aughts kids who wore out the DVDs are now the ones doing the costume shopping. And if you need another reason to love the pick, Miley is Dolly’s goddaughter, which makes number one and number six a true family affair.

Worth noting that the lone superhero to crack this entire top ten is a woman who also drums in a punk rock band. That’s the kind of role model I can get behind. Spider-Man? Old news. And there’s no new movie to credit here, which means the kids are picking her on pure merit.

Specifically the Thriller era, so we’re talking red leather jacket and at least a loose attempt at the choreography. If your kid can pull off the zombie shoulder roll, they’ll absolutely crush this one. Credit the Antoine Fuqua biopic, “Michael,” that hit theaters last spring and put the moonwalk back in heavy rotation.

Admittedly, I had to look this one up. Turns out, she’s a jester trapped in a digital circus having a slow-motion existential crisis, which tells you this is for the tween and up set–not the toddlers. If your kid is asking for it, they’re too old for the cute stuff and whether you knew it or not, you’re officially in a new stage of parenting. The hat is non-negotiable, though.

Baby Yoda by any other name, and still the single most efficient way to make a small child look even smaller and more adorable. The ears make it truly irresistible and though your stroller may not float, it can still be part of the costume.

And there you have it. Ten costumes, roughly four decades, and one dumpling. Whoever your child opts into being this year, may the wig defy gravity and the candy be plentiful.

So while the Instagram-worthy six-cheese macaronis and truffled mashed potatoes sure look tasty, how many of us can really spend that much to make one side? If you’re stressed about Thanksgiving costs this year, here are some of the best Thanksgiving meal deals of 2026 to help you stay on (or under!) budget and still get to enjoy feeding your family their Turkey Day favorites.

If you like the sound of spending $39 to feed 10 people, you need only swing through Aldi. Each year the grocery chain publishes a shopping list that helps customers maximize how many people they can feed for as little as possible, while still enjoying all their favorite seasonal dishes. This year’s list includes a 16-lb. whole turkey, stuffing ingredients, dinner rolls, and more.

Amazon announced a Thanksgiving meal deal you can have delivered right to your door, same-day, and you don’t have to be a Prime member to order. If you have Amazon Grocery in your city, you can get a full Thanksgiving meal for $25 now through Nov. 26 while supplies last. The meal includes:

The shipping giant is also running some seasonal specials (and Prime members do get extra discounts), like up to 40% off charcuterie board items and party snacks, and frozen turkey as low as $0.79 per pound.

This meal deal isn’t as easy on the budget, but it comes almost completely ready-made (you still have to roast the bird) and is steeply discounted compared to its usual price. Fresh grass seed can take longer to sprout than the bag suggests, especially as fall cools off. A slow start is usually normal, and a few simple changes can help it along...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall is when a lot of homeowners get around to overseeding cool-season lawns. You rake out the thin spots, spread the seed and set the sprinkler going. Two weeks later, plenty of those patches still look like bare dirt, and it's tempting to blame the seed.

Chances are, the seed is fine. Anyone who has spent time seeding a lawn knows some grasses are just slow, and a couple of the usual fall picks can take weeks to show anything. Fall is still a smart time to seed, though. The ground stays warm from summer while the air cools off, and the rain usually picks back up.

Grab the bag and check what's in it. A blend might mix ryegrass, fescue and bluegrass, and those don't keep the same schedule. Ryegrass can be up in about a week, while bluegrass may take a month, so a new blend looks spotty at first. And green doesn't mean done – new grass still needs several more weeks to root in.

The rest happens underground. Cool-season seed generally won't germinate until the soil is above about 50 degrees Fahrenheit, and colder ground can leave it sitting there until spring. Push a soil thermometer (like this one from the Urban Worm Store) in to see where yours is. The seed also has to stay damp and reach dirt, not just rest on dead thatch.

Any lawn that slows down and browns a little in July, then greens back up when the nights cool off, is a cool-season lawn. Bermuda, zoysia and bahiagrass are the opposite; those warm-season grasses do better seeded in late spring or early summer, after the soil has warmed up.

Across the upper Midwest and other northern areas, the ground cools early, so the window runs from mid-August to mid-September and has usually closed by October. Farther south, in places like Tennessee, there's room to seed into mid-October. Anything sown late has less time to get established before the first hard freeze.

Perennial ryegrass is what you want when a bare spot has to look green before winter – a worn strip by the mailbox, let's say, or the patch where the dog cuts across the yard. It's often up in 5 to 10 days. Sow it early in the fall window. One option is Pennington Fairway Supreme perennial ryegrass from Lowe's, which comes in a 50-pound bag with fertilizer mixed in. It's at its best in cool, moist weather and doesn't take drought well. In the South, it mostly gets sown over dormant Bermuda for winter color, not as a permanent lawn.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

If your USDA Planting Zone is somewhere between Kansas and the Carolinas, your lawn may well be tall fescue already. Bluegrass struggles in those hot summers, but fescue's deep roots carry it through dry spells. Seed usually comes up within a week or two. GreenView turf-type tall fescue seed, available on Amazon, comes in 7-pound bags. Fescue grows in clumps rather than spreading, though, so thin spots won't fill in by themselves and need reseeding in early to mid-fall.

Bluegrass asks for patience up front. It usually takes at least two weeks to sprout and can take closer to a month. Once it's up, it spreads by underground rhizomes into a thick, soft lawn that can fill worn spots back in. It does best where summers stay fairly cool. Get it down right at the start of your fall window. Home Depot stocks a 5.6-pound bag of Scotts Turf Builder Kentucky bluegrass mix.

Keen for your grass to get a move on? Look this way...

Get down and look closely at a patch that still hasn't come up. You'll often find the seed sitting on top of old thatch or dead leaves instead of on the soil. It dries out between waterings up there; indeed, its first root may never reach the soil. Before you seed, mow the grass you already have down to about 1 1/2 to 2 inches (4–5cm), rake out the loose debris, then scratch up the surface until you can see bare, crumbly soil.

On small areas, a stiff 16-tine steel bow rake like the one Walmart carries will break up a crusted surface. Once the seed is down, rake over it lightly to work it into the top 1/8 to 1/4 inch (3–6mm) of soil, or press it in with the back of the rake. Don't worry if some seed is still showing, since bluegrass actually sprouts better with a little light.

On a breezy afternoon, soil watered at breakfast can be pale and crusty by the evening. Seed that's begun to swell can dry out and fail. Short, light sprinkles once or twice a day, and one more on days like that, keep the top inch (2.5cm) damp, not muddy. Long soaks can float seed into low spots or waterlog the soil, and an overnight rain counts as a turn.

A pulsing impact head can knock seed loose, but an oscillating sprinkler lays water down in a soft sweep. With the Melnor XT turbo oscillating sprinkler from Amazon, you can narrow the spray so it stays on the seed, not the sidewalk. For days when nobody's home, the Orbit single-outlet hose faucet timer from Home Depot can run short cycles as often as once an hour. Once seedlings have roots, water less often but more deeply.

A thin layer of screened compost over the seed helps keep the surface from drying out so fast. That layer gives the seed some protection from heavy rain, too. Spread it no more than about 1/4 inch (6mm) deep. You should still be able to see a little seed and soil through it.

Thicker isn't better. Grass seed carries only a small store of energy, and seed buried too deep can use it up before the shoot reaches light —, and fine bluegrass seed may not sprout under a heavy layer at all.

If you don't have finished compost, a bag of Scotts Turf Builder lawn soil from Home Depot is made for overseeding and top dressing.

So how long should you wait? With ryegrass or tall fescue in soil that's stayed warm and damp, about three weeks is a fair wait. Before reseeding, scrape back a little soil and look. Swollen or split seed is still working, while seed that looks dry and unchanged probably dried out or never touched the soil. Old seed can be the culprit too, so check the packaging date.

Don't count on starter fertilizer to hurry any of this along. Seed carries its own food for germination, and starter fertilizer is there to feed seedlings once roots form – too much can burn tender new grass. If your fall window has closed, it's better to stop than to keep sowing into cold soil. Some people dormant seed instead, spreading it in late fall once the soil is too cold for sprouting but before the ground freezes. Otherwise, early next fall is the more reliable time to try again.

Slow grass seed usually just needs a few more weeks. Choose the right grass for your area, sow it while the soil is still warm, and keep it damp. That will do more than any quick fix. With some patience, those bare spots may be filled in by the time you mow next spring.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8153. The Resentment of Being the Parent Who Can Never Clock Out

Maybe it’s a lack of freedom, unequal responsibilities with a partner, or both, but you’re big mad.

You had a certain expectation for what new motherhood would look like: Friends and family stopping by, your partner playing peek-a-boo with the baby, and even yourself feeling calm, patient, and present when the baby cries.

Reality might look a bit different, though. You blink, and your partner heads back to work, reading a newly cracked novel on the commute. Your friend drops by with pastries, then jets off to a yoga class. Everyone’s gone but you and the baby.

You’re at home, wading through a pile of burp cloths and hoping the baby naps long enough for you to choke down a sandwich. If you’re feeling a little ragey about that, you’re not alone. In one 2022 cross-sectional survey, nearly a third of new moms reported feeling intense anger.

But who are you actually angry with, and are you even mad, or — let's be brutally honest for a second — just jealous of their freedom and spontaneity? What’s really going on is likely more complicated than that, but there are things you can do things about it besides screaming into a pillow.

Anger is often underrepresented in research on the postpartum period, and tends to fly under the radar when moms get screened for perinatal depressive and anxiety disorders, as it can occur without elevated depressive symptoms, says Christine Ou, Ph.D., lead author of the aforementioned survey, assistant professor at the University of Victoria in Canada, and founder of the school’s Parent-Child Lab. “So asking only about depression may miss mothers who are struggling [with anger],” she says.

In a 2018 review, which Ou co-authored, researchers found that several factors contributed to moms’ anger, including a feeling of powerlessness and a misalignment between expectations and reality.

But you can also feel angry simply because having a newborn is hard. Moms were often mad because “their needs were compromised, and they were exhausted or stressed,” says Ou, as to why many new moms reported feeling anger. That’s pretty par for the course during the newborn haze, but being stuck at home — especially without help or breaks — can intensify those emotions.

Babies can bring a lot of joy, but staying at home around the clock with one is no picnic. First, newborns operate on an unpredictable schedule and demand constant supervision, making it feel like a logistical nightmare to get out of the house. Compounding that, mothers have historically been cast as the ‘default parent,’ says Paige Bellenbaum, L.C.S.W., founding director of The Motherhood Center, a clinic in New York City that provides care for women with postpartum depression (PPD). In traditional families, they’re “the ones physically with the baby most of the day and night, carrying most of the mental and emotional load, and managing the logistics, often while preparing for their own return to work,” says Bellenbaum.

Even if parents split duties pretty evenly within their own orbit, external factors can still throw that balance off. Take the fragmented, inadequate, and deeply unequal parental leave in the US: Often the dad or non-birthing partner ends up returning to work first. When that happens, the parent who remains at home “may feel envy, anger, or a sense of abandonment,” says Bellenbaum. Being home day in and day out with a baby can be isolating, even if you do get help from family or well-meaning visitors, she adds.

It's not just one person returning to work that creates this isolation. Reliable childcare can cost as much as your monthly mortgage these days, which means many birthing parents may make the tough but economical decision to stay home with the baby. “Everyone else can come and go, while she remains responsible for the baby, with no real opportunity to step away,” says Ou.

You could argue that the parent who’s heading into the office doesn’t necessarily want to be away from their family nor view it as an “escape.” Nevertheless, they “get to step back into their former life, stopping for coffee on the way into work, using the bathroom when they need to, and feeling useful and connected to the outside world,” says Bellenbaum. Plus, heading back to work can restore elements of their pre-baby life they may have been missing, like adult conversation, structure, control, and a sense of mastery and accomplishment, she adds. Meanwhile, the mom at home takes a 30-second shower and sings Wheels on the Bus for the 40th time in a row.

It’s normal to feel a lot of emotions in the postpartum phase — joy, frustration, rage, loneliness, anxiety, sadness, gratitude, you name it, says Ou. But that mix can make it hard to figure out exactly what you’re feeling.

While postpartum anger can happen independent of PPD, the two are clearly linked. For instance, Ou’s survey found that anger and PPD can also occur at the same time; in fact, those who screened positive for depressive symptoms had almost four times the odds of reporting intense anger. (But the survey couldn’t establish which came first.)

It’s not surprising: Imagine telling people you’re feeling trapped in your house — and no one seems to care. “When the circumstances behind a mother’s anger don’t change, when she remains overwhelmed, unsupported, or unheard, she may start to feel helpless or hopeless, which could contribute to depression,” says Ou. Maybe your partner acknowledges the struggle but doesn’t actually change anything, or you don’t feel comfortable or safe expressing your anger. Both can contribute to the development of PPD.

You might feel guilty for feeling trapped in the first place. After all, aren’t moms supposed to want to soak up as much time as possible with their babies? And, in a country where parental leave isn’t guaranteed, isn’t it a privilege to be at home with your newborn? Despite these arguments being flawed — they’re ignorant of the realities of newborn needs and nonexistent help for moms — this narrative can put a lot of pressure on moms, or even make you feel like you’re not doing right by your child. “Guilt and shame about being angry can add to that distress, potentially contributing to or worsening depressive symptoms,” says Ou.

First, know that it’s normal to be angry or irritable—period. But if you notice yourself getting worked up, take stock of how often you get angry, and how mad you get. If anger is frequent, intense, difficult to manage, or affecting your relationships or everyday life, that warrants a discussion with your doctor, says Ou. As is “feeling scared by your anger, or that you have little control over your reactions,” she adds. Postpartum Support International offers a peer support group for postpartum anger and rage, which may be a potential resource.

A screening from your healthcare provider can also be helpful since it may factor in other symptoms like crying and sadness, changes in sleep or appetite, a lack of interest in the baby, a sense of hopelessness or helplessness, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, according to Bellenbaum. “When these are present along with the anger, PPD may be at play,” she says.

However, getting professional help is not a replacement for making changes in your home and routine, if needed, stresses Bellenbaum. These tactics can help.

Since anger often stems from a lack of equality, it helps to start by looking at the division of labor in a partnered relationship. “Who gets more opportunities to sleep?” says Ou. “Who can leave without making arrangements? Who notices what needs doing, and who is responsible for making sure it happens?” Assessing this together allows you both to see who’s shouldering more of the work. “When that load is shared more equitably, resentment tends to ease, and a sense of shared responsibility emerges,” says Bellenbaum.

If and when you identify the areas of inequality, the partner should take “more ownership of tasks, night shifts, and the mental planning, not just ‘helping’,” says Bellenbaum, who recommends a card-based system called Fair Play that helps partners rebalance household work and divide invisible mental labor (like remembering to schedule doctor appointments). “Instead of splitting every chore 50/50, each partner takes full ownership of specific responsibilities, divided in a way that both people feel is fair,” she says.

“Genuine off-duty time means someone else is fully responsible for the baby,” says Bellenbaum. In other words, mom’s not on standby. She’s not listening for cries or manning the monitor, and she’s also not checking her phone or expecting a call because her partner feels the baby “wants mommy,” she explains. That can be hard, especially if the mom is afraid to leave the baby or feels guilty about being away, but it’s a worthwhile exercise for everyone. Otherwise, it “can make it harder for her partner to learn to care for the baby on their own,” she says.

Non-partnered parents need breaks, too. “Friends and family can bring food, do laundry, or hold the baby for half an hour,” says Ou. Run errands alone one evening while the baby stays home with a loved one. “A grocery run might be a chore, but it can also mean getting out of the house, being alone, and deciding what happens next without having to respond to a baby and their needs,” she says.

If a new mom in your life is dealing with anger or isolation, there are ways you can support her. Instead of asking what she needs, be specific and offer choices, like "I can do some laundry for you or bring over food for you. Which would help more?” says Bellenbaum.

If going out with friends or on a date night feels like too much for the mom, that's okay. "Separating from the baby is hard, and it often takes small steps before big ones,” says Bellenbaum. In this case, offer to watch the baby while she goes for a walk, go grocery shopping with her while you push the stroller, or hold the baby at the salon while she gets a haircut.

The bottom line? Feeling angry because your world feels small right now doesn’t make you a bad mom. “You can love your baby and resent having so little freedom over your own time,” says Ou. “Both things can be true.” It just means you need more sleep, a conversation with other adults, or an hour or two out of the house, and having those needs met only makes you a better parent to your baby.

#8152. Pyometra: Signs, Causes, and Care (Vet Answer)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Your female dog is drinking more, panting, lethargic, and you know something just isnât right. Never ignore that feeling. You know your dog better than anyone else, and if you think something is wrong, it probably is. And if your dog hasnât been spayed, you could be seeing signs of pyometra: infection of the womb or uterus that can turn deadly if left untreated.

Any dog with a uterus can develop a uterine infection, and, although rare, even dogs that have had a laparoscopic or âkeyholeâ spay, where only the ovaries are removed, can be at risk of pyometra. So, what is pyometra? Read on to find out.

An infected uterus or womb, sometimes referred to in practice as a âpyoâ, is a relatively common condition affecting entire female dogs. It occurs most commonly in middle-aged to older dogs, but cases have been reported in dogs as young as 9 months.

In dogs, the uterus splits into two branches or âhornsâ that allow multiple fetuses to be carried on each side. Female dogs come into season or estrus around every six months once they reach sexual maturity. This is when she becomes fertile and receptive to mating. If she becomes pregnant, all being well, she will deliver a litter of puppies approximately 63 days later. Sometimes there can be a âphantomâ or âfalseâ pregnancy, also known as pseudopregnancy, where the fluctuating hormones surrounding estrus and mating prepare the dog for pregnancy, even when fertilization hasnât occurred.

Every time a dog goes through estrus, her cervix relaxes and opens, and the lining of the uterus thickens in preparation for mating and pregnancy. Ordinarily, the cervix helps prevent dirt, debris, and harmful bacteria from entering the uterus, so when the cervix is open, the risk of contamination and infection increases. If fluid and bacteria accumulate, infection can set in over the following 2-3 weeks, resulting in pyometra.

There are two types of pyometra: open and closed.

The more common and less dangerous of the two, an open pyometra occurs when there is infection in the uterus, but the cervix remains open. Dogs with an open pyometra are often diagnosed more easily because owners notice a foul-smelling discharge coming from the vulva, or that their dog becomes obsessed with licking her nether regions.

Because the pus can drain out of the uterus, an open pyometra tends to be less of a threat than one that is closed. However, an open pyometra can become closed, and vice versa.

A closed pyometra occurs when the cervix has shut, locking infection inside the body. It is a far more dangerous situation because the problem is not always immediately obvious, and, as the infection continues, pus fills and stretches the uterus. This can bring a risk of septicemia (infection of the bloodstream) and uterine rupture, both of which carry a high risk of mortality.

The signs of pyometra usually appear around 2-3 weeks after estrus. As mentioned above, dogs with an open pyometra may have a yellow, greenish, or brown discharge from the vulva which, if you get close enough to discover, smells pretty awful. However, dogs that are quite clean may lick up any discharge before you notice, so itâs important to be aware of the other signs of pyometra, which include:

With each season a dog experiences, her risk of uterine infection increases. At each estrus, the cervix opens, and the repeated thickening of the uterine wall reduces its ability to contract and expel fluid and contaminants. Dogs over 7 years old are typically at higher risk, but pyometra can affect even young dogs.

The most common bacteria involved in pyometra is Escherichia coli (E. coli), responsible for around 90% of cases, usually from fecal contamination.1 Obesity, recessed vulvas, chronic diarrhea, and thick coats that regularly become soiled increase the incidence of fecal contamination of the vagina and uterus, putting dogs at a much greater risk for pyometra.

Studies have also shown that diet can affect the growth of pathogenic E. coli and therefore influence pyometra risk.2

The use of synthetic hormones to prevent embryo implantation or induce abortion in the case of accidental mating, or to suppress or delay estrus, has also been found to increase the risk of pyometra.3

Your vet will diagnose pyometra based on a combination of the history, clinical signs, and examination. They will usually perform a brief abdominal ultrasound. Pyometra appears as fluid inside the uterine horns, visible on ultrasound as discrete black circles or tubes.

pyometra in dogs,ultrasound findings and diagnosis

They will also perform some bloodwork to check for signs of septicemia and assess kidney function, hydration status, and rule out any other underlying issues.

The fastest and most definitive treatment of pyometra is to perform an ovariohysterectomy â spay the dog.

The first step in treating pyometra is to start antibiotic therapy and intravenous fluids. Depending on the severity of the situation, your vet may recommend that your dog stay overnight on these treatments before proceeding with surgery, or they may want to go ahead right away.

Occasionally, mild cases of pyometra can be successfully managed using a combination of hormonal treatments and antibiotics. However, dogs that have had one episode of pyometra have a much higher chance of having another, which is why surgery is usually recommended. Once the ovaries and uterus have been removed, a dog can never get pyometra again.

The surgical removal of the ovaries and uterus will completely eliminate the risk of pyometra. Dogs that are spayed earlier in life also have a significantly lower risk of mammary cancer.

In the last decade, advice regarding the timing of spaying has changed, and most vets recommend waiting until after the first season to ensure she has reached sexual maturity. For small breeds, the first season might occur at around 6 months, while for large or giant breeds, the first season may not happen until they are at least 12-18 months old.

In a keyhole or laparoscopic spay, only the ovaries are removed (ovariectomy); the uterus is left behind. This has become a popular option due to the perceived reduction in pain, discomfort, and recovery time. However, when performed on young, healthy dogs, the most challenging part of a routine spay is trying to convince the patient to stay quiet and calm after surgery!

Theoretically, by removing the hormonal factor, ovariectomy should prevent pyometra. However, in the case of ovarian remnant syndrome, where fragments of ovarian tissue are left behind, uterine infection can occur.

Breeding from a dog that has (or has had) pyometra is not recommended. The circumstances that allow pyometra to form â open cervix, thickened uterine walls, contamination â can also make pregnancy riskier for the dog.

Additionally, pyometra can damage the uterine lining, reducing fertility and increasing pregnancy risks.

Before surgical spaying became common practice, allowing dogs to mate and have litters was likely seen as the best way to avoid pyometra. This is probably where the old wivesâ tale that âyou should let your dog have puppiesâ originated. These days, with millions of unwanted puppies in need of homes, and surgical sterilization being a relatively safe routine procedure, there is no longer any real justification behind the idea that dogs should have a litter.

If you think your dog might have a pyometra, do not delay treatment â the longer you wait, the worse things will get. If you are worried about costs, reach out to local charities or speak to your veterinarian â there may be payment plans or charitable funds available to help.

A dog is never too old to get a pyometra, so even if your dog is considered elderly, unless they have health conditions that make surgery or anesthesia too much of a risk, itâs far better to have them spayed when theyâre healthy rather than risk them getting a pyometra in old age.

Pyometra is a relatively common â and entirely preventable â disease in female dogs. Infection of the uterus can make your dog incredibly sick, and if left untreated, can even be fatal. Signs of pyometra usually appear 2-3 weeks after a season and include increased thirst & urination, lethargy, inappetence, fever, discomfort, and, in the case of an open pyometra, vaginal discharge.

If you suspect your dog may have pyometra, contact your vet immediately â do not delay.

If your dog hasnât been spayed, talk to your vet. Remember, prevention is always better than cure.
