November can feel like the end of things, but if you put these cottage garden and prairie favorites in the ground this month, you can enjoy beautiful early flowering displays

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November often feels like the end of the growing season in many backyards. Annual and perennial borders have likely died back for the year, and deciduous trees and shrubs stand have lost their leaves. Yet while the air is getting fresher, you can still work a little magic in your cooling soil. Because as it turns out, this month is a prime time for sowing some classic hardy flower seeds.

Many pretty cottage garden favorites, native prairie wildflowers, and pollinator staples actually need a winter chill to thrive. In nature, wild flower seeds drop from seed heads in late fall, settle into the cool earth, and take part in a natural winter cycle known as cold stratification. Exposure to freezing and thawing breaks down the tough seed jackets of key annual and perennial flower types, prompting the embryo to awaken as soon as spring conditions become favorable.

Sowing these flower seeds in November gives them a big head start. Seeds planted now establish strong roots. This means healthier conditions in spring, with sturdier stems, superior drought resistance, and prolific displays that can bloom a month ahead of spring-sown counterparts. By taking advantage of these planting conditions now, you lay the groundwork for an effortless explosion of color next season.

Keep in mind your USDA hardiness zone, your local climate, and weather conditions before deciding on specific plants and a sowing strategy. Successfully sowing flowers in November comes down to matching your plant variety with the right late-season sowing technique. There are a few primary approaches you can try with these flowers, depending on your region and weather. In mild winter climates (zones 7-10), you can try fall sowing (directly outdoors) so seeds germinate before winter, overwintering as frost-hardy rosettes that bloom in April.

In colder northern climates (zones 3-6), there is also dormant sowing. This is where seeds are sown directly into garden beds once the ground is cold enough to prevent immediate germination. Soil temperatures consistently below 45°F (7°C) allow seeds to sit dormant until early spring. For native perennial flowers or regions with erratic thaws, the best approach is winter sowing. This means sowing in outdoor containers and placing in a protected area, like an unheated cold frame, to shield seeds from rodents and heavy downpours while still providing natural chilling.

Before sowing, ground preparation is vital. Check soil temperatures before you start sowing with a good soil probe. Budget-friendly Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter, available from Amazon gives a reliable read on current moisture and temperature levels. Then clear away thick, suffocating leaves, remove weeds, and lightly rake the top inch (2.5cm) of soil into a fine, crumbly tilth. Pay attention to seed packet instructions regarding sowing depth, as this can have a big effect on germination. Some larger seeds may require burying an inch deep, while fine wildflower seeds need light to germinate and need to be surface-sown with just a whisper of sand or light compost.

Water the seedbed gently with a fine mist to settle the soil without dislodging the seeds, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Mark each row clearly with durable weatherproof tags, and cover vulnerable beds with breathable floating row covers, mesh, or clean straw to deter birds. Whether sowing directly in the soil or indoors, these gorgeous flowering picks are all good to go this month…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Sweet peas (Lathyrus odoratus) are the quintessential cottage border bloomers. They are celebrated for their intoxicating scents and ruffled hues, which can cascade across trellises from late spring through early summer. These vintage darlings thrive in cool weather. Sowing sweet peas in November allows the seeds to develop deep roots while temperatures are low. This leads to more prolific flowering displays, with longer, sturdier stems. If you fancy a floriferous blend of lavender, violet and maroon blooms, buy Sweet Pea Burgundy Mix Sweet Peas from Eden Brothers.

In milder climates (zones 7-10), you can direct-sow sweet peas along sunny, well-draining trellises. In colder zones (3–6), sow seeds indoors in deep root-trainer tubes or biodegradable pots, and keep in an unheated greenhouse, sheltered porch, or cold frame. Sweet pea seeds have hard shells, so nick these with a nail file (or soak in room-temperature water for 12 hours prior to planting) to speed up moisture absorption. Plant seeds an inch (2.5cm) deep in rich, organic-rich soil, and pinch the central tips once seedlings develop 3 sets of true leaves for bushier plants.

With their luminous, silky petals, California poppies (Eschscholzia californica) bring effortless cheer to borders, gravel gardens, and sunny slopes. These tough-as-nails wildflowers thrive in sandy or rocky soils, making them ideal for challenging areas where other ornamentals struggle. However, because they have brittle taproots that resent disturbance, they should be direct-sown where they are intended to bloom. Buy Marde Ross & Co California Dreaming California Poppy Seed Mix from Amazon for a near-neon flush of tangerine, melon and magenta blooms.

You can sow seeds now in regions with milder winters (zones 7-10). In these areas, fall rains will trigger late-fall germination, establishing fern-like foliage that bursts into bloom by April. To sow California poppies, scatter them over the soil in an area that drains well and has full sun. Lightly rake the seeds into the soil so they are barely covered, as poppy seeds require light to germinate. If you have colder or very wet winters, it’s best to wait until spring to sow these seeds.

Offering the vertical grandeur of delphiniums without the fussy growing requirements, annual larkspur (Consolida ajacis) produces epic flowering spires in shades of royal purple, lavender, rose, and white. This cottage garden classic is a cool-season annual that is ideal for November sowing. In fact, waiting until spring often results in poor, erratic germination, as seeds need a period of stratification to break dormancy. For a shock of saturated purple-blue spires, buy QIS Dark Blue Larkspur Seeds from Eden Brothers.

Direct-sow in a rich, sunny, well-drained bed. Cover very lightly with an eighth of an inch of fine compost or sand. Winter rain and freezing nights should satisfy the seed's chilling requirements, triggering early emergence in spring. Fall-sown larkspur often blooms up to a month earlier than spring-sown seeds, beating the summer heatwaves that can cause these cool-season annuals to fade. If your winters are very cold, try winter sowing in containers.

Also known as cornflowers, bachelor’s buttons (Centaurea cyanus) are cherished vintage annuals. Their blue ruffled blooms erupt in late spring and summer to create a dazzling contrast with cottage perennials and ornamental grasses (though you can get varieties in shades of pink, purple and white). Also cold tolerant, they are naturally adapted to late-season sowing. Sowing in November helps it to grow strong roots that can withstand hotter summer days far longer than spring-started plants.

Sow in a bright, sunny border with average to poor, well-draining garden soil. Sow at roughly a quarter-inch (0.6cm) deep, firming the soil gently. For the best results, ensure the area with seeds doesn’t erode or get waterlogged over winter. In mild winter regions, seeds will sprout within a few weeks; in northern climates, they will sleep until early March, flowering from late spring all the way to July. Buy SVI Store’s Bachelor Button Mix Seeds from Amazon for a lively mixture of floral heirloom tones.

Black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia hirta) are prairie icons that light up borders from early summer well into fall. With their sunny yellow petals and chocolate-brown cones, these pollinator-friendly perennials and biennials are often bought as transplants. Hardy in zones 3-9, they are super tough. However, their seeds possess dormancy inhibitors that can lead to patchy germination in spring soil. November sowing solves this problem naturally. By scattering now, you allow the rhythm of winter rains, snow cover, and sub-freezing nights to break dormancy smoothly.

Clear away heavy mulch and scatter seeds thinly over the surface. They require light to germinate, so press them into the soil without burying them. While fall-sown plants spend their first spring developing roots and crowns, many will reward you with late-summer blooms in the first year. Buy Harris Seeds’ Rudbeckia Goldilocks Seeds from Walmart for a ruffled twist on the dazzling classic. Just keep in mind that many varieties benefit from cold exposure, but not all, so know your type before you sow.

With their delicate, two-toned blooms and graceful spurs, columbines (Aquilegia spp.) bring woodland romance and grace to borders, cottage beds, and rockeries. Native across North America and Europe, Aquilegia species are hardy down to zone 3. Seeds require 4-6 weeks of cold, damp stratification, making November sowing the easiest, most reliable way to propagate them. Buy Blue Star Columbine Seeds from Eden Brothers for a vivid bounty of iconic violet-blue and white blooms.

Select a site that receives gentle morning sun and dappled afternoon shade with rich, well-draining soil. Some varieties require sunlight to trigger germination, so check the seed packet. Scatter seeds onto the soil surface and press lightly into the earth, but don’t cover with soil. If you live in an area with winter gales or heavy rains, you can winter-sow columbines into ventilated plastic jugs in a shaded outdoor spot. Seedlings will emerge in spring, providing pretty nectar for returning hummingbirds.

Purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) is a perennial staple in the sustainable, pollinator-friendly yard. Featuring daisy-like blooms and spiky cones, echinacea feeds native bees and butterflies in summer, while offering seed cones for goldfinches in fall. Seeds have evolved to weather harsh winters before germinating, making November a great time for sowing. Buy Purple Coneflower Heirloom Seeds by the Kviter Store from Amazon for a generous supply of purple drifts.

Broadcast seeds in a sunny spot with well-drained, average soil. Echinacea seeds need minimal light filtering through to sprout, so rake them into the earth no more than an eighth of an inch deep, firming the soil. Winter's freeze-thaw cycles settle the seeds, softening their husks so that strong roots push down early in spring. While coneflowers focus heavily on root establishment in the first year, November-sown echinacea tend to bloom reliably by the second season.

Your gardening season doesn’t have to be over in November. Taking a little time this month to start off some pretty cottage garden and pollinator favorites is such a rewarding investment in future backyard bloomers. By partnering with winter’s cold cycles rather than fighting them, you give these key annuals and perennials a real head start on early spring beauty. Using seeds is also a cost-effective way to get more flowers. If some don’t germinate or establish, you haven’t lost a lot of money. So grab a few seed packets, prep your beds, and get planting. It’s time to start looking forward to an effortless run of blooms well ahead of the neighbors.

#8101. Who’s a Scaredy Cat? Keeping Cats Safe This Halloween

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Halloween can be an exciting night for families, but all that activity can leave cats feeling unsettled. Strange costumes, unfamiliar visitors, and a doorbell that rings non-stop can be overwhelming, even for cats that usually enjoy meeting new people.

The biggest concern is that a frightened cat may try to escape, while decorations, candy, and other seasonal hazards can create additional risks. A few simple changes around the home can help keep cats safe while everyone else enjoys the festivities.

Even households that don't celebrate Halloween can be affected by the extra noise and activity around the neighborhood. Excited children, unfamiliar costumes, barking dogs, loud music, and parties can create an unusually stressful environment for cats.

A frightened cat may bolt when strangers approach the house, and there's no guarantee it will head somewhere safe. A cat that escapes could become lost or run into traffic while trying to get away.

Keeping cats indoors is therefore one of the most important Halloween precautions. Even cats that normally spend time outside should remain indoors, with windows and doors securely closed.

With trick-or-treaters arriving throughout the evening, the front door may open far more often than usual. Every time it does, there's another opportunity for a cat to slip outside unnoticed.

Keeping a cat in a separate room when visitors arrive can reduce the risk, particularly if several people are coming and going. Making sure your cat is microchipped and that the registration details are up to date also improves the chances of being reunited if they do escape.

The simplest approach is to keep your cat away from the entrance for the entire evening rather than relying on everyone to remember to watch out for it.

Halloween decorations can look appealing to curious cats, but anything within reach may become a potential plaything. Curious cats can chew decorations or swallow small pieces, so it's best to avoid edible decorations and keep other items out of reach.

Carved pumpkins lit with real candles need particular care. A cat could knock one over, risking burns or even starting a fire.

Battery-operated candles offer a safer alternative. Another option is to place pumpkins outside or in a window where the cat can't reach them.

It can be tempting to dress a cat up for Halloween, especially when everyone else in the household is wearing a costume. However, many cats find clothing uncomfortable or frightening, and restrictive outfits can cause unnecessary stress.

Some cats need to wear garments for medical reasons, such as a surgical vest to protect stitches after an operation. Halloween costumes are different because they generally serve no practical purpose for the cat.

Pay attention to how a cat responds to clothing and accessories. If they seem uncomfortable or distressed, leave the costume off. There are plenty of ways to include a cat in the celebration without dressing them up.

Candy presents several potential hazards for cats. Chocolate and certain other sweets contain ingredients that can be toxic to pets, while wrappers can become choking hazards if swallowed. Even sweets that aren't directly poisonous aren't suitable cat treats, and excess sugar can contribute to health problems.

Crinkly plastic wrappers can be particularly tempting because they appeal to a cat's instinct to chase and play with small objects. Itâs all fun and games when a cat bats them around, but they could end up swallowing them.

Keep Halloween treats in a closed container somewhere the cat can't access, and make sure children understand that sharing their candy with pets isn't safe. If a cat manages to eat candy, contact a vet promptly for advice.

Cats often cope with stress by hiding somewhere they feel safe. Providing a quiet room away from visitors and noise gives them the chance to retreat until the activity dies down.

A bedroom can work well, provided it has fresh water, a litter tray, and a favorite blanket or other familiar bedding. Guests should know that the room is off-limits so the cat isn't disturbed while resting.

Giving a cat this private space can be especially helpful during parties or evenings when the front door is opening repeatedly.

It's sensible to check on a cat throughout Halloween, particularly when the household is busy. These checks help confirm that the cat is comfortable and hasn't slipped out unnoticed.

However, checking in doesn't mean coaxing a frightened cat out of its hiding place. If they have chosen a quiet spot and appear settled, let them stay there.

The aim is to make sure the cat is safe without adding more attention or activity when it would rather be left alone.

Keeping a cat safe doesn't mean they have to be excluded from the evening entirely. Cats that dislike costumes can still feature in a Halloween photoshoot without wearing anything themselves. After all, theyâre already wearing the best outfit! Dressing as a character known for having a feline companion is another way to include a cat without making them uncomfortable.

A scary movie marathon can also be a relaxed way to spend the evening together. A soft, Halloween-themed blanket and a favorite treat might encourage a cat to settle on a lap, provided it enjoys that kind of attention.

Cat-friendly treats can be offered while the humans enjoy their own candy, and cats that like catnip may appreciate a Halloween-themed toy with a little dried catnip.

Halloween should be enjoyable for the whole household, but cats don't understand why the neighborhood suddenly becomes noisier or why strangers keep appearing at the door. Keeping them indoors, removing potential hazards, and providing somewhere quiet to retreat can make the night safer and more comfortable for everyone.

#8100. 13 Easy Holiday Mocktail Recipes For Entertaining Guests (Or Just Yourself)

Sometimes you just need a special bevvie.

I love a good drink — whether it’s a canned cocktail or a jam jargarita, sign me up. But even I sometimes fall back on a good old mocktail, whether I just can’t handle a red wine hangover tomorrow or because I’m hosting and there needs to be an NA option. These easy holiday mocktail recipes are perfect for those moments when you need to whip up a big batch of something festive to drink that’s safe for the whole family. Some are nonalcoholic versions of cocktails you know and love, while others are just fun, festive drinks to serve in place of something spiked.

Since they make nonalcoholic and boozy ginger beer, ginger beer-based recipes are some of the easiest to make into mocktails on the fly. All The Healthy Things’ bevvie is bubbly, fruity, and slightly herby — and it looks so stinking cute with “frosted” cranberries on top.

I love it when a mocktail recipe makes up for its lack of booze with an overabundance of fun in another form. In Averie Cooks’ recipe for caramel apple cider, it’s a homemade caramel sauce all around the rim — I’m in. You could totally use store-bought sauce to save time, but if you have to simmer the cider anyway, it might be fun to try.

If you’re making drinks for guests who don’t mind something super sweet (kids will lose it for this stuff), you’ve got to make Princess Pinky Girl’s Grinch punch. It’s a bright green blend of sherbet, green Hawaiian Punch, Sprite, and juice, so it will hurt many people’s teeth. But sweet-toothed friends, this one’s for you.

Holiday party snuck up on you and you’re in charge of drinks? Whip up this super easy holiday punch from Damn Delicious. All you have to do is mix together some ginger ale, pineapple juice, and cranberry juice, and load it up with some fresh fruits before serving.

Want a more decadent drink for a movie marathon at home? You have to try Princess Pinky Girl’s apple cider float recipe. It’s basically like a milkshake and apple cider had a baby and then dressed it up in warm, seasonal spices.

Think about how happy you’d be if you showed up at a holiday party and there was a self-serve vat of hot chocolate waiting for you. Well, be the change you wish to see in the world with Princess Pinky Girl’s Crockpot peppermint hot chocolate. While technically not a mocktail in that it’s not imitating a cocktail, a gussied-up take on hot chocolate still feels really festive and exciting to try.

This apple cider shrub mocktail from Budget Bytes is the drink if you like a not-so-sweet mocktail that tastes almost like it could be boozy. The drink has a few steps that’ll make you look like a professional bartender, but it’s easy enough that even a first-timer around a cocktail shaker can pull it off. Bonus points: They’re also incredibly cheap to make.

Dirty soda, as a drink category, got plenty of attention this year thanks to the cast of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives. So if you need a fun NA drink to serve your reality TV-loving friends, what could be better? Princess Pinky Girl’s recipe will teach you how to get the perfect balance of flavors if it’s your first time wading into dirty soda territory.

Haute & Healthy Living’s pomegranate sparkler looks like the perfect thing to swirl around in one hand while you make a cozy dinner. It still feels special — when else do most of us spring for pomegranate juice? — and has seasonal touches that give you all the festive feels of a cocktail.

Our Love Language Is Food’s spiced cider mocktail proves that as long as you have a fancy glass and a sugar-and-spice rim, you can make your beverage feel celebratory. These just look aggressively clink-able.

Want to make a big batch of punch for the party? Haute & Healthy Living’s recipe blends apple juice, orange concentrate, and cranberry cocktail, plus a few extra touches to bring it to life. It’s so easy to make, you can refill the bowl in a few minutes mid-party.

If you just can’t with all the sweet this and spiced that, Simply LaKita’s blackberry thyme mocktail is perfect for you. It’s simple, fizzy, and way less dessert-in-a-glass-inspired that many winter mocktails tend to be.

Which mocktails are you adding to your hosting repertoire this year?

#8098. 22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

Two registered dietitians on what to read before a packaged snack goes in the cart, and the brands they buy for their own kids.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 06, 2026

Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.

Labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something. The truth is, most of it is noise. The part that matters is on the nutrition label. For a run of dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy and pack as-is, we asked two registered dietitians who shop that aisle for a living what they actually look for.

Robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a new product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read. Here’s what they’re looking for, and the snacks they reach for without overthinking it.

Kaiden scans the label’s ingredients first. “That matters to me more than anything else,” she says. She wants simple, real-food ingredients and the least processed option available. There’s a practical reason to start there, notes Manaker. Ingredients appear in order by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.

The claims on the front get much less of their attention. “Made with real fruit” doesn’t tell you how much fruit is actually in there, says Kaiden, and “no artificial flavors” doesn’t automatically make something a nourishing snack. Even the regulated claims are narrower than they sound, explains Manaker. “Good source of fiber” means the product provides 10 to 19% of the daily value per serving. “Gluten free” matters for kids with celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity and does nothing nutritionally for anyone else.

The label lists added sugars and total sugars separately. Total sugars include the naturally occurring sugars in ingredients like fruit and milk, says Manaker. Added sugars are the ones put in during processing, and those are the numbers to take into consideration. The targets for added sugar are lower than most parents expect. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend no added sugars for children under 10, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises less than 25 grams, about 6 teaspoons, per day for kids 2 and older.

Kaiden also looks at where the sugar comes from. She passes on high-fructose corn syrup and would rather see a small amount of honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar. “Those are still added sugars, so the amount matters, but the source and processing matter to me, too,” she says. If cane sugar is on the list, she prefers it farther down.

Protein and fiber make a big difference in how satisfying a snack is. Kaiden balances a carbohydrate-rich food with protein and some healthy fat, like fruit with nuts, cheese or plain yogurt. “That combination helps slow digestion and supports steadier energy through the afternoon,” she says. For a substantial afternoon snack, she suggests around 5 to 10 grams of protein and at least 3 grams of fiber, depending on a child’s age, appetite and activity level. Those numbers can come from the snack as a whole. No single bar has to do everything.

Most U.S. children don’t get the recommended amount of fiber, says Manaker, so small additions help. Fruit, veggies, beans, whole-grain bread or crackers, and nuts or seeds where school rules allow are all easy lunchbox sources.

Hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils are an automatic no for Kaiden. Partially hydrogenated oils contain industrial trans fats, which are particularly harmful to heart health. High-fructose corn syrup, a highly processed sweetener that adds sugar without meaningful nutrition, is another pass.

Seed oils get a lot of negative press, but Kaiden’s position helps clear up confusion: When there’s a comparable option, she opts for extra virgin olive oil or avocado oil instead of seed oils because of the difference in processing. Many seed oils are extensively refined, and some are extracted using solvents such as hexane. “That processing is why I personally prefer other options,” she says, “not because all seed oils are harmful or because using hexane means unsafe amounts remain in the food.”

She’s also not rigid about it. Some Simple Mills crackers contain sunflower oil, and she still buys them for the almond-flour base. “I look at the whole product rather than letting one ingredient make the decision for me,” she says.

Unfamiliar names aren’t automatically a problem, either. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Tocopherols are forms of vitamin E that can help preserve freshness. “I care more about what an ingredient actually is than whether its name is easy to pronounce,” says Kaiden.

Read the ingredients even on brands you buy regularly, Kaiden cautions, because formulations change, and one good product doesn’t mean everything from that brand makes the cut.

To make shopping easier for you, we asked the nutritionists exactly what they’re tossing in their carts. Take notes!

Kaiden’s favorite snack doesn’t sound like a dietitian’s pick at all. “Potato chips!” she says, naming José Andrés Extra Virgin Olive Oil Potato Chips, made with potatoes, extra virgin olive oil and salt. “I want my kids to enjoy their food, and a simple-ingredient chip can absolutely fit into a balanced lunchbox. Add a sandwich and some fruit or vegetables, and you have a lunch that’s nourishing and enjoyable.” Potato chips? Say less.

#8097. “My Husband & I Just Had A Threesome With Another Woman” & 57 Other Anonymous Mom Confessions

The moms are really going there this week.

There’s tired... and then there’s whatever moms are feeling right now. It’s not the kind of tired that you can knock out with a quick nap (as if we even have time for one, pssh). It’s the type of tired where you’ve been running on empty so long, you don’t even remember what not being tired feels like. And this week’s confessions are chock full of women at exactly that point.

There’s a mom who just wants a single good night’s sleep, a mom who’s beyond exhausted by her mother-in-law’s boundary-pushing, a mom who’s so angry all the time she needs something to change and doesn’t know what. There’s a physician mom who’s bordering on burnout, and a teacher mom who literally got spat on by a student. Some moms are at an impasse with their kids (those teen years are tricky!).

Underneath a lot of it is the same frustration: not enough help. No partner who sees their struggles and jumps in. No village swinging by to check in. In fact, one mom says she’s jealous of anyone who has help they didn’t have to pay for.

You’ll find bits of good news tucked in here, too, like one mom who finally feels like she’s coming out on the other side of things. So no matter what you’ve got on your mind, you’ll likely find a relatable confession in the bunch. Here’s this week’s roundup.

Scary Mommy Confessions are a tried-and-true part of what makes our site so fun. If you want to anonymously confess, look for our weekly callouts on Instagram. And to browse past Confessions, take a look here.

I’m so jealous of people with grandparent help. Or any help that we didn’t pay for.

My parents never call. Tired of being the only one that ever reaches out. So I’m done.

I just want one good night’s sleep. I’m so tired of being tired.

It weirds me out that my MIL calls my 3-year-old daughter her best friend.

So not excited for the holidays this year. So expensive! Can it be January already?

Finally back in the dating world after a 20-year marriage. I just want to keep having sex!

I think I’m ruining my kids because I can’t self-regulate, and I then yell when frustrated.

Mid-30s desire for a career change is reeeeeeal.

His depression and grumpy mood are slowly killing my love for him. We live on edge 24/7.

Why Cats Freeze in Harnesses: Because a cat's body relies heavily on sensory feedback from skin and nerves for orientation, placing clothes or a harness on them is like "blindfolding" their body, causing them to temporarily lose balance until they adapt.

Testing vs. Clinical Trials: The hosts differentiate between harmful animal testing and ethical clinical research. Modern veterinary trials often involve treating pet patients with naturally occurring conditions (like cancer or coronavirus), generating medical advancements that aid both humans and animals.

Trying to make compost from fallen leaves takes forever, right? Not if you know this gardeners’ trick to get it ready to use in your yard in time for spring.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Making free compost from fall leaves is such an easy win, and with these smart hacks you’ll have a nutritious mix ready to enrich your garden soil by spring. While creating traditional leaf mold compost can take up to two years, this quick and easy method speeds up decomposition to bring garden-ready compost in 4-5 months. What’s more, it’s mess-free!

Want to know the secret? Any compost pile relies on tiny organisms, way too small for us to see without a microscope, to break plant matter down. These microbes are responsible for around 80-90% of the chemical decomposition process when making compost, and this method simply creates the ideal conditions for the speediest members of this recycling workforce to flourish.

It’s cheap, too, as you’re going to make compost in a black trash bag. Heavy-duty contractor bags such as Brute Super Tuff Bags, available from Walmart, are best as they’re much stronger than those designed for residential use. Your reward will be a rich and crumbly, well-structured compost that will feed plants as well as help soil hold moisture. Spread it as a mulch onto perennial borders and around shrubs to lock moisture in and deliver nutrients to roots. Dig it into veggie beds to fuel healthy crops, or mix with coco coir to make your own potting mix. You can even steep a scoop in a bucket of water for a couple of days to make a compost tea that’ll help protect your plants from disease.

Ready? Part of the Weekend Wins series, making a quick compost from fall leaves is one of those easy garden jobs that brings a big reward. Here's what to do.

Not all leaves break down at the same speed, and many species have evolved strong defences against microbes. Oak, beech, sycamore, horse chestnut, holly, laurel and magnolia leaves are all high in a compound called lignin that acts as a protective armor against microbes. They’re also rich in tannins, a compound that effectively halts the digestive action of microbes, so they're slow to decompose.

Instead, use foliage that’s thin, flexible and soft to make compost from autumn leaves. Maple, ash, elderberry, willow and fruit tree foliage are all far lower in lignin and tannin so they’ll break down in a fraction of the time. It doesn't matter if a few high-lignin, high-tannin leaves get mixed in, but keep them to a minimum. And don't worry if you're not sure about tree identification: just avoid using thick, leathery or glossy leaves.

Cutting the leaves up into smaller sections also speeds up the process by increasing the surface area and exposing the less protected innards of the foliage for the microbial feasting. Shredding leaves before composting is the equivalent of chopping a log into kindling: you give the microbes plenty of vulnerable material that quickly gets the process going.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The chopped-up material won’t mat together like whole leaves do, and it'll absorb water rather than repelling it, both also speeding decomposition.

Shredding leaves is easy to do, even if you don’t have a leaf shredder. Simply run your lawnmower over the leaves multiple times or tip the foliage into an old trash can and shred with a string trimmer or weed whacker.

In any compost pile you need to mix carbon – the ‘browns’ – with nitrogen – the ‘greens’ – for microbes to work efficiently. And this applies when you make compost from fall leaves, too. Leaves are very high in carbon so, to get a good balance of browns and greens to keep those microbes happy, you need to add some nitrogen.

Grass clippings are super-high in nitrogen: use a lawnmower to shred leaves on your lawn and the job’s done for you. Coffee grounds are also nitrogen-rich so toss those in, and if you have access to free chicken manure, that works a treat, too. Aim for one part greens to three parts brown.

To kickstart the decomposition process, toss a shovelful or two of garden soil – or homemade compost if you have it – into the mix. This will be packed full of microbes that will immediately get to work.

Microbes work best in damp conditions so pour water over the leaf mix, unless of course it's recently rained and the leaves are already wet. Aim for moist not wet, as you don’t want the leaves sitting in water.

Making compost this way requires oxygen so when you tie the sack closed (using a zip tie is easiest) don’t squash all the air out of the sack first. So this air can be replaced, delivering a fresh supply of oxygen, use a sharp knife to punch air holes into the sack. Around 15 holes in a regular contractor sack is about right, and try to distribute them well around the sides and base of the sack.

Those microbes are going to generate plenty of heat as they get to work, and you can help retain that warmth by storing the bag in a sunny, sheltered spot so the black plastic absorbs lots of solar heat. Tucking the bag against a south-facing wall or shed-side is ideal as here it'll enjoy plenty of sunshine and be shielded from cold northerly winds.

When you make traditional leaf mold compost, you rely on the battalion of slow-working fungi among the microbial army to do the hard work. But in this accelerated composting method, you want to encourage the fast-working bacteria contingent to head up the recycling force. To do this, you need to regularly aerate the compost and add fresh oxygen, and the easiest way to do this is to give the bag a shake, flip it over or simply kick it along the ground every few days.

Do all these steps and your homemade compost will be ready to use in 4-5 months, right on time for when your garden wakes up in spring. You’ll know when it’s ready, even without opening the bag. While the microbes are busy breaking down the leaf mix, the contents will feel warmer to the touch; once they’re done, the temperature of the bag with match the ambient air temperature.

When you do open the bag, the compost should smell earthy, like a fresh forest floor. If you notice a slightly sour note, simply leave the sack open for a week or so to allow the compost to air.

Then you’re all ready to use your free compost to give your garden plants a nutritious boost for healthy growth, abundant blooms and bumper crops. Making a quick compost is one of the best ways to use fallen leaves in your garden so put this easy task on your list of garden jobs to do in fall.

Waterlogged soil is the prime reason potted plants fail in fall and winter, and this speedy solution couldn't be simpler.

This great-value gardening tool transforms lawns in fall, fast, if you want lush grass next year for next-to-no effort.

Plant fast-growing bulbs in your lawn and enjoy drifts of lavender-hued blooms in a few weeks.

Why your boomer parents keep defending instead of hearing you, and how to break the stalemate.

One of the most painful things about being an adult child is realizing that your parents may never become the people you keep hoping they will be. You can be 38, 48, or 58 years old, with a career, children, a mortgage, and a fairly sophisticated understanding of your own emotional life, and still find yourself on the phone with your mother feeling 12 years old.

You tell her something hurt you. She tells you that you are too sensitive. You try to explain why the comment landed badly. She reminds you that she did the best she could. By the end of the conversation, you're not sure whether you're asking for an apology, trying to be understood, or hoping (once again) that this time she will respond differently.

In my work with adult children navigating conflict with their boomer parents, I see a recurring pattern: The adult child experiences a parent's rigidity, defensiveness, or denial as evidence that the parent doesn't care.

Sometimes that interpretation is accurate. There are parents who are cruel, manipulative, dismissive, or unwilling to take responsibility. But often, what looks like malice is also a generational mismatch in how people understand emotional responsibility, conflict, and attachment.

Many boomers were raised in families where children were expected to adapt to adults, not the other way around. Feelings were often treated as private matters, discipline was framed as character-building, and parents were not necessarily expected to explain themselves or repair a rupture after an argument. For some, love was expressed through provision, sacrifice, and showing up materially. The idea that a parent should validate a child's emotional experience — even when the parent remembers the event differently — can feel foreign, or even accusatory.

That history can help explain why a parent responds to “That hurt me” with “Well, I did my best,” or to “I need you to listen” with a list of everything they have done for you. The adult child is asking for emotional recognition in the present. The parent hears a verdict on their entire history as a mother or father. One person is trying to talk about impact; the other is defending intent. They are having two different conversations, and both leave feeling unseen.

This is the pattern I want adult children to understand... not because it excuses harmful behavior, but because it can change what you do next.

If you interpret every defensive response as proof that your parent has no love for you, you may keep escalating the argument in search of a kind of recognition they are not currently able to offer.

You may explain more, provide more examples, produce more evidence, and try increasingly precise language. Meanwhile, your parent may become more entrenched, because each new explanation feels like another charge they have to defend against.

A reframe can help: instead of asking, “Why won't my parent admit they hurt me?” try asking, “What kind of response is this person actually capable of giving me?” That is not the same as accepting the response or deciding it is enough. It is an assessment of reality. You can want your parent to understand you and also recognize that they may not have the emotional vocabulary, flexibility, or willingness to do so.

Sometimes a more effective conversation begins with a smaller, more concrete request. Rather than asking a parent to acknowledge an entire pattern of emotional neglect, you might say, “When I tell you something is hard, I need you to listen before you tell me what I should have done.” Rather than trying to settle the history of your relationship over dinner, you might say, “I'm not asking you to agree with my memory. I'm asking you not to tell me I'm making it up.”

The goal is not to shrink your needs to make them palatable. It is to make the request clear enough that you can see whether your parent is willing to meet it.

There is also a difference between understanding a parent's limitations and organizing your life around them. If a parent repeatedly dismisses your feelings, violates boundaries, or uses guilt to control you, you are allowed to limit what you share, shorten visits, decline certain conversations, or take space.

A generational explanation is not a hall pass. It can offer context, but it does not erase impact or require you to keep making yourself available for the same injury.

I also encourage adult children to notice when they are still approaching a parent as though the right argument will finally produce the childhood experience they missed. This is deeply human. We want our parents to see us, to be curious about us, to take responsibility when they hurt us. But sometimes the work is grieving the parent we needed while deciding what kind of relationship is possible with the parent we actually have.

That grief can coexist with affection. You can understand that your mother was doing what she knew how to do and still wish she had done something different. You can appreciate what your father provided and still name what was missing. You can have compassion for the conditions that shaped your parents without making those conditions your responsibility to repair.

The most useful question may not be whether your parents are bad people or whether you are asking too much. It may be whether the relationship you have today can hold the kind of honesty you want to bring to it. If it can, try a smaller, clearer conversation. If it cannot, boundaries may be more productive than another attempt to persuade.

Growing up doesn't always mean finally getting your parents to understand you. Sometimes it means learning to understand the limits of the relationship... and deciding, with care and without self-abandonment, what you want to do with that knowledge.

#8092. The Woman Keeping Pets and People Together | Heroes of the Pet World

As we drove through the beautiful mountain scenery surrounding Lake Chapala, I wasnât sure what to expect. Julie Wittmann picked me up early in the morning, and now we were on our way to help distribute food to families who needed extra help feeding their pets.

When we arrived, large sacks of cat and dog food had already been divided into individual portions by a team of Pet Food Bank Lakeside volunteers who gather every week to prepare the food for distribution. We moved the bags into two piles, one for each community they would serve, ready to be collected by volunteers who would take them to families in need.

It was simple work, but it was part of a much greater effort.

Pet Food Bank Lakeside is an independent partner of FoodBank Lakeside, which provides âdespensasâ (bags of basic groceries and household essentials) to families experiencing financial hardship. Families receiving assistance are asked how many pets they have, helping connect the two programs. The pet food program now provides food for more than 1,200 dogs and cats each month.

Next, Julie and I headed to the small town of Santa Cruz, joined by FoodBank Lakeside leader Steve Motenko, his wife Karen, their granddaughter, her best friend, and Javier, a cheerful local with a kind heart. Javier knows the families in the community and helps coordinate the deliveries.

Everyone we met was struggling financially. For most, that hardship was compounded by illness, age, or disability. We met a woman who was completely blind and several people who used wheelchairs.

Just like us, many have pets, and just like our own cats and dogs, theirs are companions, confidants, and cherished members of the family. For some of the people we met, who spend much of their time at home because of age or a health condition, their pet may be their most constant companion.

Looking at them, it was impossible to see a dog or cat as simply another expense. These animals were part of the family. They brought comfort, protection, affection, and, very often, a little joy into lives that could use more of it.

That is something Julie and FoodBank Lakeside understand well. Helping someone feed their pet is not just about putting food in a bowl. It is about helping preserve a very important relationship.

As we moved from house to house, we also carried treats for the dogs we met along the way. They quickly learned that the cars arriving meant something good was coming.

One particularly enthusiastic dog decided not to wait for us at home. He followed our cars from one house to the next, keeping pace for two or three stops as if he had appointed himself our unofficial escort.

It was a small, funny moment in an otherwise emotional morning, and it brought plenty of smiles from everyone.

What I noticed most was how happy most of these people were to see the volunteers arrive.

These were not strangers arriving at a doorstep with a bag of food. There were smiles, conversations, and a sense of familiarity that comes from years of showing up for the same community.

One of the women who had received help from the FoodBank for her cat had passed away only days before we arrived. Karen told me through tears that they had known each other for six years and had become very close. She described her as one of the sweetest women she had known.

The friendship had grown both ways. Over the years, the woman had prepared plant cuttings for Karen and given her handmade embroidery pieces as Christmas gifts. These were small gestures, but they spoke of a relationship that had grown far beyond a food delivery.

Her cat was still there, and the womanâs daughter was relieved to know that the pet food program would continue to help care for it.

I found that moment difficult to forget. The woman was gone, but the connections she had made remained in Karen's memories, in the plants she had shared, in the handmade gifts she had given, and in the cat still waiting at home.

That is something you cannot measure in bags of food, but in kilos of love instead.

Julie did not set out to create a large pet food program.

After moving from Portland, Oregon, to the Lake Chapala area, she began looking for ways to help animals in her new community. When COVID-19 disrupted daily life, she asked local veterinarians what they believed was needed most.

Local rescue groups were also concerned that families who could no longer afford to feed their dogs might eventually have to surrender them or turn them loose.

Julie started small. She bought large 25-kilogram bags of food, repackaged them herself, and drove into local communities to distribute them. As local groups organized despensas for families in villages around Lake Chapala, Julie saw an opportunity to make sure the pets were not forgotten. Over time, that small effort became Pet Food Bank Lakeside.

A partnership with FoodBank Lakeside allowed the program to reach more families. FoodBank Lakeside already knew which households were struggling and how many pets they had. The two programs could work together to help both people and animals.

Today, Julie has a community of volunteers helping with the work that she once did herself. In its six-year update, Pet Food Bank Lakeside reported more than 20 volunteers and the ability to prepare a month's supply of food in under two hours.

Julie and her volunteers also visit local schools to teach children about pet care.

For Julie, education is one of the most important ways to prevent animals from being misunderstood or mistreated.

âEducating children is particularly important,â Julie explains. âWhen they understand that the weird-looking dog has scabies, and that what it needs is medication, we prevent that dog from being mistreated and left aside.â

Her point is simple. Children need to understand what they are seeing before they can respond with compassion.

She sees the same principle in the way children learn what animals need.

âThe only way for kids to understand that it is not normal for dogs to spend all day tied up to a post is to let them know that this is not normal, to teach them what dogs are, what they need, and how they can enrich each other's lives.â

Those lessons can have an impact long after a food delivery is over.

During our morning together, I saw another example of how those values can be passed to the next generation. Steve and Karen's granddaughter and her best friend helped deliver the pet food.

I loved seeing teenagers take part in helping people who were struggling. There was something hopeful about watching them learn through experience that their time, effort, and kindness can make a difference.

Julie is helping animals today, but she is also trying to shape how children understand animals tomorrow.

Steve Motenko has watched Julie's work grow from those early days when she was repackaging large bags of food herself, into a community-supported program reaching more than a thousand animals each month.

He describes Julie as admirable and says she has done an extraordinary amount to help pets in the Lakeside community.

After spending a morning with her, I understood why.

What struck me was that these deliveries were about so much more than food. They were about people knowing, caring for, and looking out for one another.

Javier knew the families. Karen had formed a six-year friendship with one of the women we visited. Volunteers gathered each week to prepare food. Teenagers came along to help. Julie kept showing up for the pets.

Julie says it simply: âWe believe food scarcity shouldn't separate families from their pets.â

After spending that morning with her, I understood that belief in a more personal way.

When someone is already struggling to afford food, dealing with illness, or living with a disability, feeding a pet can seem like one more impossible responsibility. But for the people we met, their animals were not disposable. They were very important companions, bringing comfort and connection to lives that were often anything but easy.

Helping them keep those animals fed also helped them keep an important part of their lives.

By the end of the day, I felt an enormous admiration for Julie and for the people who have joined her in this work.

I had arrived thinking I was just going to help deliver pet food. Instead, I witnessed something much bigger. I saw people who had built genuine relationships with their neighbors. I saw volunteers giving their time week after week. I saw teenagers learning to help others. I saw a daughter relieved that her mother's cat would continue to receive food.

Most of all, I saw how much a small act of kindness can mean when someone is having a difficult time.

My heart felt very warm on the drive home.

I kept thinking about those bags of food we had divided into two piles that morning.

At first, they had simply looked like bags of pet food waiting to be delivered.

By the end of the day, I understood what they represented.

And, sometimes, the chance for a person and the animal they love to stay together.

When my boss passed away, I took in his older Red Heeler, Bob, so he didnât end up in the pound. I've been giving him turkey tail for his lumps, and he is overweight.

Itâs hard to walk him when it's 100 degrees out. For the last couple of months, he has been drinking so much water and urinating way more than usual. He mostly stays inside, and when I take him out to pee, the first thing when he comes back in is head for the water bowl, like he wants to replace what he just got rid of!

You have done something very kind by giving Bob a home after losing his person. It sounds like he is a senior boy who has already been through a lot, and it is wonderful that he has someone looking out for him. The increased drinking and urination you are seeing, especially since this has been going on for a couple of months, is something I would have checked rather than assuming it is just his age or the hot weather. Older dogs can develop several conditions that cause this combination of signs, including diabetes, kidney disease, and Cushing's disease.

I would schedule a veterinary examination and ask for some basic lab work, particularly blood tests and urinalysis. These can give us information that we simply cannot get from looking at Bob. Bloodwork can tell us about his blood glucose, kidney and liver function, electrolytes, and other changes that may help identify what is going on. A urine sample is just as valuable. It can show whether his kidneys are concentrating the urine properly, and can also detect glucose, ketones, protein, blood, inflammation, and other abnormalities. Depending on those results, his veterinarian may recommend some additional tests.

Please do not limit his water, even if it seems like he is drinking right back what he just urinated. In many of these conditions, the excessive thirst is the body's way of trying to replace fluid that is being lost. Taking water away can actually make him dehydrated and much sicker. Keep fresh water available at all times, and because of the heat, try to take him out during the cooler parts of the day. If you can, measuring approximately how much water he drinks in 24 hours would also be very helpful information for his veterinarian.

I would also recommend that he has the lumps properly checked rather than relying on turkey tail or other supplements. Some lumps are harmless, but others can be more serious, and we cannot tell the difference just by feeling or looking at them. A fine needle aspiration can often collect cells from a lump with very little discomfort and may give the veterinarian a much better idea of what it is. With Bob being overweight and having difficulty walking in the heat, getting his medical issues sorted out first will also make it much safer to work on his weight and mobility.

He has clearly found someone who cares about him, and sometimes the most loving thing we can do for an older dog is simply to find out what his body is trying to tell us.

#8090. New York's New AI Law Prohibits Bots From Dangerous Behaviors With Minors

Starting in January, New Yorkers can file complaints with the attorney general if chatbots cross a line with their kids.

Artificial intelligence is everywhere now. It has become part of most Americans’ work and personal lives at an unprecedented pace, popping up in our inboxes and social media apps even when we haven’t opted into a chatbot ourselves. Examples of the harm have rolled in, from staggering numbers of deepfake nudes being created of children to teens who turn to AI for advice during a mental health crisis. But in New York, new legislation will try to rein in the technology and the risks it poses to minors.

The new law, which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, prohibits companies with AI chatbots “from offering unsafe features to minors, including chatbots that pretend to be human, build emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage in sexually explicit conversations.” Companies would have to block these features on the accounts of anyone under 18, or any user whose age has not been verified. The law requires chatbot providers to verify users through multiple age assurance methods.

Once verified, that age information must be deleted. It was signed into law by Gov. Kathy Hochul on Oct. 28, 2026.

According to Gov. Hochul’s website, the legislation prohibits AI chatbots from, among other things:

Violations of the new law could result in fines of up to $25,000 per infraction. The attorney general will publish a new website where New Yorkers can file complaints. New York’s new law is an attempt to curtail the behaviors that are most harmful to kids, experts say.

The story of Adam Raine — a teenager who died by suicide, and whose conversations with ChatGPT exposed that it offered to write his suicide note for him — is one example of why humanizing chatbot behaviors like these are targeted by this law. Surveys have shown kids ages 11 to 16 can’t really articulate what AI is, and many ascribe human-like consciousness and emotions to chatbots.

According to a 2026 Common Sense Media report, nearly 9 in 10 kids ages 9 to 17 (86%) interact with AI, including about one in four who use it on a daily basis. More than half of kids (57%) who use AI said they’ve used it to get information about their health or body; separate studies have found that AI gives misleading or inaccurate health information to users 50% of the time. Half of the respondents have asked AI for advice on decisions about their future or goals, while 37% have used chatbots to discuss their feelings or personal problems.

As always, legislation lumbers along while technology speeds ahead unchecked. Until the laws catch up to AI, parents can feel alone in the fight to protect their kids. Fraser says this law on its own is not enough to protect them either.

“Legislation alone cannot guarantee safety. Companies have got to do their part, and there has got to be accountability,” she says. “The Meta settlements are a great example of what industry self-regulation looks like. It doesn’t work. There’s got to be third-party independent accountability because companies, for all sorts of reasons, can’t always take five steps back to see what it is that they’re doing. Sometimes they can't see the risks that are right in front of them. So I do think that the law is a step in the right direction. We need these types of laws, but we also need the companies to do their part.”

As New York readies to enforce its new youth AI protections, just this week Google, Meta, and TikTok filed a lawsuit against the state of California, challenging its legislation prohibiting addictive social media features on children’s accounts. The law bans the platforms from offering “psychologically exploitative features” to minors, including autoplay videos, endless scroll, and personalized recommendations that contribute to “compulsive use.” The companies argue the government is trying to impose its judgment over parents'.

This article was originally published on November 5, 2026

If you're thinking of cleaning your deck with vinegar, take care not to make this mistake...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Somewhere in the pantry there's probably a gallon of white vinegar that already cleans the coffee pot and the shower door. Vinegar costs next to nothing and smells like salad dressing instead of bleach; many people use vinegar to clean a deck for exactly those reasons, without a second thought about where the rinse water goes.

Out in the yard, white vinegar already has a few honest jobs. Some gardeners use vinegar in the garden to scrub crusty clay pots and burn back weeds in sidewalk cracks. That same weed-killing action is part of the problem on a deck, though. Acetic acid burns plant tissue on contact, and a bucket of rinse water doesn't stop at the edge of the boards.

It also matters what the deck is made of. A cedar deck that has never seen a drop of stain, for example? Well, that doesn't play by the same rules as Trex, a major composite brand that actually approves vinegar for one particular job. Check the maker's care guide before any cleaner goes on.

On some composite boards, the answer is a qualified yes. If your boards are one of Trex's current lines, white vinegar is on the approved list for hard water deposits: the chalky white spots a sprinkler leaves when it keeps hitting the same boards.

Rinse well afterward; everyday dirt gets warm soapy water and a soft-bristle brush instead, scrubbed down into the embossed grain. Be aware that Trex says anything containing acid or bleach can lighten the color of its boards, so try a small spot near the steps first.

Other brands say less. TimberTech's care guide doesn't mention vinegar at all, and it points owners toward its own diluted deck cleaner or, for railings, a pH-neutral detergent. It also warns against citrus cleaners, solvents and several brand-name deck cleaners on its current capped boards. When a manufacturer hasn't approved a product, using it anyway means guessing how the surface will react.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Wood decks raise a different question, and the finish on top matters more than the boards underneath. Acids aren't foreign to deck care – oxalic acid brighteners are a standard step for pulling gray discoloration out of bare wood before a fresh coat of stain.

That's prep work for unfinished boards, though; once paint or stain goes on, the can it came in has the final word. Some finish makers approve only their own cleaners, and washing a stained deck with straight vinegar again and again means working outside those directions with no way of knowing how that particular finish will hold up.

Then there's everything growing below the deck rail. Household vinegar is about 5% acetic acid, the same acid sold in stronger form as a weed killer, and it damages leaf tissue wherever it lands.

Picture that rinse water running off the edge of the deck onto a bed of hostas or a row of fall lettuce – leaves that it soaks can turn brown and crispy, and seedlings take the worst of it. The acid doesn't hang around in the soil, and lawn grass along the edge usually recovers better than broadleaf plants do. A natural label? It sadly doesn't change any of that.

The broom comes out first, since scrubbing wet leaves only smears them across the boards. Home Depot's 7-pattern Ames hose nozzle set has a soft shower setting for soaking the deck and a narrow jet for packed gaps. Warm water and a squirt of dish soap handle ordinary grime on wood and composite alike.

Brushes are where the two big composite brands part ways. Trex wants soft bristles, and Home Depot also carries a soft-bristle Unger scrub brush that threads onto a standard broom handle. TimberTech calls for medium-to-stiff nylon on its composite instead. Do one section at a time and rinse it before the suds dry.

Mildew and gray weathering on a wood deck usually need something stronger than soap. Walmart carries DEFY's powdered wood cleaner, an oxygen-based formula for exterior wood that mixes up in a bucket.

Now, at least one stain maker warns that chlorine bleach can damage both the finish and the bare wood fibers, and it's hard on any plants it splashes. Capped composite needs more caution here (TimberTech's guide says its own diluted cleaner is the safe bet). Think about where the bucket water goes, too, especially if the deck slopes toward a fish pond or a storm drain. A label that says biodegradable means the product breaks down eventually, not that it's harmless to fish and other pond life along the way.

Pressure washers are tempting on a big deck, but a narrow stream held too close can tear up the surface of wood boards and leave the fibers fuzzy. Composite brands set firm limits. On Trex Transcend, Enhance and Select boards, the limit is 3,100 psi with a fan tip held at least 8 inches (20.3cm) from the surface, though the company doesn't recommend pressure washers at all on its early-generation lines. TimberTech caps pressure at 1,500 psi, for rinsing only, with the spray running along the grain.

Decks that get washed twice a year are far less likely to need anything harsh. Trex ties its spring and fall schedule to pollen and leaf litter, since that buildup is what mold grows on. Leaves wedged between boards can hold water against the surface long after a rain, and a putty knife slid down the row clears them out quickly. Shady corners and boards under overhanging branches usually go green first.

Keep the vinegar, just not as the everyday deck cleaner. On Trex boards with chalky sprinkler spots, it's the fix the company itself approves, and the potting bench can use it too. Day-to-day grime comes off with warm soapy water and a brush that won't scuff the boards, ideally on a gray afternoon when the sun isn't drying the suds faster than you can scrub.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8088. Tiffani Amber Thiessen Talks Parenting Teens, Period Talks & Her Witchy Era

The “Saved By The Bell” alum has come full circle and is now playing a principal and mom.

Tiffani Amber Thiessen’s face is burned into the brains of every elder Millennial who watched countless Saved by the Bell episodes and dreamed of dressing exactly like Kelly Kapowski. Of course, we’ve all left the 1900s behind and have grown into adults — parents and women with careers.

Like the rest of us, the 52-year-old mom of two kids — Harper, 16, and Holt, 11 — has left high school in the rear view mirror, but her career continues to flourish. And she’s still in the classroom, in a way: Coven Academy, the witchy dark academia series in which she stars as the principal of Crescent Veil Academy, just got renewed for a second season.

You can also find her on Instagram, where her account is a delightful mix of food, fashion, humor, nostalgia, and life as a woman who is finding power and peace as she enters her 50s.

Recently, Thiessen partnered with Always on its “Period Talks Don’t Have to Be Scary” campaign, which addresses what is often a real hurdle for parents: talking about periods with their kids. Research has found that 43% of moms struggle to start the first-period talk because they feel unprepared. So Thiessen wants to share her own experiences while offering practical advice to parents who want to open and informative with their tweens and teens... even if can be awkward at times.

She recently sat down with Scary Mommy to talk about periods, parenting, her new show, and her family’s holiday traditions.

Scary Mommy: Gen Z and Millennial moms have done a lot to break period stigma with our kids. How have you done that with your kids?

Tiffani Amber Thiessen: I think the generation I grew up in didn’t talk about these things. Now kids are much more open, and I have a very open relationship with both my children. It never fully takes away the scariness of intimate talks, whether it’s periods, the body, or growing up. But I think parents who understand that it isn’t one big, intimidating conversation, but many small, casual talks, can take the edge off.

Partnering with Always has been lovely because they’re trying to prepare parents with what to do and how to have that first conversation. Being prepared gives you the confidence.

SM: I found that I was a lot more scared than my daughter was. Did you feel that?

TAT: Most parents feel that way. You don’t realize until afterward that it really isn’t that scary. I found it to be a bonding moment. I’d tell my kids that over half the population menstruates, so it’s not a big deal. Keeping it casual and a little funny helps. Building that competence between parent and child is what lets your daughter take it on, and it’s a badge of honor.

SM: I love asking this: What’s your best piece of parenting advice?

TAT: It goes back to having an open conversation about anything. When I became a parent, I wanted to be open to receiving anything my kids share, whether it’s hard or difficult. I wanted them to feel comfortable and know I would never judge. We’ve all been in crazy places, and my kids are super open with me, about the fun stuff and the stuff that isn’t so fun. Keeping that conversation free of judgment is probably the most important thing in parenting.

SM: Have you ever wanted to judge, though?

TAT: I can secretly judge, is that okay? [laughs]

TAT: Most of the things my kids tell me I’ve either witnessed, been through, or know someone who has. It’s really not that crazy.

SM: Let’s switch gears to Coven Academy. And you just got renewed for Season 2?

TAT: Monday! We had high hopes and wanted to find an audience that saw the specialness of the show, and I think we did. It’s done very well on Disney+ and Hulu, so we’re over the moon to do it all over again.

SM: There are so few shows made for this demographic: tweens, mostly girls. It’s so good to have something that speaks to kids in that space.

TAT: The witch aspect is having a moment on social media, but it’s not really about spells and potions. It’s about found family, sisterhood, and having each other’s backs. I have a teenage daughter, and she has a wonderful group of girls she can count on. Everybody should have that, especially women.

SM: How has it been going from being a student on a hugely popular show to a headmistress on set with the younger generation?

TAT: It feels natural. I have kids of my own now. The last few shows I’ve been fortunate to do have had younger casts, and I really enjoy working with young adults. I may give them advice, but I get a lot from them, too. We did a lot of night shoots, and I’d see these kids at 3 a.m. doing their TikToks while I was struggling. Their energy kept me going through those nights.

SM: The holidays are coming up. Do you have any family traditions you want to share?

TAT: We’re very traditional in that it’s all about family. We do Christmas morning and Christmas Eve dinner. For the last 15 or 16 years, we’ve alternated between my husband’s family in Texas and ours. This year it’s our turn to go to Texas. We leave the day after Christmas and spend the week and New Year’s with my in-laws. All the cousins are together, and we look forward to it every year.

SM: What have you been cooking lately, or what are you planning for the holidays?

TAT: My kids like the traditions. Thanksgiving is classic turkey and stuffing, plus my mom’s famous cream cheese pie. For Christmas we usually do enchiladas, which I’ll probably make again this year. We usually switch it up for Christmas because everybody’s over turkey.

SM: Dennis Haskins recently passed away. He was your principal on Saved by the Bell, and now you’re playing a principal. Do you have any remembrances to share?

TAT: I have so many. He was our solid one; our anchor. I know it was probably hard for him, being the only adult on a kids’ show. He handled it with such grace and gave us a safe place. He was part of us, and he could be young, but he was still a strong personality. He always made us feel protected, and he’s very much missed.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
