#8087. The Best Compost Tumblers of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

By Jenn Ryan, Glenda Taylor, Additional research provided by Mark Wolfe

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:00 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Composting has numerous benefits, and having a compost tumbler makes the process even easier. In addition to recycling kitchen, lawn, and garden waste into a helpful soil amendment, composting helps keep significant amounts of organic waste out of landfills. As lawn care and gardening enthusiasts, we wanted to find out just how easy these contraptions made the task, so we tested several. For 8 weeks, we filled and turned tumblers, yielding over 100 pounds of plant-enriching compost.

After testing, we selected the RSI Maze 65-Gallon Compost Tumbler as our favorite due to its overall ease of use and smart design, but it’s not the only great option. Ahead, learn more about how these products fared in testing, and discover which considerations are worth bearing in mind when you’re shopping for the best compost tumbler.

Bottom line: Compost tumblers simplify composting, offering various features to suit different needs. Our tests highlight top models for efficiency and ease of use.

We tested each of these composters, from assembly to everyday use, to determine the best picks for both small and large home gardens.

The 65-gallon RSI Maze Compost Tumbler makes controlling the bin simple and smooth, even when fully loaded, with a geared handle and ratchet lock. The bin features air vents on all sides and large sliding covers that simplify loading and unloading. The dual-chamber design facilitates a consistent flow of garden waste in and compost out. This is a suitable size for medium to large gardens and landscapes.

The 65-gallon (8.69-cubic-foot) bin is made of UV-protected high-impact plastic. The frame is made of rust- and corrosion-resistant zinc-coated steel. It offers 15 inches of ground clearance for unloading compost via a cart.

We loved the size of this composter as well as its hand crank, which made it easy to turn even when the composter was full. We filled it with organic vegetable and fruit scraps, dry leaves, and dry grass.

This tumbler’s crank was a unique feature. Rather than having to roll the barrel, the crank allowed us to turn the bin with ease and “stop” it in a position where it was easiest to empty it. It is heavy, though, so users should be mindful of where to place it. Once it’s full, it’s difficult to move.

What our tester says: “I found this product to be high quality. It’s very durable, thanks in part to its rust-resistant zinc coating. Additionally, it’s relatively simple to assemble, and it’s easy to use.”—Jenn Ryan, Product Reviews tester and writer

Read our full review: RSI Maze Two-Stage Compost Tumbler

Get the RSI compost tumbler at Amazon, Lowe’s, Tractor Supply Co., or The Home Depot.

The FCMP Half-Size Rolling Composter is a compact, affordable pick ideal for one or two people who don’t generate much compostable waste. The ground-rolling design gives this unit a low profile that easily tucks away in small spaces, such as a balcony, patio, or garage. Built-in ergonomic handholds help make rolling less awkward. Aeration holes and deep fins break up clumps inside the chamber to maximize oxygen penetration.

The 19-gallon (2.5-cubic-foot) bin is made of recycled UV-inhibited BPA-free polyethylene. To speed decomposition, the manufacturer recommends turning the bin about twice a day.

The assembly of this product couldn’t have been easier. The composter came almost completely assembled—all we needed to do was place it on the stand and slide the door on. Although we loved the size and portability of this composter, it was too small for a large garden and would make a better option for urban composters, those with a small garden, or those who want to use compost for indoor or potted plants.

During testing, the composter needed to be turned frequently; for balance, using two hands was best. We also found it challenging to turn because it is not attached to the base; it merely sits on the stand, and both the stand and the composter can slide off balance. We found that the turning process was best done slowly, but people with mobility challenges may find this composter difficult to use, as it’s low to the ground and needs to be turned by hand.

We also found that the door was a bit tight and tricky to open and close when filling with compost and emptying. For emptying, the composter needs to be lifted, which can also be a challenge when it is full and heavy.

Overall, this composter makes a great option for those with smaller gardens, those who want zero-fuss assembly, or those who want a small but sturdy composter they can easily store out of sight.

Get the FCMP half-size compost tumbler at Amazon.

The Miracle-Gro Tumbling Composter provides a convenient place to recycle veggie scraps and houseplant debris while fitting easily into a small space. The hexagonal 18.5-gallon (2.47-cubic-foot) chamber features aeration holes and mixing bars for better oxygen infusion. Tight-locking slide doors keep out pests. For easy loading and unloading, toppers on the frame lock the bin rotation.

The UV-protected plastic chamber is built to withstand exposure to weather. The powder-coated stainless steel frame makes it easy not only to load, unload, and rotate the bin, but also to sweep or blow out debris from underneath. The composter requires some assembly, but that is made easy with step-by-step directions via a QR code. The package includes a pair of water-resistant, no-slip grip garden gloves.

Assembly for this composter was simple thanks to the included QR code that walked us through each step with 3D images—no app download required. We loved that this composter was easier to turn in a more compact size—perfect for one- or two-person households with small gardens or for urban gardeners. Since it is a smaller size, we found that the bin remained easy to turn even as it filled with compost. Its small size also makes it convenient for placing in a more conspicuous location as opposed to large dual-bin composters.

On the downside, we found that the door on this compost bin was a bit too tight and difficult to open with one hand. The frame of the composter is narrow, and combined with the fact that the composter is just inches from the ground means only a shallow dish or trough will fit under the frame to empty the compost. (In testing, we used an old sled for emptying and transporting the compost out of this tumbler.)

Get the Miracle-Gro compost tumbler at Amazon.

The RSI Maze 48‑gallon compost tumbler can be used for uninterrupted composting thanks to its dual-chamber design. The geared crank handle made turning easy, even when loaded. We liked its UV-protected barrel and galvanized steel frame, which are made especially for outdoor use.

Assembly posed a small challenge as some of the components were pretty tight and had to be forced into place. But once built, it worked smoothly and reliably. The sliding doors and ratchet lock held the drum in position, allowing easy collection of finished compost into a cart or bucket placed underneath.

The only drawback we noted was the assembly process, but that’s a one‑time obstacle worth dealing with as the daily ease and performance thereafter make up for it. Overall, the Maze tumbler delivers high usability with long-term value and minimal maintenance.

Get the Maze compost tumbler at The Home Depot.

We found the Genesis compost tumbler to be robust yet compact enough for backyard composting. We’re sold on its “rodent‑proof” design, too. Its secure sliding doors and solid construction succeeded in keeping the little critters out during our testing. We also liked the internal mixing rods and multiple ventilation points—the compost in this tumbler seemed to biodegrade more quickly than in the others we tested.

Despite its sturdy materials and tight assembly, we found it lightweight enough to rotate comfortably. Its design takes up only a small footprint but still offers substantial capacity. The UV-resistant barrel and powder-coated frame are built for long-term outdoor exposure.

On the downside, we think the doors could be wider, which would making loading and removing compost slightly less cumbersome. Still, for its build quality, ease of use, and continuous composting capability, we think the Genesis tumbler is a solid value.

Get the Genesis compost tumbler at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or The Home Depot.

This tumbler earned its keep with a design built for efficiency and ease of use. Its dual‑compartment barrel allowed us to continue adding fresh scraps while older material matures in the opposite chamber. For anyone serious about continuous composting, a dual chamber is essential.

Made of steel, the two‑leg stand not only gives the tumbler a solid foundation but also elevates it off the ground, offering added protection against rodents. We found this model especially well made and sturdy.

We only had one gripe: the doors had a tendency to slide open at times as we rotated the barrels. Once, we were turning the handle while looking at something else, and we lost about half of our compost before we noticed. We ended up taping the doors shut to keep them closed. Still, it might just have been our model, and this tumbler is otherwise well-built.

Get the Exaco compost tumbler at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

With its built-in, wheeled tea-collecting base, the Good Ideas compost tumbler does double duty. It comes with a rugged, FDA-approved recycled plastic body, and upon arrival, it was fully assembled, so we didn’t have to put anything together. That was impressive.

Its twist-off lids provide a tight closure, backing up the manufacturer’s claims that it’s pet- and rodent-safe. We liked how durable and easy to use this model was from day one. It sits low, so there’s no chance of it blowing over in high winds. The compact yet spacious barrel is a boon for busy gardeners who want to produce a good amount of compost.

However, the large capacity means that once we got it full, rotating the tumbler required significant effort, as the material inside got heavier. Despite that, we think this model is likely to last for years, and with its compost tea collection, it’s a hard one to beat.

What our tester said: “The Good Ideas compost tumbler really impressed me—not only is it pest-proof and made from high-quality materials, it also produces compost tea for fertilizing my plants.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Good Ideas compost tumbler at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Walmart.

We tested the best compost tumblers using a rubric that scored assembly, ease of use, and mobility when empty and full. We also noted the quality of instructions, including whether physical and digital versions were available. Each model was loaded with a mix of wet and dry compost materials—fruit and vegetable scraps, herbs, leaves, and grass—to evaluate how easy it was to turn under different conditions.

Points were awarded based on performance, with higher scores going to models that were simpler to assemble, turn, and empty. After testing, we averaged the points to determine our Best Overall pick and to rank the remaining models by their standout features.

Several characteristics can help shoppers determine which tumbler is the best composting tumbler for their needs. The type, intended use of the bin, amount of space available, and garden environment are some of the key considerations, as well as a few more, all detailed below.

Composting outdoors uses aerobic (i.e., oxygen-loving) microorganisms to break down organic waste quickly. Previously, home gardeners had to turn their compost piles manually with a garden fork to supply adequate oxygen. Compost tumblers, on the other hand, fully enclose the pile inside a vented barrel. They are mounted on a frame to make the barrel easier to turn, which eliminates the slow, back-breaking process of turning with a fork. The most important difference among the types of compost tumblers is in the way they turn. The tumblers rotate by one of three turning methods: ground rolling, central axis, and handle-operated.

A ground-rolling spinning compost bin has two separate pieces: the barrel (or bin) and the base. The base has a curved upper surface that cradles the bin, holding it in place without fasteners. Rollers built into the curved surface of the base allow the loaded bin to spin freely when pushed or pulled.

Because they sit at ground level, ground-rolling compost tumblers are a good choice for those who live in cold climates. The reduced exposure to wind and cold allows the bin to retain heat. The added warmth keeps composting microbes active instead of allowing them to go dormant in the cold.

Central-axis compost tumblers are built on a metal compost tumbler framework with an axle running through the midpoint of the bin. The framework serves two purposes. First, it elevates the bin to a height that reduces bending and stooping while filling, turning, and emptying the bin. Second, the axle allows the bin to spin freely to aerate its contents.

Central-axis compost bins are a good choice for those who suffer from back problems, since these bins allow the user to load and unload the material from a standing position rather than a stooping one. Some models also feature wheels, so users can easily relocate the bin to a different area of the yard or garden.

Handle-operated compost tumblers use gears to make turning the barrel much easier. The geared handle matches up with a gear built into the end of the bin. When the operator cranks the handle, it turns the bin in a smooth, controlled manner.

Handle-operated tumblers require less physical strength than other types of tumblers. This kind of tumbler might be a good choice for children, older adults, or gardeners with reduced physical strength. Buyers can also find a few electric composters that generate their own heat and are designed to be used indoors.

Before buying one, shoppers will want to determine exactly how they intend to use the bin. For instance, will it be used primarily for kitchen scrap disposal with a countertop composter like a Vego composter? Or, will it also process weeds, grass clippings, and other garden debris? Will it be filled irregularly, with additional content added periodically until it’s full? Or will it receive a steady stream of material on a regular basis?

For processing small amounts of kitchen scraps and occasional houseplant debris, a compost tumbler in the 15- to 25-gallon size range works well. To compost greater quantities on an irregular basis, such as at the end of a gardening season, large compost tumbler (50 to 80 gallons) can meet that challenge. For a steady stream of debris, dual composter tumblers can easily handle consistent loads, as they process and finish compost on one side while the user feeds new material on the other.

Indoor countertop models make good composting for beginners, since they do all the work for you. Using an indoor countertop model can let you see if composting is something you want to do on a larger scale.

Although some versions use steel, compost tumblers typically have an ultraviolet (UV)-protected plastic bin with a frame made of tubular steel or plastic. Since plastic resists both weather and corrosion and transfers heat slowly, it makes an ideal material for the bin.

Metal compost tumblers allow internal heat to escape more quickly in cold weather, slowing the composting process, and they can corrode over time. Tubular steel frames are the standard for central-axis and handle-operated tumblers. Most ground-rolling bins feature a plastic base, some of which include a reservoir for capturing the liquid runoff from the bin, called “compost tea,” another useful gardening medium.

Indoor models (like the Lomi Composter we tested) contain additional materials, such as silicone, that are designed to seal the unit, minimizing odor.

Bin capacity is measured in either gallons or cubic feet; 1 cubic foot equals 7.48 gallons. The smallest compost tumblers hold about 15 gallons, or about 2 cubic feet, while the largest holds more than 80 gallons, or 10.7 cubic feet.

Shoppers will also want to consider the amount of material and how often they want to compost. Typically, it takes at least 10 weeks to fully process a batch of compost. For this reason, many gardeners operate two tumblers simultaneously or use a dual-chamber tumbler. With a dual-chamber bin, users can add to one bin for 10 weeks, then close it, allow it to process, and gradually fill the second bin.

Tumbling helps provide air to compost and reduce moisture, both of which are vital in the decomposition process. Look for a compost bin with built-in aeration structures, such as air holes or vents in the walls, fins on the interior walls, flat sides, and mixing bars.

As the material inside breaks down, it can become compacted. Turning the bin loosens the material and breaks down the clumps. Air holes and vents allow the exchange of gases in the microorganisms within the decaying matter, letting excess moisture escape. Flat walls, such as in a hexagonal shape, force the material to tumble rather than slide. Additional texture comes from features such as fins and bars that help stir the material and add oxygen.

An enclosed compost tumbler also helps composters avoid pests like rodents and insects. The lids on these units thread, latch, or slide into tracks, which prevents rodents and other small animals from entering. Durable, heavy-duty plastic is difficult for rodents to chew through, and steel makes the bin virtually impossible to penetrate. Bears even find them challenging—though we don’t suggest putting that claim to the test if you don’t have to! Avoid adding animal favorites, such as meat scraps, bones, and items with high fat content, to the bin.

A foul odor emanating from the bin is an indication that the compost is either poorly aerated or that the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the compost ingredients is out of balance. Compost tumblers are specially designed to deal with the first issue quickly and easily. Simply rotating the bin once or twice each week infuses oxygen into the mix and promotes the growth of beneficial aerobic-composting microbes. If the compost smells like rotten eggs, it needs air. In that case, simply spin the bin.

Just as keeping a pet requires consistent care and attention, so does composting, only in this case, the “pets” are millions of aerobic microbes. These microbes need a consistently warm, moist environment with the right kind of “food.” Their food initially consists of about 30 parts carbon to 1 part nitrogen. Nitrogen comes from green compost ingredients, such as vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, and grass clippings. Carbon comes from so-called brown ingredients, such as autumn leaves, straw, sawdust, and paper. One way to ensure an adequate supply of carbon with kitchen scraps is to include paper products, like coffee filters, used paper towels, and tea bags, in the mix. When users add new scraps to the bin, they can cover the scraps with shredded newsprint or cardboard.

A properly working compost tumbler should heat up from the activity of the microbes and produce a somewhat sweet, earthy scent. If the ingredients are far out of balance, the microbes cannot process the compost efficiently, possibly causing unpleasant odors. If the mixture is slimy or has an ammonia odor, the nitrogen level is too high. It needs brown ingredients. If too much carbon is in the bin, it won’t heat properly; it needs green ingredients.

Compost tumblers offer numerous advantages over stationary compost piles. For starters, they’re neat. They enclose the mess for a tidier appearance. Moreover, they’re fast and easy to turn. Users only have to spin the tumbler for a minute or two instead of the half hour that it takes to turn a compost pile with a garden fork. Gardeners can move them into a garden shed or garage for efficient winter composting; however, a stationary pile simply goes dormant during cold weather.

Of course, different gardeners may have unique needs or physical limitations that impact how easily they can use a compost tumbler. Generally speaking, to distribute the compost, users can simply dump it from an elevated bin into a wheelbarrow. However, cold-weather gardeners who process compost outdoors may prefer a bin that sits directly on the ground. This is because a tumbler on an elevated frame would be exposed to cold on all sides; the composting process would slow down and stop with the rapid cool down. A bin directly on the ground would be insulated from that effect longer.

But some characteristics appeal to almost everyone. A wider opening makes it easier to load and unload, and, unlike latches and threaded lids, sliding covers rarely get clogged with debris. Exterior handgrips on the bin or a hand crank make it easier to rotate the bin.

There are several benefits of composting with a tumbler, with one of the largest draws being its impact on reducing landfill waste. On top of that, users get to take advantage of their own compost to promote a healthy garden, landscape, and houseplants. It also helps avoid the traditional downsides of composting: the amount of work involved, the mess and odors associated with it, the fear of attracting animal pests, and more. Compost tumblers eliminate these nuisances.

New to composting? Keep reading to learn more about using and maintaining your new compost tumbler.

Set up the outdoor compost tumbler in a sunny location to promote the rapid growth of composting microbes. Fill it (either all at once or over several weeks) with a mix of kitchen scraps, shredded newspaper, garden debris, grass clippings, fallen leaves, and other scraps. Moisten the mixture (it should feel like a not-quite-saturated sponge) and close the lid.

The time it takes to make compost varies depending on the temperature, time of year, and the balance of the ingredients inside. It’s possible to have garden-ready compost within 10 weeks if all of the right conditions come together.

For optimal processing and to eliminate odors, turn the compost tumbler two to three times per week—or more often if the manufacturer recommends it.

The compost should have the feel of a gently wrung-out sponge. As the material is processed and builds heat, moisture evaporates. Check the bin weekly and add water as needed.

Yes—at least we think so. Compost tumblers save time, reduce waste, and produce nutrient-rich compost faster than traditional piles. That being said, if you need compost and don’t want to wait, you can find bagged compost at garden and DIY centers.

Not usually—when properly sealed, compost tumblers deter pests far better than open compost piles.

Yes, air holes promote oxygen flow, prevent odors, and support the microbes responsible for decomposition.

Choose based on waste volume. We recommend opting for 15 to 25 gallons for small households, and 50+ gallons for large gardens.

Glenda Taylor is a contractor, product tester, and writer focusing primarily on construction, DIY tools, and home appliances. She tests a wide range of power tools as well as other home improvement, household, and lawn-and-garden products.

#8086. HELP WANTED: Scientists Seeking Senior Dogs To Unlock the Secrets of Aging

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

What if your senior dog could help scientists learn more about how dogs age, and potentially help future generations of dogs live healthier lives?

That is the opportunity behind a major clinical trial from the Dog Aging Project, a research collaboration focused on giving us a better understanding of canine aging. The project is currently looking for older, healthy dogs to participate in the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs, better known as TRIAD.

This study is attracting renewed attention following a recent 60 Minutes report on the Dog Aging Project and its work investigating why dogs age the way they do and how their golden years might be made healthier.

TRIAD is not simply asking how long dogs can live. Researchers are trying to understand if a medication called rapamycin can influence the aging process and improve health in older dogs.

Rapamycin, also known as sirolimus or Rapamune, is a macrolide drug with immunosuppressive and antitumor properties. This medication has been used in human medicine for more than two decades, including in patients who have undergone kidney transplantation.

The interest in rapamycin and aging comes from a different area of research. Studies in laboratory organisms found that rapamycin can extend lifespan in several species, including mice, yeast, worms, and flies. Now, researchers want to find out whether those benefits could extend to our pets.

The Dog Aging Projectâs TRIAD trial is a multicenter study involving researchers and veterinary hospitals at universities across the United States, including Tufts University. The TRIAD trial is investigating whether rapamycin can influence lifespan and, importantly, promote healthy aging in companion dogs.

For veterinary science, one of the most interesting parts of aging research is the difference between lifespan and healthspan.

Lifespan is how long an animal lives. Healthspan is the portion of that life spent in good health.

Living longer is great, but what matters just as much is how dogs feel during those extra years. More time with the family means less if a dog is struggling with chronic illness, having trouble getting around, or experiencing cognitive decline. The goal isn't just to add years to a dog's life. It's to help them enjoy more of those years feeling good.

TRIAD is examining several areas of canine health, including cognitive function, heart function, immunity, and cancer incidence.

The current TRIAD recruitment drive is specifically aimed at older dogs that meet the study's eligibility requirements. To be considered for the study, dogs must:

Be able to cooperate with examinations, including blood collection and cardiac ultrasound, without sedation

Have normal diagnostic findings at enrollment

Clinical trial sites are located throughout the United States.

For families who decide to participate, it is important to consider that this is a three-year commitment. During the first year, dogs receive either rapamycin or a placebo. Once that year is over, the medication stops, but the study continues. Researchers will follow the dogs for another two years to see how they age and whether any differences emerge over time. In total, owners will bring their dogs to a clinical trial site seven times during the three-year study.

When it comes to getting older, dogs and humans have quite a lot in common. Dogs are susceptible to many of the same age-related conditions we are, including cognitive decline, arthritis, heart disease, cancer, and other chronic health problems. And since they share our homes and daily environments, a great deal of what researchers learn from studying aging in dogs can be extrapolated to humans.

The recent 60 Minutes report touched on this connection, including research into canine dementia. It's an area worth paying attention to, especially as more dogs live into their senior years.

There's also a practical advantage. Dogs age much faster than humans. This allows researchers to track changes in their health over a few years instead of waiting decades. That's a big deal when you're trying to understand what happens as the body ages.

But this isn't just about what dogs can teach us about ourselves. What researchers discover will help dogs, too.

Aging isn't a single disease that can be treated with one medication. As dogs get older, several things can start changing at once, sometimes as a domino or cascade effect after an initial problem or illness. Maybe getting up becomes harder, walks get shorter, or a dog who's always been sharp seems a little confused. Sometimes these changes happen gradually, and it's easy to chalk them up to old age.

The more we learn about what's actually happening in an aging dog's body, the better chance veterinarians have of spotting problems earlier and finding ways to help dogs feel good for as long as possible.

Due to the eligibility requirements, not every dog will qualify for TRIAD, but that doesnât mean they canât contribute to canine aging research.

The Dog Aging Project also has a broader research community known as the DAP Pack, which welcomes dogs of different ages, sizes, breeds, and backgrounds. The project explains that dogs who do not qualify for TRIAD can still make a meaningful contribution to understanding canine aging.

Itâs important to include all kinds of dogs in this research, not just a particular breed or size. A dog's genes, lifestyle, environment, size, and even their health history can all play a role in how they age. The more variety researchers can study, the better picture they can get of why some dogs stay healthy well into their senior years while others develop health problems earlier.

When it comes to canine aging, the goal isn't just to help dogs live longer. It's to help them feel good for more of those years, stay active, and keep enjoying life with their families.

And anyone who's lived with a senior dog knows that two dogs of the same age can be worlds apart. One 10-year-old may still be eager for walks, playtime, and whatever the family has planned that day. Another might be struggling with mobility or dealing with several health problems. So, what makes the difference?

That's part of what makes the TRIAD study interesting. Rapamycin has shown promising results in other species, but researchers still need to find out whether it can make a meaningful difference in dogs. That's a question that needs to be tested, and your pup may be part of this!

For owners of senior dogs, taking part in research like this is a chance to help scientists get some answers. What they learn could help us better understand why dogs age differently and what might help them stay healthier as they get older.

So, if you have a pup in their golden years, check out the Dog Aging Project and see how your four-legged friend might become part of this research.

#8085. Newborns Are Experiencing Life-Threatening Bleeding As More U.S. Parents Decline Vitamin K Shot, Studies Find

Researchers say rising vaccine hesitancy is to blame.

Two new studies published this week highlight a sharp increase in life-threatening bleeding incidents in American newborns, which coincide with a rise in parental refusals of vitamin K shots at birth. Vitamin K is an essential component that allows blood to clot; babies are born deficient. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has recommended a vitamin K shot be administered at birth since 1961 in order to prevent severe internal bleeding, which can result in brain bleeding and even death up to six months after birth.

The studies both address the correlation between a rise in parents refusing vitamin K shots and severe bleeding incidents. One study assessed 5.2 million infants; the number of babies who didn’t receive the shot jumped from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Those numbers align with an uptick in bleeding events among American babies — between 2017 and 2025, the incidence of bleeding by 6 months increased from 225 to nearly 400 per 10,000 births.

The second study found that between 2017 and 2025, “the percentage of newborns who received injectable vitamin K decreased from 97.7% to 95%.” The rate of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) increased by 215% and 347% respectively. Only 19% of infants diagnosed VKDB had received their boost of vitamin K at birth.

Both study’s authors point to waning trust in public health following the COVID-19 pandemic, and the rise anti-vax sentiment in recent years thanks to HHS secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s crusade against the childhood vaccine schedule.

“Increases in VKD and VKDB — peaking in 2025 — occur against the backdrop of eroding trust in public health in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, increasing vaccine hesitancy, and growing parental unease about interventions in newborns. As with childhood immunizations, vitamin K prophylaxis may be a victim of its own success; the rarity of VKDB may leave today’s families largely unaware of its grave consequences,” wrote study authors.

Parents who declined vitamin K shots for their babies cited concerns about outcomes or effectiveness, toxicity of the ingredients, risk of cancer, and a desire for “natural” alternatives, researchers also found. In the 1990s, one study sparked concern there may be a link between vitamin K shots and an increased risk of childhood cancer. Since then, multiple studies have been done to investigate the potential link, and there was found to be no association between the two.

According to the AAP, the vitamin K shot has been proven to be safe and effective; it has been recommended for 65 years now. Vitamin K is a naturally occurring nutrient made in our intestines, and found in many types of food. It doesn’t cross the placenta well, so babies are born deficient and without the gut bacteria to produce their own. Without a vitamin K shot, babies are 81 times more likely to develop VKDB. For every five babies who develop VKDB, one will die.

A vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, but headlines around recommended childhood shots have sown mass confusion over the past year. In March, a federal judge determined that Health & Human Services (HHS) secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. violated federal law by changing the childhood vaccine schedule in January and dismissing long-standing members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. His ruling resulted from a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Diseases Society of America, and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. The judge called Kennedy’s actions “dangerous,” saying they “have sowed chaos and confusion for parents and pediatricians across the country.”

It’s likely pediatric vaccines will remain a hot political topic heading into 2027. On the heels of midterm elections, the AAP issued a statement congratulating a number of newly elected and re-elected pediatricians, and urging Congress to make evidence-based children’s health policies a priority.

There was a time when any tree injury had us reaching for cans of black tar and wound dressings, but is sealing really a good idea? Here’s the truth about what your trees need

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some garden wisdom isn’t really wise at all. Have you ever heard that sprinkling used coffee grounds around hydrangeas adds oodles of acid to the soil, or that peony buds won’t open unless ants tickle their petals? Far from being wisdoms, these are classic examples of garden folklore: ideas that have been repeated so often across fences and forums that people simply assume they are true.

Welcome back to Garden Mythbusters, where we aim to separate fact from fiction with persistent gardening beliefs. We have already examined whether gravel at the bottom of pots truly helps drainage and the idea that bulbs need to be planted pointy side up. Here’s another one that you might not even have suspected was a myth: the idea that when you sever a branch or clean up storm damage, you must slather the fresh wood with pruning paint or tar sealant to prevent rot, pests, and disease.

For generations, we’ve been encouraged to buy sealants and dressings to protect our damaged trees. Watching an oak or maple bleed sap feels alarming, and reaching for a sealant seems like a responsible way to shield against infection. But should you really seal a tree wound? Indeed, could slathering a cut with wound dressing be doing more harm than good? It seems true tree recovery requires a much simpler approach. Let’s set the record straight once and for all…

To understand why tree wound sealants became a thing in the first place, there’s a simple (and admittedly silly) explanation. We are prone to anthropomorphism, which means that we think all life forms are prone to reacting like us. So we project our own biological experiences onto plants and wildlife. People once imagined tree wounds needed sealing because they assumed that trees heal like humans, basically.

When a person suffers a deep scrape or laceration, the protocol is clear: clean the cut, stop the bleeding, apply antiseptic ointment, and seal the opening to block external pathogens while our cells heal. Gardeners back in the day figured trees would also need a protective Band-Aid to keep tree sap in and bugs and disease out. When a heavy limb snapped in a summer gale or was lopped off during seasonal pruning, the exposed heartwood looked vulnerable, and any sap seemed alarming.

Gardeners made the mistake of thinking that if they left this tree damage exposed to the elements, wood-boring beetles could march right in, airborne fungal spores might colonize the moist sapwood, and the tree would might bleed to death. By the early 20th century, several petroleum-based asphalt paints, chemical tar compounds, and thick sealants were marketed as miracle aids for healing. The problem? Beneath those seemingly protective layers, the reality was far from protective.

It wasn't until the late 20th century that arborists and tree scientists found that routine sealants can cause more harm than good. They ran rigorous, controlled trials on tree wound dressings and they found that painting tree wounds does not prevent decay or add protection. In study after study, sealed wounds rotted faster and suffered more internal structural breakdown than wounds left exposed to the open air.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Today, leading forestry institutions and the International Society of Arboriculture (ISA) advise against the routine application of wound paints and sealants. The core problem is that wound dressings alter the microclimate of the cut surface. Asphalt paints and sealants dry into an imperfect crust. As the tree barks expand and contracts in shifting weather and humidity, the paint hairline-cracks. Rainwater seeps into these tiny fissures, but the sealant prevents that moisture from evaporating.

When you apply sealant on a tree wound, it traps water inside the wound, allowing bacteria to thrive and fungi to cause decay. The sealant also impedes the tree’s natural healing process. Thick dressings physically smother living plant cells along wound margins, impairing the tree's ability to produce vital callus tissue. By attempting to protect the wound, growers may seal pathogens inside the tree, while locking out the fresh air that recovery demands.

That’s not to say you can’t help out a stressed tree. There are amendments you can add at the ground level to help tree roots with the process of recovery. For example, a light sprinkling of mycorrhizal fungi can assist with rejuvenation. You can buy PureMyco Mycorrhizal Fungi Root Inoculant from Amazon to encourage root growth in stressed trees. But in terms of the trunk or branch, the general opinion now is that clean, unsealed tree cuts heal best on their own.

It’s rare to find a general rule without exceptions. This new expert opinion that sealant should not be used for most tree wounds also has a few exceptions. There are a couple of scientifically backed occasions where dressings can be an essential defense. These exceptions do not exist to help the tree heal faster. Rather, they serve as a barrier to protect specific species against insect-borne epidemics.

The primary time when you might use a sealant safely involves native oak species and elms. In regions where oak wilt or Dutch elm disease are prevalent, fresh pruning cuts or storm tears can result in a leaking sap that attracts beetles that spread deadly diseases like oak wilt and Dutch elm disease. If an oak or elm suffers accidental storm breakage or requires emergency trimming during the high-risk growing season (spring through mid-summer), It’s wise to apply a very thin layer of plain, water-based latex paint or specialized tree wound spray over the cut surface.

A safe sealant option in this case is Tanglefoot Tree Sealant Aerosol, available from Walmart, which is beneficial for emergency summer cuts on oak and elm. The goal is to mask the scent of sap from foraging beetles. Once outside this active insect window, even oaks and elms should be pruned cleanly and left unpainted.

To understand why artificial sealants are generally unnecessary, just bear in mind that trees do not heal like animals do. Trees don’t have the same circulatory system that humans do. Human wounds need closing to prevent loss of bloom, but trees don’t have these issues. Instead, when you prune a tree, the tree initiates a process called tree compartmentalization.

Research led by USDA Forest Service plant pathologist Dr Alex Shigo revealed that trees cannot replace or regenerate damaged heartwood. Instead, they build walls to seal off injured tissue from the rest of the tree. This is called compartmentalization of decay in trees (CODIT). The moment a branch is severed, the tree activates an internal defense consisting of multiple boundaries. Simultaneously, the outer edges of the wound produce swollen ridges of tissue known as callus wood.

Trees start compartmentalizing as soon as you prune them. Cells near the cut area form a cork layer between the wound and the healthy wood inside. Cork is dense and moisture-resistant and quickly forms a natural dressing. At the same time as the tree starts building a callus around the wound, the edge of the cut starts making healthy tissue. This new wood starts growing on the outside, but continues inward until the entire cut surface is covered. This can take years, but ultimately the wound is overgrown. And it works best if you leave the cut alone and let the tree manage it.

Because trees rely on specialized anatomical structures to build their natural defense walls, your pruning technique matters far more than anything that comes out of a can. Proper cuts empower the tree’s natural CODIT defense system, while improper cuts compromise its defenses. Make sure you always use sharp, sterilized pruners or saws. The sharper the blades, the cleaner the cuts. If you need a hand saw, the Fiskars 10-Inch Folding Soft Grip Handsaw, available from Walmart, gives a good grip when cutting through thicker tree branches.

Always cut outside the branch collar when pruning. Look for the junction where a limb meets the parent branch or trunk. The swollen shoulder of textured wood is the branch collar. This collar is packed with cells hardwired to generate those CODIT barrier walls. Make your cut just outside this swollen collar. Never make a flush cut against the trunk, as slicing into the collar invites trunk rot. Don’t leave a 6-inch (15cm) dead branch protruding from the trunk, either, as this is also damaging. The tree cannot compartmentalize dead tissue inches away from the collar.

Large branches are heavy and prone to tearing the trunk if cut from the top. To prevent this, first make a shallow upward cut on the underside of the limb, about 12 inches (30cm) from the trunk. Cut one-third of the way through. Then from above, cut through the limb from the other direction, 2-3 inches (5-8cm) out from the first cut. The branch should break cleanly between the cuts without tearing bark. Finally, make a single, clean cut just outside the branch collar to remove the stub. Once you’re done, leave the cut bare and allow the fresh wood to dry and air-heal.

Storms can rip major limbs from trees, leaving jagged stumps and stripped bark. The secret to storm recovery is acting quickly to clean up jagged breaks so those natural compartmentalization mechanisms can engage. First, never approach trees that are tangled in utility lines or have hanging widow-maker branches suspended overhead. Call professional utility crews or an ISA-certified arborist for high-canopy work.

Always wear safety equipment like a hard hat, safety glasses and sturdy gloves. And avoid uprooted trees or split trunks. They could shift in the wind and fall. After that, assess the damage and determine what can be saved. Wind often twists branches off, tearing strips of living bark down the trunk. Using a sharp utility knife or hand chisel, trim away any loose, jagged flaps of bark, creating a smooth, clean margin around the wound. Keep the healthy inner cambium intact.

Jagged, splintered branch stumps cannot seal properly. Trace the shattered limb back to the nearest healthy branch union or just outside the branch collar, and make a clean, flat saw cut. If a storm strips more than 50% of a tree's canopy, or if the main trunk has split down the center, structural recovery is unlikely. However, if more than half of the canopy remains intact, the tree possesses sufficient power to compartmentalize the damage and rebuild its crown over several seasons.

Pruned or storm-stressed trees need moisture rather than fertilizer. Apply a 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of organic wood mulch over the roots, keeping it 6 inches (15cm) away from the trunk flare. Our team favorite is Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help regulate ground conditions and retain moisture to support damaged trees.

It can be difficult to resist the urge to bandage a damaged tree, especially when a favorite suffers a traumatic break. But these tree-loving insights can hopefully give you the confidence to step back a bit and let Mother Nature lend a helping hand. Trees are ancient, resilient entities, equipped with extraordinary internal defense mechanisms that have preserved them beautifully for many, many years. So skip artificial wound dressings and focus on making precise cuts outside the branch collar, smoothing ragged storm tears, and supporting root health with mulch and consistent hydration, and you’ll give your trees the ability to heal themselves.
